recipes.title: Spicy Moroccan Fish (Chraime)
recipes.description: White fish fillets simmered in a thick, pungent tomato sauce loaded with paprika, cumin, and cayenne pepper. A staple of Moroccan Friday night dinners and holiday tables.
ingredients: 4 firm white fish fillets (cod, halibut, or sea bass), about 6 oz each
1/2 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice (about 3 lemons)
1/2 lemon, diced into small pieces with rind intact
1 tsp salt, plus more to taste
1/4 cup fresh cilantro, roughly chopped, for garnish
directions: Begin by preparing the fish. Pat the fillets dry with paper towels and place them in a shallow dish. Season both sides generously with salt and pour the lemon juice over them. Turn the fillets to coat evenly, then cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour. This step firms the flesh, removes any residual fishiness, and allows the lemon to begin gently curing the surface of the fish.

While the fish marinates, prepare the sauce base. Set a wide, deep skillet or saute pan over medium heat and add the olive oil. Once the oil is shimmering, add the diced garlic. Cook the garlic for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring frequently, until it turns soft and fragrant but has not taken on any color. Burnt garlic will make the entire sauce bitter, so keep the heat moderate and stir often.

Add the ground cumin, sweet paprika, and cayenne pepper to the garlic. Stir the spices into the oil and toast them for exactly 1 minute. You will notice the oil turning a deep red-orange color and the kitchen filling with a warm, smoky aroma. This brief toasting step blooms the essential oils in the spices and deepens their flavor significantly.

Pour in the water and add the tomato paste. Stir vigorously to dissolve the paste completely into the liquid, scraping up any spiced bits from the bottom of the pan. Add the diced lemon pieces (rind and all) to the sauce. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer and let it cook uncovered for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. The sauce should begin to thicken slightly and the oil will start to separate from the tomato — this is the sign that the water has evaporated from the tomatoes and the flavors have properly concentrated.

Remove the fish from its marinade and gently nestle the fillets into the simmering sauce in a single layer. Spoon some of the sauce over the tops of the fillets. Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover the pan with a lid, and let the fish simmer gently for 10 to 15 minutes. The fish is done when it flakes easily when pressed with a fork and is opaque throughout. Be careful not to overcook — the residual heat will continue cooking the fish even after you remove it from the burner.

Taste the sauce and adjust the seasoning with additional salt, pepper, or a squeeze of fresh lemon juice if needed. Transfer the fish and sauce to a serving platter. Garnish generously with the chopped fresh cilantro. Serve warm or at room temperature alongside crusty bread for mopping up the sauce. This dish also tastes wonderful cold the next day, making it an excellent make-ahead option for Shabbat.
recipes.tip: The diced lemon with the rind is the secret weapon of this dish — it provides a sophisticated bitterness that balances the heat and sweetness of the paprika. Cook the sauce until the oil visibly separates from the tomato before adding the fish; this concentration step is what separates a great Chraime from a mediocre one.

recipes.title: Iraqi Chickpea Sambousak
recipes.description: Golden fried turnovers with a filling of mashed chickpeas, deeply caramelized onions, and turmeric. A highlight of the Iraqi Hanukkah and Purim tables.
ingredients: 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
Neutral oil (canola or vegetable), about 2 cups
directions: Start by making the dough. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Make a well in the center and pour in the warm water and olive oil. Using a wooden spoon, stir from the center outward until a shaggy dough forms. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead firmly for 5 minutes, pushing the dough away from you with the heel of your hand, folding it back over itself, and rotating it a quarter turn. The dough should become smooth, slightly tacky, and spring back when poked with a finger.

Shape the dough into a ball and place it in a lightly oiled bowl, turning once to coat all sides. Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and place it in a warm, draft-free spot (such as an oven that has been briefly heated to 200°F and then turned off). Let the dough rise for 1 full hour until it has doubled in size and feels pillowy and light.

While the dough rises, prepare the filling. Drain and rinse the chickpeas thoroughly. Place them in the bowl of a food processor and pulse 6 to 8 times until you achieve a chunky, crumbly texture — similar to the consistency of a rough tuna salad. Do not over-process into a smooth hummus-like paste; the textural contrast is essential to a good sambousak.

Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the finely diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, for 10 to 12 minutes until the onion is deeply golden and caramelized. The slow caramelization brings out the natural sweetness of the onion, which will balance the earthiness of the chickpeas.

Add the turmeric, salt, and pepper to the caramelized onions and stir for 30 seconds to toast the spice. Add the pulsed chickpeas to the skillet and mix everything together thoroughly. Cook the mixture for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, to allow the flavors to meld. Taste and adjust the salt. Transfer the filling to a plate and let it cool to room temperature before assembling.

Once the dough has risen, punch it down gently and turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Divide the dough into 24 equal pieces (each about the size of a large marble). Roll each piece into a ball between your palms, then use a rolling pin to flatten each ball into a circle roughly 4 inches in diameter. Try to keep the center of each circle slightly thicker than the edges — this prevents the filling from bursting through during frying.

Place 1 level tablespoon of the cooled chickpea filling in the center of each dough circle. Fold the dough in half over the filling to create a half-moon shape. Press the edges firmly together with your fingertips, then crimp the sealed edge by pressing with the tines of a fork. This both decorates the sambousak and ensures a tight seal that will not open during frying.

Pour the neutral oil into a large, deep skillet to a depth of about 1/4 inch. Add the peeled carrots to the oil — this is a traditional Iraqi technique that keeps the frying oil clear and prevents it from burning and smoking too quickly. Heat the oil over medium-high heat until it reaches 350°F (a small piece of dough dropped in should immediately sizzle and float to the surface).

Fry the sambousak in batches of 4 to 5 at a time, being careful not to crowd the pan. Cook for about 1 minute per side, flipping once with a slotted spoon, until both sides are an even, deep golden brown. Remove to a wire rack set over a baking sheet and let them drain for a minute. Serve warm. These are best eaten within a few hours of frying, though they can be reheated in a 350°F oven for 8 minutes.
recipes.tip: Frying the carrots in the oil alongside the turnovers is a time-honored Iraqi technique — the carrots absorb impurities and sugar from the dough that would otherwise burn and darken the oil. Replace the carrots if they blacken.

recipes.title: Sheet Pan Spinach & Cheese Bourekas
recipes.description: Layers of golden puff pastry encasing a rich filling of feta, ricotta, mozzarella, and fresh spinach. Cut into elegant diamonds and topped with everything bagel seasoning.
ingredients: 2 sheets store-bought puff pastry, thawed according to package directions
2 cups fresh spinach, chopped and squeezed extremely dry
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
directions: Preheat your oven to 375°F and position the rack in the center of the oven. Line a large rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.

Prepare the spinach first, as this is the most critical step for preventing a soggy boureka. If using fresh spinach, blanch it in boiling salted water for 30 seconds, then immediately transfer to an ice bath. Drain and place the spinach in the center of a clean, lint-free kitchen towel. Gather the corners of the towel and twist tightly, wringing out every last drop of moisture. You should end up with a compact ball of very dry spinach. If using frozen spinach, thaw it completely and squeeze it dry using the same towel method. Any residual moisture will create steam during baking and make the bottom pastry soggy.

In a large bowl, combine the crumbled feta, ricotta, cottage cheese, and shredded mozzarella. Add the 2 whole eggs, the squeezed dry spinach, a pinch of nutmeg, and a generous grinding of black pepper. Mix thoroughly with a spatula until everything is evenly combined. Taste the filling — the feta provides saltiness, so you may not need additional salt. Set the filling aside.

Unfold one sheet of puff pastry onto the prepared baking sheet. If there are any cracks or tears, press them together with dampened fingers. Use a rolling pin to gently stretch the pastry so it covers most of the baking sheet in an even layer.
Spread the cheese and spinach filling evenly over the pastry, leaving a 1/2-inch border around all edges. Use the back of a spoon or an offset spatula to create a smooth, uniform layer.

Carefully unfold the second sheet of puff pastry and lay it over the filling, pressing it down gently to eliminate any air pockets. Pinch the edges of the two pastry sheets together to seal. Using a sharp knife, score the top pastry into diamond shapes by cutting diagonal lines in one direction about 2 inches apart, then cutting diagonals in the opposite direction. Do not cut all the way through to the bottom — you are only scoring the top layer.
Brush the entire top surface with the egg wash (yolk beaten with water), making sure to get into the scored lines. Sprinkle the everything bagel seasoning evenly over the top.

Bake for 50 to 55 minutes until the pastry is a deep, rich golden brown and has puffed up dramatically. The internal temperature should reach at least 180°F. Remove from the oven and let cool on the pan for 5 minutes — this allows the cheese to set slightly so the bourekas hold their shape when cut. Use a sharp knife to cut along the scored lines into individual diamond-shaped portions. Serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.tip: The single most important step is squeezing the spinach completely dry. Excess moisture is the number one cause of soggy bourekas. A clean kitchen towel works far better than paper towels for this task — twist and wring it like you are wringing out a washcloth.

recipes.title: Persian Gondi (Chickpea Dumplings)
recipes.description: Cardamom-scented chicken and chickpea flour dumplings simmered gently in golden broth. The quintessential Persian Shabbat starter, served in nearly every Iranian Jewish home on Friday nights.
ingredients: Fresh basil and mint for serving
directions: Begin by preparing the onion puree. Place the roughly chopped onions in a food processor and process until you have a smooth, liquid puree. You want this to be completely smooth with no chunks remaining, as any onion pieces will cause the dumplings to have an uneven texture and may cause them to crack during cooking.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the ground chicken, ground turkey, chickpea flour, pureed onion, oil, ground cardamom, turmeric, salt, and pepper. Using your hands or a sturdy wooden spoon, mix and knead the mixture for a full 2 minutes until it becomes completely unified and cohesive. The texture should feel like soft, slightly sticky playdough — it should be firm enough to hold a clear thumbprint when you press your finger into it, but soft enough that you could cut through it easily with a spoon.

If the mixture feels too wet and loose, add chickpea flour 1 tablespoon at a time until it reaches the right consistency. If it feels too dry and crumbly, add a teaspoon of water at a time. Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours, and ideally 4 hours or overnight. This resting period is not optional — the chickpea flour needs time to hydrate and absorb the moisture from the meat and onion, which is what gives the dumplings their characteristic structure and prevents them from falling apart in the broth.
When you are ready to cook, bring the chicken broth to a gentle boil in a large, wide pot. Add the whole chickpeas, carrot halves, and turnip quarters to the broth.

Remove the gondi mixture from the refrigerator. Wet your hands thoroughly with cold water (this prevents sticking) and form the mixture into balls about 1.5 inches in diameter — roughly the size of a golf ball. You should get approximately 12 to 14 dumplings. Place them on a plate as you work, keeping your hands wet at all times.

Gently lower the dumplings into the simmering broth one at a time, spacing them apart so they have room to expand (they will nearly double in size). Reduce the heat to maintain a very gentle simmer — vigorous boiling will break the dumplings apart. Cook uncovered for 1.5 to 2 hours. The dumplings are done when they have expanded noticeably, float easily, and are tender and cooked through when you cut one in half to test.
Serve the gondi in shallow bowls with plenty of the golden broth, a few chickpeas, and pieces of the cooked carrot and turnip. Garnish with fresh basil and mint leaves torn over the top.
recipes.tip: The refrigeration step is non-negotiable. Without it, the chickpea flour has not hydrated, and your dumplings will disintegrate in the broth. Test one dumpling first — if it falls apart, knead in a bit more chickpea flour and chill for another 30 minutes before proceeding with the rest.

recipes.title: Classic Gefilte Fish with Chrain
recipes.description: Handmade poached fish patties from a blend of carp, whitefish, and pike, served cold with the traditional spicy beet horseradish known as chrain. A cornerstone of Ashkenazi holiday tables.
ingredients: 6 medium onions, finely minced or grated
Fish heads and bones (reserved from filleting)
6 large carrots, peeled and left whole
1 large fresh horseradish root, peeled and grated
directions: Start by making the poaching stock, as it needs to be simmering before you add the fish. Place the fish heads, bones, and trimmings in a very large, wide stockpot or kettle. Add the quartered onions, whole carrots, celery stalks, salt, and peppercorns. Pour in 10 cups of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to a gentle simmer. Skim off any gray foam that rises to the surface during the first 10 minutes. Let the stock simmer while you prepare the fish mixture — it should cook for at least 20 minutes before you add the patties.

In a very large mixing bowl, combine all three types of ground fish with the finely minced onions, eggs, sugar, matzah meal, ice water, salt, and white pepper. Mix the mixture thoroughly with your hands or a wooden spoon for 3 to 4 minutes until it becomes sticky, smooth, and holds together when you squeeze a handful. The ice water is important — it keeps the mixture cold during handling, which results in a lighter, more delicate texture in the finished gefilte fish.

Wet your hands thoroughly with cold water. Take a generous handful of the fish mixture (about 1/3 cup) and shape it into a fat oval patty, roughly 3 inches long and 2 inches wide. The patties should be plump and well-formed — not too thin, or they will fall apart during poaching. Place each formed patty on a wet plate as you work. You should get approximately 12 patties.

Carefully slide the fish patties into the simmering stock one at a time, spacing them apart. Try to arrange them in a single layer if possible. The stock should barely cover the tops of the patties — add a splash of water if needed. Return the liquid to a very gentle simmer (never a full boil, which would cause the patties to break apart).

Cover the pot partially with a lid and let the gefilte fish poach at a gentle simmer for 25 to 30 minutes. The patties are done when they feel firm to the touch and have turned uniformly opaque. Do not stir or flip them during cooking.

Turn off the heat and let the gefilte fish cool completely in the pot, submerged in the stock. This is essential — as the stock cools, it will form a natural jelly that is a traditional hallmark of homemade gefilte fish. Once cool, carefully transfer the patties and carrot slices to a storage container. Strain the stock through a fine-mesh sieve and pour it over the fish. Refrigerate overnight or for at least 6 hours.

To make the chrain, combine the freshly grated horseradish with the grated cooked beets, white vinegar, sugar, and a pinch of salt. Mix well and taste — it should be bracingly sharp with a sweet beet undertone. Adjust vinegar and sugar to your preference. Store in a sealed jar in the refrigerator.
To serve, remove the gefilte fish from the jellied stock and arrange on a platter. Place a round of poached carrot on top of each patty. Serve cold with a generous spoonful of chrain on the side.
recipes.tip: The fish heads and bones in the poaching liquid are what create the natural jelly — do not skip them. Ask your fishmonger to save them when filleting. For the lightest texture, some cooks add a tablespoon of seltzer water to the fish mixture. The gefilte fish tastes best made a full day ahead.

recipes.title: Sephardic Agristada Fish (Lemon-Egg Sauce)
recipes.description: Fried white fish bathed in a velvety, custard-like lemon-egg sauce. An elegant Sephardic classic passed down through generations of Syrian and Turkish Jewish families.
ingredients: 2 lbs firm white fish (cod, halibut, or grouper), cut into 2-inch cubes
1/3 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice (about 2 large lemons)
directions: Pat the fish cubes completely dry with paper towels and season them on all sides with salt and pepper. Set up a dredging station with two shallow bowls: one containing the flour seasoned with a pinch of salt, and the other containing the 2 beaten eggs.

Dredge each fish cube first in the seasoned flour, shaking off any excess, then dip it into the beaten egg, allowing the excess to drip back into the bowl. This double coating creates a thin, delicate crust that will turn beautifully golden when fried.

Heat 1/2 cup of neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers and a tiny piece of flour sizzles immediately when dropped in. Working in batches to avoid crowding the pan, fry the coated fish cubes for about 2 minutes per side until they are golden brown and crisp on all surfaces. Transfer the fried fish to a plate lined with paper towels and set aside while you prepare the sauce.

To make the Agristada sauce, crack the 4 eggs into a medium mixing bowl and whisk them until smooth and frothy. In a separate small bowl, combine the 2 cups of warm water with the 2 tablespoons of flour and whisk vigorously until there are absolutely no lumps remaining — even tiny flour lumps will create an unpleasant grainy texture in the finished sauce.

Slowly pour the flour-water mixture into the whisked eggs in a thin, steady stream while whisking constantly. Then add the oil, lemon juice, salt, and white pepper. Whisk until the mixture is completely homogeneous.

Pour the sauce mixture into a clean saucepan set over medium-low heat. This is the most critical step: stir the sauce continuously with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, scraping the bottom and sides of the pan at all times. The sauce must never come to a boil — if it boils, the eggs will scramble and the sauce will become lumpy and grainy instead of velvety smooth. Cook for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring without pause, until the sauce thickens to a consistency that coats the back of the spoon. When you run your finger through the sauce on the spoon, it should leave a clean line that does not fill back in.

Arrange the fried fish cubes on a serving platter. Pour the warm Agristada sauce generously over the fish, making sure every piece is well coated. The sauce can also be served on the side in a gravy boat. This dish is delicious served warm immediately after preparation, but it is also traditionally served at room temperature or even cold, making it an excellent make-ahead dish for Shabbat or Passover.
recipes.tip: The key to a perfect Agristada is patience and constant stirring over low heat. If you see even the smallest curd forming, immediately remove the pan from the heat and whisk vigorously until smooth, then return to very low heat. The sauce should be silky and pourable, like a thin custard.

recipes.title: Authentic Israeli Hummus
recipes.description: Silky-smooth, cloud-like hummus with a spicy tatbilah dressing. The secret is over-cooking the chickpeas until they practically melt and processing with high-quality tahini for a full 8 minutes.
ingredients: 1 cup high-quality raw tahini (Al Arz or similar)
1/2 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice (about 3 lemons)
1 1/2 tsp salt, plus more to taste
10 pickled shifka peppers (or sport peppers), stems removed
directions: Place the dried chickpeas in a large bowl and cover with at least 4 inches of cold water. Add 1 teaspoon of baking soda and stir to dissolve. The baking soda begins breaking down the chickpea skins and softens the beans, which is essential for achieving the ultra-smooth texture. Let the chickpeas soak for a minimum of 12 hours and up to 24 hours at room temperature.

Drain and rinse the soaked chickpeas thoroughly under cold running water. Transfer them to a large pot and cover with fresh cold water by at least 3 inches. Add 1/2 teaspoon of baking soda. Bring to a boil over high heat.

As the chickpeas begin to boil, you will see the skins floating to the surface and a layer of foam forming. This is where the magic happens: using a fine-mesh skimmer or slotted spoon, skim off the floating skins and foam continuously for the first 10 minutes. Removing these skins is the single most important step for achieving hummus that rivals the best hummusiya stands in Tel Aviv. The more skins you remove, the smoother your hummus will be.

Reduce the heat to a steady simmer and cook the chickpeas for 45 to 60 minutes until they are extremely soft — much softer than you would cook them for a salad. They should crush effortlessly between your fingers with zero resistance. If in doubt, cook them longer. Under-cooked chickpeas are the primary reason homemade hummus turns out grainy instead of creamy.

Drain the chickpeas, reserving 1/2 cup of the cooking liquid. Measure out 4 cups of the cooked chickpeas (save any extra for garnishing). While the chickpeas are still hot, add them to the bowl of a food processor along with the garlic cloves, lemon juice, and salt. Process for 3 full minutes, scraping down the sides once halfway through.

Add the tahini to the food processor. Now process for a full 8 minutes without stopping. Yes, 8 minutes — this is not a typo. This extended processing time incorporates air into the hummus and breaks down every last particle of chickpea, transforming the mixture from grainy to impossibly fluffy and light. If the hummus seems too thick during processing, add ice water 1 tablespoon at a time through the feed tube. The finished hummus should be lighter in color than when you started and have a mousse-like consistency.
To make the tatbilah, place the lemon juice, shifka peppers, garlic, and olive oil in a small blender or food processor. Pulse until you have a coarse, chunky sauce with visible pepper pieces.

To serve, spread the hummus onto a shallow plate using the back of a large spoon, creating a circular swoosh with a well in the center. Drizzle generously with extra virgin olive oil, letting it pool in the well. Spoon the tatbilah over the top and dust with a light sprinkle of sweet paprika. Serve immediately with warm, fresh pita bread.
recipes.tip: Three things separate incredible hummus from mediocre hummus: removing the skins while boiling, cooking the chickpeas until they are mushy-soft, and processing for 8 full minutes with the tahini. Do not skip or shorten any of these steps.

recipes.title: Iraqi Kubbeh Batata (Potato Meat Dumplings)
recipes.description: Crispy fried dumplings with a creamy mashed potato shell encasing a fragrant filling of ground beef seasoned with cinnamon and nutmeg. Perfect for Passover since they use matzo meal instead of flour.
ingredients: 5 medium Yukon Gold potatoes (about 2.5 lbs), peeled and quartered
Neutral oil, about 1/2 inch deep in a skillet
directions: Place the peeled and quartered Yukon Gold potatoes in a large pot of heavily salted cold water. Bring to a boil and cook for 18 to 22 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender and a fork slides through them with no resistance. Drain the potatoes in a colander and let them steam dry for 5 minutes — removing excess moisture at this stage prevents the potato dough from becoming gummy.

While the potatoes are still hot, mash them thoroughly with a potato masher or pass them through a ricer for the smoothest result. You want absolutely no lumps. Let the mashed potatoes cool until they are warm but no longer hot (about 10 minutes). Beat 1 of the eggs and add it to the potatoes along with the matzo meal and salt. Mix with a spatula or your hands until a smooth, pliable dough forms. The dough should hold together when squeezed without cracking. If it seems too dry and crumbly, add a teaspoon of water at a time; if too wet and sticky, add matzo meal a teaspoon at a time.

While the potatoes are cooling, prepare the filling. Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add the finely diced onion and cook for 3 minutes until softened. Add the ground beef and break it up with a wooden spoon, cooking until no longer pink, about 5 minutes. Drain any excess fat. Season with the cinnamon, nutmeg, salt, and pepper. Stir well and cook for 1 more minute to toast the spices. Transfer the filling to a plate and let it cool completely — hot filling will melt the potato dough and make assembly impossible.

To assemble the kubbeh, take a golf-ball sized portion of the potato dough (about 2 tablespoons) and roll it between your palms into a smooth ball. Using your thumb, press a deep well into the center of the ball, rotating it to create a cup with walls about 1/4 inch thick. Place 1 tablespoon of the cooled meat filling into the well.

Gently close the potato dough around the filling, pinching the edges together at the top. Roll the sealed ball gently between your palms to smooth out any cracks, then flatten it slightly into a thick patty about 3 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Repeat with the remaining dough and filling, placing the assembled kubbeh on a parchment-lined plate.
Beat the remaining egg in a small bowl. Brush both sides of each kubbeh patty with the beaten egg wash — this creates a beautiful golden crust during frying and helps hold the patty together.

Heat 1/2 inch of neutral oil in a large, heavy skillet over medium heat until a drop of egg wash sizzles on contact (approximately 350°F). Fry the kubbeh in batches of 3 to 4, without crowding, for 3 minutes per side until deeply golden brown and crispy. Transfer to a wire rack to drain. Serve hot.
recipes.tip: Yukon Gold potatoes are essential — they have a naturally creamy, buttery texture that holds together far better than Russet potatoes, which can become dry and crumbly. If the potato dough cracks when you try to close it around the filling, your potatoes may need a touch more moisture.

recipes.title: Homemade Falafel (Green Herb Style)
recipes.description: Vibrant green on the inside from generous handfuls of fresh cilantro and parsley. Made from soaked (never cooked) chickpeas for the perfect crispy-outside, fluffy-inside texture.
ingredients: 2 cups dried chickpeas (never canned or cooked)
1 cup fresh cilantro, packed (stems and leaves)
1 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, packed (stems and leaves)
Neutral oil for deep frying (at least 3 inches deep)
Pita, tahini, Israeli salad, and pickles for serving
directions: Place the dried chickpeas in a large bowl and cover with cold water by at least 4 inches. Soak for 12 to 18 hours at room temperature. The chickpeas will absorb a great deal of water and roughly double in size. This is the foundational step of great falafel — you must use dried chickpeas that have been soaked but never cooked. Canned or pre-cooked chickpeas lack the raw starch needed to hold the falafel together during frying, and they will crumble apart in the oil.

Drain the soaked chickpeas thoroughly in a colander. Spread them on a clean kitchen towel and pat dry, removing as much surface moisture as possible. Excess water will make the mixture too wet and result in falafel that splatter and fall apart in the fryer.

Place the drained chickpeas in the bowl of a food processor along with the cilantro, parsley, onion quarters, garlic, cumin, coriander, cayenne, salt, and black pepper. Pulse the mixture in short bursts, scraping down the sides between pulses, until you achieve a coarse, granular texture similar to the consistency of kosher salt or coarse cornmeal. This typically takes 15 to 20 pulses. Do not over-process into a smooth paste — falafel made from a paste will be dense, heavy, and gummy rather than light and airy.

Transfer the falafel mixture to a bowl, cover, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to overnight. This resting period allows the flavors to meld and the chickpea starch to hydrate further, which improves the binding.

When you are ready to fry, remove the mixture from the refrigerator. Sprinkle the baking soda and sesame seeds (if using) over the surface and fold them in gently with a spatula — do not overmix. The baking soda creates a slight chemical leavening that makes the falafel puff up in the hot oil, resulting in a lighter, airier interior.

Fill a deep pot or Dutch oven with neutral oil to a depth of at least 3 inches. Heat the oil to exactly 350°F, using a deep-fry thermometer to monitor the temperature throughout the frying process. Line a baking sheet with a wire rack for draining.

Using wet hands or a falafel scoop, form the mixture into balls about 1.5 inches in diameter. You can also shape them into slightly flattened discs for more surface area and crunch. Do not pack them too tightly — a gentle hand results in a lighter falafel.

Fry the falafel in batches of 4 to 6, being careful not to crowd the pot (crowding drops the oil temperature and causes greasy falafel). Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once or twice, until the falafel are a deep, rich golden brown on all sides. Remove with a slotted spoon and place on the wire rack to drain. The interior should be bright green and steaming when you break one open.
Serve immediately in warm pita bread with tahini sauce, Israeli chopped salad, pickled vegetables, and a drizzle of amba or hot sauce.
recipes.tip: Never use canned or cooked chickpeas — this is the single most important rule of falafel making. Raw, soaked chickpeas contain the ungelatinized starch needed to bind the mixture. Also, maintain your oil at exactly 350°F — too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks; too cool and the falafel absorb excess oil and become greasy.

recipes.title: Moroccan Carrot Salad
recipes.description: Tender carrot coins tossed with toasted cumin seeds, garlic, turmeric, paprika, and tamarind. A vibrant, tangy salad that tastes even better the next day.
ingredients: 2 lbs carrots, peeled and cut into 1/4-inch thick rounds
1 small hot pepper (serrano or bird's eye), minced (optional)
directions: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Add the carrot rounds and cook for exactly 9 minutes. You want the carrots to be fork-tender — a fork should slide through with some resistance but no crunch — but not mushy or falling apart. This precise cooking time preserves the carrots' structure so they hold their shape when tossed with the dressing. Drain the carrots immediately in a colander and shake off excess water.

While the carrots cook, prepare the spice base. Heat the olive oil in a large, wide skillet over medium heat. Add the whole cumin seeds and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds until they become fragrant and begin to pop — this toasting step activates the volatile oils in the cumin and gives the salad its distinctive warm, earthy aroma.

Add the minced garlic and hot pepper (if using) to the skillet and stir for 1 minute until the garlic is soft and fragrant but has not taken on any color. Add the ground turmeric and sweet paprika and stir for 30 seconds — the oil should turn a vivid golden-red color.

Add the drained carrots to the skillet and toss gently to coat them in the spiced oil, being careful not to break the carrot rounds. Add the tamarind paste and toss again. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring gently, to let the carrots absorb the spices.

Remove the skillet from the heat. Squeeze the lemon juice over the carrots and toss one final time. Season with salt to taste. Transfer the salad to a glass bowl or container, let it cool to room temperature, then cover tightly and refrigerate overnight.

The overnight rest is not merely a suggestion — it is what transforms this from a good side dish into a magnificent one. The carrots spend the night absorbing the cumin, turmeric, tamarind, and garlic, deepening the flavor profile dramatically. Before serving, bring the salad to room temperature and top with a generous handful of freshly chopped cilantro.
recipes.tip: Do not skip the overnight refrigeration. The salad will taste twice as good the next day as the carrots fully absorb the spices. This makes it an ideal make-ahead dish for Shabbat or holiday meals.

recipes.title: Fluffy Matzah Ball Soup
recipes.description: Crystal-clear golden chicken broth with cloud-like matzah balls that practically dissolve on the tongue. The undisputed centerpiece of the Passover Seder table, but beloved all year round.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (4-5 lbs), cut into pieces
2 large onions, halved (skin on for color)
6 large carrots, peeled and cut into chunks
4 parsnips, peeled and cut into chunks
1 cup matzo meal (regular, not cake meal)
1/4 cup schmaltz (rendered chicken fat) or neutral oil
1 tbsp seltzer water (optional, for extra fluffiness)
directions: Begin with the broth, which needs at least 2 hours of simmering. Place the chicken pieces in a very large stockpot and cover with 14 cups of cold water. Starting with cold water and bringing it slowly to a boil extracts the maximum flavor and gelatin from the chicken and bones, resulting in a richer, more full-bodied broth.

Set the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. As the water heats, impurities will rise to the surface as a gray, foamy scum. Using a large spoon or fine-mesh skimmer, skim this foam off diligently for the first 10 to 15 minutes. This skimming step is what produces a clear, golden broth rather than a cloudy one.

Once the foam has subsided, add the halved onions (leave the skins on — they contribute a beautiful golden color to the broth), carrots, parsnips, celery, dill, parsley, salt, and peppercorns. Reduce the heat to maintain the gentlest possible simmer — you should see lazy bubbles rising slowly to the surface, not a rolling boil.

Simmer the broth uncovered for 2 hours, adjusting the heat as needed to maintain that gentle simmer. The broth will reduce slightly and turn a deep, rich gold. After 2 hours, remove the pot from the heat. Strain the broth through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean pot, pressing gently on the solids to extract all the liquid. Discard the chicken and vegetables (or save the chicken meat for another use). Let the broth cool slightly, then refrigerate until the fat solidifies on the surface. Remove and discard the fat (or save it — this is schmaltz).

While the broth simmers, prepare the matzah ball mixture. In a mixing bowl, whisk the eggs until frothy. Add the chicken stock, schmaltz (or oil), nutmeg, ground ginger, and salt. Whisk to combine. Fold in the matzo meal gently with a spatula — do not beat or overmix, as this develops gluten and produces dense, heavy matzah balls. If using seltzer for extra fluffiness, fold it in last. The mixture will be wet and soft.

Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate for a minimum of 1 hour, and up to 4 hours. This rest is essential — the matzo meal needs time to fully absorb the liquid, which gives the matzah balls their structure and prevents them from falling apart in the water.

When you are ready to cook the matzah balls, bring a very large pot of well-salted water to a gentle boil. Wet your hands with cold water and gently form the mixture into balls about the size of golf balls (roughly 1.5 inches in diameter). Do not pack them tightly — a light touch is the secret to fluffy matzah balls. You should get about 12 balls.

Carefully drop the balls into the gently boiling water. Cover the pot with a tight-fitting lid, reduce the heat to a simmer, and cook for 45 minutes. Do not lift the lid during this entire time — the steam trapped inside is what makes the matzah balls expand and become light and fluffy. Peeking lets the steam escape and results in dense, heavy balls.

To serve, reheat the strained broth until steaming hot. Place 1 or 2 matzah balls in each bowl, ladle the hot broth over them, and add a few pieces of fresh carrot (cook them separately in the broth for 15 minutes before serving if desired). Garnish with fresh dill fronds.
recipes.tip: For the fluffiest possible matzah balls, fold in 1 tablespoon of seltzer water at the end and use a very light hand when forming the balls. The number one rule: do not lift the lid during the 45-minute cooking time. The steam is doing all the work.

recipes.title: Moroccan Harira Soup
recipes.description: A thick, hearty tomato-based soup brimming with chickpeas, lentils, fresh herbs, and fine noodles. The traditional dish for breaking the Yom Kippur fast across Moroccan Jewish communities.
ingredients: 3 large carrots, peeled and diced into 1/4-inch pieces
3/4 cup dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in water
directions: Drain and rinse the chickpeas that have been soaking overnight. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed soup pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion, carrots, and celery. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 to 7 minutes until the vegetables have softened and the onion is translucent.

Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the harissa paste, turmeric, ginger, cinnamon, and ground coriander. Stir to coat the vegetables in the spices and toast for 1 minute — the spices should become very aromatic and the oil will take on a golden hue.
Add the tomato paste and stir it into the vegetable mixture, cooking for 1 minute to caramelize it slightly. Pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices and stir to combine.
Add the drained soaked chickpeas, green lentils, and red lentils. Pour in the 8 cups of stock and stir well. Bring the soup to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady, gentle simmer.

Cover the pot and let the soup simmer for 60 to 90 minutes, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes. The soup is ready for the next step when the chickpeas are completely tender — they should smash easily between your fingers with no chalky center. The red lentils will have dissolved into the broth, acting as a natural thickener, while the green lentils will hold their shape.
Add the vermicelli noodles and stir them in. Continue simmering uncovered for 15 more minutes until the noodles are tender and the soup has thickened to a hearty, stew-like consistency.

Remove the pot from the heat. Stir in the fresh parsley, cilantro, and lemon juice. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt, pepper, and additional lemon juice as needed. The soup should be thick enough that a spoon stands up in it, and the flavor should be complex — warm from the spices, bright from the lemon and herbs, and deeply savory from the slow-cooked legumes.

Serve in deep bowls with additional fresh herbs on top and crusty bread on the side. This soup thickens considerably as it cools, so when reheating leftovers, add water or broth 1/4 cup at a time until it reaches your desired consistency.
recipes.tip: Make this the day before Yom Kippur — the flavors deepen overnight and the soup becomes even more satisfying. The lentils and noodles will continue to absorb liquid, so keep extra broth on hand when reheating.

recipes.title: Iraqi Kubbeh Hamusta (Sour Soup)
recipes.description: Semolina dumplings stuffed with spiced ground beef, simmered in a tart, lemony celery broth. The crown jewel of Iraqi Jewish cooking and a labor of love that rewards every minute of effort.
ingredients: 1 tsp ras el hanout (or a mix of allspice, cinnamon, and cumin)
directions: Begin by making the soup broth. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add the diced carrots, cubed potatoes, and celery. Pour in 8 cups of water and add the turmeric and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer. Add the juice of half a lemon. Let the broth simmer while you prepare the dumplings — it should cook for at least 20 minutes before you add them.

To make the meat filling, heat a small skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and finely diced onion, breaking the meat up with a wooden spoon. Cook until the beef is browned and no pink remains, about 6 to 7 minutes. Drain off any excess fat. Add the ras el hanout (or spice mixture), salt, and pepper. Stir well and cook for 1 more minute. Transfer to a plate and let cool completely. If you are finding the assembly challenging, you can freeze the filling for 15 minutes — cold filling is much easier to work with.

To make the semolina dough, place the fine semolina in a large bowl. Add the oil and rub it into the semolina with your fingertips. Gradually add the warm water, mixing with your hands, until a smooth dough forms that holds together without crumbling but is not sticky. The dough should feel like wet sand that clumps together when squeezed. If it is too dry, add water a teaspoon at a time; if too wet, add semolina a tablespoon at a time.

This is the most important technique: keep a bowl of water beside you and wet your hands constantly throughout the entire assembly process. Semolina dough cracks when it dries out, so wet hands are non-negotiable. Take a piece of dough about the size of a walnut and roll it into a ball between your wet palms.

Using your thumb, press a deep hole into the center of the ball, rotating it while pressing to create a cup with thin, even walls (about 1/4 inch thick). If the walls crack, wet your fingers and smooth the cracks closed. Place 1 tablespoon of the cooled meat filling into the cup.

Pinch the opening closed, smoothing the seam with wet fingers. Gently flatten the sealed dumpling into a thick patty about 2 inches in diameter. Place on a plate or tray. Repeat with the remaining dough and filling — you should get 15 to 18 dumplings.

Bring the soup broth back to a steady boil. Carefully drop the kubbeh into the boiling soup 5 at a time, waiting a moment between each addition so the broth temperature does not drop too quickly. Once all the dumplings are in the pot, reduce the heat to a gentle simmer.

Cover the pot and simmer for 30 minutes. The dumplings will swell slightly and become tender throughout. In the last 5 minutes, add the remaining lemon juice and the chopped cilantro. Taste the broth — it should be distinctly sour and bright. Adjust with more lemon juice if needed. The word 'hamusta' means sour, so do not be shy with the lemon.
Serve the soup in deep bowls with 2 to 3 kubbeh per serving, plenty of broth, and the vegetables.
recipes.tip: The golden rule of kubbeh: always keep your hands wet. Dry hands cause the semolina dough to crack and the dumplings to fall apart in the soup. A Jerusalem grandmother's trick is to freeze the small meat balls for 15 minutes before wrapping — the cold, firm filling is much easier for beginners to handle.

recipes.title: Yemenite Chicken Soup with Hawaij
recipes.description: A deeply golden, aromatic soup spiced with hawaij — a Yemenite blend of cumin, turmeric, black pepper, and cloves. Served with fiery zhug and spongy bread.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (about 4 lbs), cut into 8 pieces
8 small onions, peeled and left whole
4 large carrots, cut into thick 1-inch rounds
10 garlic cloves, peeled and left whole
Lemon wedges and zhug for serving
directions: Place the chicken pieces in a large bowl. Squeeze the juice of 1 lemon over them and sprinkle generously with salt. Using your hands, massage the lemon and salt into every surface of the chicken pieces. Let sit for 30 minutes at room temperature. This lemon-salt massage draws out blood and impurities, resulting in a remarkably clean, bright-tasting broth.

Place the chicken pieces in a large stockpot and cover with 12 cups of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat. As the water comes to a boil, foam will rise to the surface — skim this off with a large spoon for the first 10 minutes until the broth runs relatively clear.
Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer. Add the whole peeled onions, carrot rounds, celery chunks, and whole garlic cloves. Stir in the hawaij spice blend, chopped parsley, and cilantro.
Simmer uncovered for 45 to 50 minutes. The soup will turn a deep, vivid golden yellow from the turmeric in the hawaij. The chicken should be falling off the bone and the vegetables completely tender.

Taste the broth and adjust the salt. The soup should be intensely aromatic and warming from the hawaij spices. Serve in large bowls with generous pieces of chicken and vegetables, a wedge of lemon for squeezing, and a spoonful of zhug (spicy Yemenite cilantro paste) on the side.
recipes.tip: Cut the vegetables into very large chunks so they don't disintegrate during the simmer. The lemon and salt massage on the raw chicken is the secret to the Yemenite soup's legendary clarity and brightness.

recipes.title: Moroccan S'china (Overnight Hamin)
recipes.description: The Moroccan Shabbat slow-cooked stew with brisket, marrow bones, chickpeas, white beans, potatoes, and eggs that cook for 8 or more hours overnight at low heat.
ingredients: 2 lbs beef brisket or chuck, cut into 3-inch pieces
1 cup dried white beans (navy or cannellini), soaked overnight
4-5 medium potatoes, peeled and left whole
6-8 eggs, still in their shells (rinsed clean)
1 head of garlic, top sliced off to expose cloves
directions: Begin by caramelizing the sugar, which gives the entire stew its signature deep mahogany color. Place the 1/4 cup of sugar in a dry 10-quart heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Do not stir — let the sugar melt and turn from golden to deep amber, swirling the pot occasionally for even color. This takes about 4 to 5 minutes. Watch carefully, as it can go from perfect to burnt in seconds.

As soon as the caramel is a deep amber color, carefully add the drained, soaked chickpeas and white beans directly onto the hot caramel. Stir quickly to coat the beans in the caramel — they will sizzle and steam. This caramel coating gives the beans an incredible depth of flavor and a beautiful dark color.

In a separate skillet, sear the beef pieces over high heat on all sides until they develop a deep brown crust, about 2 minutes per side. Place the seared beef on top of the beans in the pot. Arrange the marrow bones around and between the meat pieces.
Tuck the whole potatoes and the rinsed whole eggs (still in their shells) into any available spaces. Place the garlic head, cut-side up, in the center.

In a large measuring cup, combine 8 cups of warm water with the silan, smoked paprika, cumin, turmeric, and salt. Stir until dissolved. Pour this seasoned liquid over everything in the pot — the liquid should come approximately 3/4 of the way up the sides. Add more water if needed.

Bring the pot to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce the heat to medium-low and let it cook, uncovered, for 1 hour. During this initial hour, the flavors begin to meld and the liquid reduces slightly.

After 1 hour, cover the pot tightly — first with a layer of aluminum foil pressed directly onto the surface, then with the heavy lid. This double seal prevents any steam from escaping during the long overnight cook.

Transfer the pot to an oven preheated to 230°F. Cook for a minimum of 8 hours and up to 12 hours (overnight). The extremely low temperature transforms the tough cuts of meat into melt-in-your-mouth tender pieces, the beans become creamy, the potatoes absorb the rich braising liquid, and the eggs turn a deep golden brown with a creamy, custard-like yolk — these are the famous 'Huevos Haminados.'

To serve for Saturday lunch, carefully remove the lid and foil. The kitchen will fill with an incredible aroma. Gently separate the components and arrange on a large platter: sliced meat, marrow bones (spread on bread), beans, potatoes, and the peeled golden eggs. Spoon the thick, glossy sauce over everything.
recipes.tip: The caramelized sugar at the bottom is the defining feature of Moroccan s'china — it colors and flavors the entire stew. The eggs cook for so many hours that they turn golden brown throughout and develop a rich, almost meaty flavor. They are a delicacy and should not be skipped.

recipes.title: Fig & Pomegranate Braised Brisket
recipes.description: A show-stopping brisket braised low and slow with pomegranate molasses, dried figs, white wine, and honey. The ultimate centerpiece for the Rosh Hashanah table.
ingredients: 5 lb beef brisket (first cut or flat), trimmed of excess fat
3 large onions, sliced into thick rings
10 garlic cloves, peeled and left whole
directions: Remove the brisket from the refrigerator 1 hour before cooking to bring it to room temperature — cold meat will not sear properly. Preheat your oven to 300°F. Season the brisket generously on all sides with the salt, pepper, cumin, and smoked paprika, pressing the seasoning firmly into the meat.

Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven or heavy roasting pan over high heat until it is smoking hot. Carefully place the brisket in the pot, fat-side down. Sear without moving for 5 to 6 minutes until a deep, dark brown crust forms. Flip and sear the other side for another 5 to 6 minutes. The quality of this sear determines the depth of flavor in your finished dish — do not rush this step or move the meat before a proper crust has formed. Remove the brisket and set it aside on a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the sliced onion rings and whole garlic cloves to the pot, stirring and scraping up the browned bits (fond) from the bottom. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the onions are golden and softened. Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute to caramelize it slightly.

Pour in the white wine and bring to a vigorous boil, scraping the bottom of the pot to release any remaining fond. Let the wine reduce by about half, which takes approximately 5 minutes. This concentrates the wine flavor and cooks off the raw alcohol taste.

Return the brisket to the pot, fat-side up. Add the chopped dried figs, honey, pomegranate molasses, and beef broth. The liquid should come about halfway up the sides of the brisket — add more broth if needed.

Press a sheet of parchment paper directly onto the surface of the liquid and meat (this creates a seal that prevents evaporation while allowing some steam to circulate). Cover the pot tightly with aluminum foil, then place the lid on top. This triple seal ensures the brisket braises in a moist environment.

Transfer to the oven and braise for 4 to 4.5 hours. The brisket is done when a fork slides into the meat with zero resistance and the meat pulls apart easily at the grain. Check the pot once at the 3-hour mark to ensure there is still sufficient liquid.

Remove the pot from the oven and let the brisket cool in its braising liquid for at least 30 minutes. For the absolute best results, refrigerate the brisket in its liquid overnight — the flavors will deepen dramatically and the fat will solidify on top for easy removal.

When ready to serve, remove the solidified fat from the surface. Lift the brisket out and slice it against the grain into 1/4-inch thick slices. Arrange the slices in a baking dish, overlapping slightly, and pour the braising liquid and figs over them. Reheat covered in a 325°F oven for 25 to 30 minutes until heated through and the sauce is bubbling. Garnish with fresh pomegranate seeds and parsley.
recipes.tip: The single best thing you can do for this brisket is make it 1 to 2 days ahead. Cooling in the liquid keeps the meat incredibly moist, slicing cold produces cleaner cuts, and the flavors marry and deepen overnight. Reheat sliced in the sauce for the most tender result.

recipes.title: Moroccan Lamb Tagine with Prunes & Apricots (Mrouzia)
recipes.description: Fork-tender lamb shoulder braised with saffron, cinnamon, dried apricots, and prunes. A dish reserved for the most important occasions and distinguished guests.
ingredients: 4 lbs boneless lamb shoulder, cut into 2-inch pieces
32 dried apricots, soaked in 1 cup warm water for 20 min
2 tbsp Ras el Hanout spice blend
1/2 tsp Aleppo pepper or red pepper flakes
1/2 cup toasted slivered almonds for garnish
1/4 cup fresh cilantro, chopped, for garnish
directions: Pat the lamb pieces completely dry with paper towels — this is essential for proper browning. Wet meat steams instead of searing, and you will miss out on the deeply caramelized crust that forms the flavor foundation of any great tagine. Season the meat generously with salt, pepper, and a teaspoon each of cinnamon, ginger, and turmeric.

Heat 3 tablespoons of olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot (a Dutch oven is ideal) over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers. Working in batches of 4-5 pieces (do not crowd the pot), sear the lamb on all sides until deeply browned, about 3-4 minutes per side. Take your time — the difference between pale meat and well-browned meat is the difference between a flat tagine and a transcendent one. Transfer the browned meat to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium and add the sliced onions to the pot. Cook them in the lamb drippings for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are soft, golden, and deeply fragrant. The onions should melt into a near-jam consistency. Add the minced garlic, remaining cinnamon, ginger, saffron threads, and a pinch of black pepper. Stir for 1 minute until the spices bloom and the kitchen fills with an intoxicating aroma.

Return the seared lamb and any accumulated juices to the pot. Add the honey, pour in enough water or broth to come halfway up the sides of the meat (do not submerge it — this is a braise, not a stew), and bring to a gentle simmer. Cover the pot, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 1.5 hours, checking occasionally to make sure the liquid is barely bubbling, not boiling aggressively.

While the lamb braises, prepare the dried fruit. If the prunes and apricots are very dry, soak them in warm water or tea for 15 minutes, then drain. Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until golden and fragrant. Set aside — they will be added at the end as a garnish.

After 1.5 hours, the lamb should be tender but not yet falling apart. Add the prunes, apricots, and a tablespoon of orange blossom water (if using) to the pot. Replace the lid and continue cooking for another 30-45 minutes until the meat is meltingly tender and the fruit has plumped and softened into the sauce.

Remove the lid and increase the heat slightly. Let the sauce reduce and thicken for 10-15 minutes, stirring gently, until it becomes glossy and coats the back of a spoon. The sauce should have a complex sweet-savory-spiced flavor. Taste and adjust with more honey, salt, or a squeeze of lemon juice as needed.

Transfer the tagine to a serving platter or bring the pot directly to the table. Sprinkle the toasted almonds over the top and garnish with a scattering of sesame seeds and fresh cilantro. Serve over fluffy couscous, which soaks up the extraordinary sauce, or with warm crusty bread.
recipes.tip: The secret to a world-class tagine is patience: low heat, long time, and never rushing the browning or braising. The meat should be fork-tender, the sauce concentrated and glossy, and the dried fruit plump and caramelized at the edges. This tagine is actually better the next day — make it a day ahead, refrigerate, and reheat gently. The fat solidifies on top overnight, making it easy to skim for a cleaner sauce. Serve it at the center of a Shabbat table with couscous and harissa on the side. For an extra layer of complexity, add a preserved lemon (quartered) to the pot during the last 30 minutes of cooking.

recipes.title: Iraqi Overnight Chicken & Rice (Tbeet)
recipes.description: A whole chicken stuffed with cardamom and rose petal spiced rice, buried in more rice, and slow-cooked overnight. The rice at the bottom becomes a crispy, golden crust.
ingredients: 1 cup chicken gizzards, chopped into small pieces
2 1/2 cups jasmine rice, soaked in water for 30 min then drained
2 tsp whole cardamom pods, lightly crushed
8 eggs in their shells, rinsed clean
directions: In a bowl, combine 1 cup of the soaked and drained rice with the chopped gizzards, 1 teaspoon of the crushed cardamom pods, the rose petals, turmeric, tomato paste, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Mix well. This is the hashwa — the aromatic stuffing that will perfume the entire chicken from the inside.

Season the chicken inside and out with the remaining salt, pepper, allspice, and cinnamon. Stuff the cavity loosely with the hashwa mixture. Do not pack it too tightly, as the rice will expand during cooking. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine or secure the cavity with toothpicks to keep the stuffing inside.

Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large, heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Carefully sear the stuffed chicken on all sides until the skin is golden brown, about 3 to 4 minutes per side. Remove the chicken and set aside.

Pour 4 cups of boiling salted water into the pot, scraping up the browned bits. Carefully return the chicken to the pot. Cook, covered, for 5 minutes on each side, turning once. This par-cooks the chicken slightly.

Remove the chicken again. Drain the liquid and reserve it. Spread the remaining 1 1/2 cups of soaked rice on the bottom of the pot in an even layer, along with the remaining cardamom pods. Place the chicken on top of the rice, breast-side up. Pour the reserved cooking liquid around (not over) the chicken.

Set the pot over medium-low heat and cook for 30 minutes without touching it. This is the critical step that creates the tichna — the prized crispy rice crust at the bottom of the pot, similar to the Persian tahdig. You will hear the rice sizzling as it toasts.
After 30 minutes, gently nestle the rinsed whole eggs into the rice around the chicken. Cover the pot with a tight-fitting sheet of aluminum foil, then place the lid on top for a double seal.

Transfer the pot to an oven preheated to 225°F. Cook for 7 to 8 hours overnight. The extremely low heat slowly renders the chicken until it is so tender that the bones can practically be chewed, while the rice absorbs all the juices and the eggs turn golden and creamy.

To serve, carefully remove the eggs and peel them — they will be a beautiful amber color with a custard-like yolk. Remove the chicken and carve or simply pull the meat apart with forks. Invert the pot of rice onto a platter to showcase the crispy golden tichna crust on top.
recipes.tip: The 30 minutes on medium-low heat before going into the oven is the secret step that everyone fights over — it creates that crispy, golden rice bottom. Cardamom pods and dried rose petals are the unmistakable aromatics that give this dish its Baghdadi identity.

recipes.title: Iraqi Stuffed Vegetables (Mahshi)
recipes.description: Hollowed zucchini, bell peppers, and eggplants filled with a mixture of rice and spiced beef, then simmered upright in a garlicky tomato broth until the rice is fluffy and the vegetables are tender.
ingredients: 2 cups medium-grain rice, soaked in warm water for 30 min and drained
1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
directions: Prepare the vegetables for stuffing. For the zucchini: trim the tops and use a long, narrow zucchini corer or apple corer to hollow out the center, creating a tube with walls about 1/4 inch thick. Be careful not to pierce through the bottom. Save the scooped flesh for soup or discard. For the eggplants: cut off the stems, halve lengthwise, and use a spoon to scoop out the flesh leaving 1/4-inch walls. Important: sear the hollowed eggplant halves in a hot skillet with oil for 2 to 3 minutes on each side until the skin softens — this step is critical because raw eggplant skin remains tough and leathery even after boiling. For the bell peppers: slice off the tops and remove the seeds and membranes.

Prepare the stuffing mixture. In a large bowl, combine the ground beef, finely minced onion, drained rice, allspice, coriander, cinnamon, parsley, mint, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Mix thoroughly with your hands until all ingredients are evenly distributed.

Fill each prepared vegetable 3/4 full with the stuffing mixture. This is important: do not fill them all the way to the top. The rice expands significantly during cooking and needs room to grow. If you overfill, the vegetables will split open and the stuffing will spill into the sauce.

Stand the stuffed vegetables upright in a deep, wide 12-inch pot or Dutch oven, packing them close together so they support each other and remain standing. Place the stuffed zucchini (which are most likely to fall) in the center, supported by the larger eggplants and peppers on the outside.

In a large measuring cup or bowl, combine the tomato paste, warm water, minced garlic, salt, cumin, and lemon juice. Whisk until the tomato paste is fully dissolved. Pour this sauce over the stuffed vegetables — the liquid should come approximately 3/4 of the way up the sides of the vegetables. Do not submerge them completely.

Place a heatproof plate upside down on top of the vegetables to keep them from floating or tipping over during cooking. Bring the liquid to a boil over medium-high heat, then immediately reduce to a gentle simmer.

Cover the pot and simmer for 45 minutes. Check the rice inside one of the zucchini — it should be completely cooked, fluffy, and tender. If the rice still has a bite, continue cooking for 10 to 15 more minutes.

Remove the pot from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 15 minutes before serving. This resting period allows the rice to finish absorbing the liquid and firm up slightly, making the stuffed vegetables easier to serve without falling apart. Use a large spoon to carefully transfer the stuffed vegetables to a serving platter and spoon the sauce over them.
recipes.tip: Never pack the stuffing more than 3/4 full — the rice inside expands significantly and will burst the vegetables if overfilled. Searing the eggplant skin before stuffing is the difference between a palatable vegetable and a tough, chewy shell.

recipes.title: Israeli Chicken Schnitzel
recipes.description: Paper-thin chicken breast coated in sesame-studded paprika breadcrumbs and fried to a deep golden crunch. Israel's unofficial national dish and the ultimate comfort food.
ingredients: 1 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (2 large breasts)
1 cup panko breadcrumbs or fine breadcrumbs
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
Neutral oil for frying (about 1/2 inch deep)
directions: Place each chicken breast between two large sheets of plastic wrap on a sturdy cutting board. Using a meat mallet or rolling pin, pound the chicken to an even 1/8-inch thickness. Start from the center and work outward, using firm but controlled strokes. Even thickness is the single most important factor in schnitzel — if some parts are thicker than others, they will cook unevenly, leaving you with parts that are overdone and parts that are still raw. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up a three-bowl breading station in order: Bowl 1 contains the flour seasoned with a pinch of salt and pepper. Bowl 2 contains the beaten eggs. Bowl 3 contains the breadcrumbs mixed with paprika, sesame seeds, garlic powder, and onion powder.

Working with one piece at a time, dredge the chicken in the seasoned flour, making sure every surface is lightly coated. Shake off the excess — too much flour creates a gummy layer between the chicken and the coating.
Dip the floured chicken into the beaten egg, letting the excess drip back into the bowl for 3 seconds.

Press the chicken firmly into the breadcrumb mixture on both sides, pressing the crumbs into the surface with your hands to ensure they adhere well. Place the breaded chicken on a wire rack. Let the breaded pieces rest for 5 minutes before frying — this brief rest helps the coating set and prevents it from falling off in the oil.

Pour neutral oil to a depth of 1/2 inch in a large, heavy skillet. Heat over medium-high heat until the oil reaches 350°F (a breadcrumb dropped in should sizzle vigorously and turn golden within 30 seconds).

Carefully place the breaded chicken into the hot oil without crowding the pan (fry no more than 2 pieces at a time in a standard 12-inch skillet). Fry for 2 to 3 minutes per side, flipping once, until both sides are a deep, even golden brown and the internal temperature reaches 165°F.

Transfer to a wire rack — not paper towels — set over a baking sheet. Draining on a wire rack allows air to circulate under the schnitzel, keeping the bottom crispy. Paper towels trap steam and make the bottom soggy. Serve immediately with lemon wedges for squeezing over the top.
recipes.tip: The three keys to perfect schnitzel: pound to an even 1/8 inch thickness, maintain oil at 350°F, and drain on a wire rack instead of paper towels. The wire rack tip alone will transform your schnitzel from good to restaurant-quality.

recipes.title: Mejadra (Lentils & Rice)
recipes.description: Spiced lentils and fluffy rice crowned with a mountain of deeply caramelized, crispy fried onion rings. Simple, magnificent, and deeply satisfying.
ingredients: 1 1/4 cups (250g) green or brown lentils, rinsed
1 cup basmati rice, rinsed until water runs clear
4 large onions, sliced into thin rings
Neutral oil for frying onions (about 1 cup)
directions: Begin with the fried onions, as they take the longest and can be made ahead. Separate the onion rings and toss them in a bowl with the flour and a generous pinch of salt. The flour coating helps them crisp up beautifully and turn a deep brown color.

Pour about 1 cup of neutral oil into a large, deep skillet and heat over medium-high heat. Fry the onion rings in 3 to 4 batches (do not crowd the pan). Each batch should take 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions are a very dark brown — almost burnt-looking. They will crisp up further as they cool. This is critical: if your fried onions are merely golden, they will be soft and bland. They need to be deeply dark brown to achieve the sweet, caramelized flavor that defines great mejadra.
Remove the fried onions with a slotted spoon and spread them on a plate lined with paper towels. They will become crunchy as they cool. Set aside.

Cook the lentils. Bring a pot of salted water to a boil. Add the rinsed lentils and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until they are al dente — tender but still holding their shape with a slight firmness at the center. Drain and set aside.

Toast the spices. Place the whole cumin seeds and coriander seeds in a dry skillet over medium heat. Toast for 1 to 2 minutes, shaking the pan frequently, until the seeds become very fragrant and you can hear them beginning to pop and crackle. Transfer to a mortar and pestle or cutting board and crush them lightly — you want them cracked, not powdered.
In a medium pot with a tight-fitting lid, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the rinsed basmati rice and the crushed spices. Stir for 1 minute to toast the rice and coat it in the oil.

Stir in the cooked lentils and 1 1/2 cups of water. Add the salt. Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce the heat to the lowest possible setting. Cover tightly and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid.

Remove the pot from the heat, keeping the lid on. Place a clean, folded tea towel between the pot and the lid (the towel absorbs excess steam and prevents the rice from getting soggy). Let the pot sit undisturbed for 10 minutes.
Fluff the rice and lentils with a fork. Transfer to a large serving platter and top with a generous, towering mound of the crispy fried onions. Serve with a bowl of yogurt or labneh on the side.
recipes.tip: The fried onions must be very dark — almost burnt-looking — to achieve the right deep, sweet, caramelized flavor. They will crisp up more as they cool. Make double the onions; they disappear fast and everyone will want more.

recipes.title: Pomegranate Glazed Salmon
recipes.description: Salmon fillets with a tart, glossy pomegranate molasses glaze, scattered with jewel-like pomegranate seeds and fresh herbs. An elegant lighter option for the New Year.
directions: Begin by making the pomegranate glaze, which needs time to reduce and concentrate. In a small saucepan, combine the pomegranate juice (or pomegranate molasses thinned with water), honey, soy sauce, minced garlic, and a pinch of red pepper flakes. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the glaze has reduced by about half and coats the back of a spoon. It should be thick and syrupy, like warm honey. Set aside to cool slightly — the glaze will continue to thicken as it cools.

While the glaze reduces, prepare the salmon. Remove the fillets from the refrigerator 15-20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off — cold fish cooks unevenly, with the outside overdone before the center is warm. Pat the fillets completely dry with paper towels. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Preheat your oven to 425°F and line a baking sheet with aluminum foil (for easy cleanup) and parchment paper on top. The high heat is essential for developing a caramelized glaze on the surface of the salmon while keeping the interior silky and moist.

Place the salmon fillets skin-side down on the prepared baking sheet. Brush a generous layer of the pomegranate glaze over the top and sides of each fillet — use about two-thirds of the glaze, reserving the rest for a final coat. The layer should be thick enough to see, like a shiny lacquer.

Bake for 10-12 minutes for 1-inch thick fillets, or until the salmon flakes easily when pressed with a fork but is still slightly translucent in the very center. The carryover heat will continue cooking the fish for 2-3 minutes after you remove it from the oven, so err on the side of undercooking rather than overcooking. Overcooked salmon is dry and chalky; properly cooked salmon is silky, moist, and luscious.

Remove the salmon from the oven and immediately brush with the remaining glaze while the fish is still hot — the heat helps the final coat adhere and gives the surface an incredible glossy sheen. If you have pomegranate seeds, scatter them over the glazed salmon now, pressing them gently into the surface.

Let the salmon rest for 2-3 minutes before serving. Transfer to a platter and garnish with fresh pomegranate seeds, thinly sliced scallions, and toasted sesame seeds. The visual presentation — jewel-red seeds against the deep burgundy glaze on pink salmon — is stunning and makes this a showpiece dish. Serve with roasted vegetables, herbed rice, or a simple green salad.
recipes.tip: The glaze must be reduced until thick and syrupy before applying — thin, watery glaze will not stick to the fish and will just pool on the pan. Do not flip the salmon during cooking — cook it skin-side down the entire time, which protects the delicate flesh and allows the glaze to caramelize beautifully on top. This dish is spectacular for Rosh Hashanah (fish head symbolism + pomegranate symbolism) and can be served warm or at room temperature for Shabbat lunch. For an even more impressive version, broil the glazed salmon for the last 90 seconds to caramelize the surface, watching like a hawk to prevent burning.

recipes.title: "Indestructible" Holiday Challah
recipes.description: A foolproof challah recipe with a triple rise and a glossy double egg wash. For Rosh Hashanah, shape into a round spiral and add honey to the dough. This recipe has never failed anyone.
ingredients: 1 3/4 cups warm water (110°F — warm to the touch but not hot)
4 large eggs + 1 egg for egg wash
Optional for Rosh Hashanah: 2 tbsp honey added to the dough, raisins
directions: In a large mixing bowl or the bowl of a stand mixer, dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water. Stir gently and let the mixture sit for 10 minutes until it becomes foamy and bubbly on the surface. This step activates the yeast and confirms it is alive. If the mixture does not foam after 10 minutes, your yeast is dead and you need to start over with fresh yeast.
Whisk in the olive oil and 4 eggs until fully combined. If making the Rosh Hashanah version, add the honey at this stage.

Add the salt and then begin adding the flour, 1 cup at a time, stirring after each addition. After about 6 cups, the dough will become too stiff to stir with a spoon. Turn it out onto a well-floured surface (or switch to the dough hook on your stand mixer).

Knead the dough for 8 to 10 minutes, adding flour as needed, until the dough is smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky but not sticky. It should pass the 'windowpane test' — if you stretch a small piece between your fingers, it should form a thin, translucent membrane without tearing. If it tears immediately, continue kneading for a few more minutes.

Shape the dough into a ball and place it in a large, lightly oiled bowl, turning once to coat all surfaces. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and place in a warm, draft-free location. Rise 1: Let the dough rise for 1 hour until it has doubled in size. When you press a finger into the dough, the indentation should spring back slowly.
Punch the dough down firmly to release the gas. Re-cover and let it rise again. Rise 2: 30 more minutes. This second rise develops more complex flavor and a finer crumb structure.

Turn the dough out and divide it in half (for 2 loaves). For each loaf, divide the half into 3 equal pieces for a classic 3-strand braid. Roll each piece into a long rope about 14 inches long, tapering the ends. Lay the 3 ropes side by side, pinch them together at the top, and braid by alternating the outer strands over the center. Pinch the bottom ends together and tuck both ends under the loaf. For Rosh Hashanah, roll the dough into one long rope and coil it into a round spiral shape.

Place the braided loaves on parchment-lined baking sheets. Beat the remaining egg and brush the loaves with a thin, even layer of egg wash. Rise 3: Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let rise for 1 hour until the loaves are puffy and have increased in size by about 50 percent.

Preheat your oven to 375°F. Brush the risen loaves with a second coat of egg wash — this double application is what gives the challah its signature deep, glossy mahogany crust. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the loaves are a rich golden brown and sound hollow when you tap the bottom.
Let the challah cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes before slicing. The interior will continue to set as it cools.
recipes.tip: The triple rise is what makes this recipe 'indestructible' — even beginners get a soft, pillowy result. If the top is browning too quickly before the interior is done, tent the loaf loosely with aluminum foil for the last 10 minutes of baking.

recipes.title: Uri Scheft's Chocolate Babka
recipes.description: A towering, laminated babka with swirls of Nutella and dark chocolate chips running through a rich, buttery brioche-like dough, finished with a sticky sugar syrup glaze.
ingredients: 120g (1 stick + 1 tbsp) unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes, at room temperature
170ml (3/4 cup) whole milk, at room temperature
directions: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine the flour, eggs, sugar, milk, and yeast. Mix on low speed for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms, then increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the sides of the bowl.

With the mixer running on medium speed, begin adding the butter one cube at a time. Wait for each cube to be fully incorporated before adding the next — this process takes about 8 to 10 minutes total. The dough will look like it is falling apart after the first few additions; this is normal. Continue kneading patiently and it will come together into a smooth, glossy, elastic dough that pulls cleanly away from the bowl. Add the salt during the last minute of kneading.

Wrap the dough tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours and ideally overnight (up to 12 hours). The cold rest firms the butter, making the dough much easier to roll out thinly, and allows the gluten to relax.

Remove the chilled dough from the refrigerator. Divide it in half. Working with one half at a time on a well-floured surface, roll the dough into a large rectangle approximately 18 inches wide by 9 inches tall. The dough should be about 1/4 inch thick.
Spread half of the Nutella evenly over the entire surface of the rectangle, going all the way to the edges. Scatter half of the chocolate chips over the Nutella layer.

Starting from the long (18-inch) side, roll the dough into a very tight cylinder, keeping it as even as possible. Pinch the seam closed. Using a sharp serrated knife, cut the cylinder in half lengthwise down the entire length — you will now have two long strips with the chocolate layers fully exposed.

Lay the two strips side by side, cut sides facing up. Cross one strip over the other to form an X. Then twist the two halves together, keeping the cut sides facing upward as much as possible to showcase the chocolate swirl layers.
Carefully transfer the twisted babka into a greased 9x5-inch loaf pan. Repeat the entire process with the second half of dough.

Cover the pans loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let the babkas rise at room temperature for approximately 2 hours until the dough has risen to about 1 inch above the rim of the pans and looks puffy.
Preheat the oven to 350°F. Bake the babkas for 30 minutes, rotating the pans halfway through, until the tops are deep golden brown and the internal temperature reaches 190°F.
While the babkas bake, make the sugar syrup. Combine the sugar and water in a small saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Let it boil for 1 minute, then remove from heat.

As soon as the babkas come out of the oven, brush them generously with the hot sugar syrup — use all of it. The syrup soaks into the hot bread and keeps the babka incredibly moist for days. Let the babkas cool in their pans for 10 minutes, then turn them out onto a wire rack to cool completely.
