recipes.tip: Adding the butter cube by cube is the most tedious part, but it is what creates the laminated, pull-apart layers that make babka so special. Chilling overnight makes the dough dramatically easier to handle. The sugar syrup applied immediately after baking is what keeps the babka moist — do not skip it.

recipes.title: Yerushalmi Kugel
recipes.description: A Jerusalem institution — thin egg noodles tossed in dark, bitter caramel with a bold, unexpected kick of black pepper. Sweet, peppery, and addictive.
ingredients: 1 (16 oz) package thin egg noodles (vermicelli or thin spaghetti)
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper (measured generously)
directions: Cook the noodles in a large pot of salted boiling water according to the package directions until they are just al dente. Drain thoroughly and set aside.

In a deep, heavy 6-quart Dutch oven or cast-iron pot, combine the sugar and oil over medium heat. Stir constantly with a long-handled wooden spoon or heatproof spatula. The sugar will first dissolve into the oil, then begin to bubble vigorously.

Continue stirring for 11 to 12 minutes. This is the critical step that defines the dish. The caramel must turn very dark amber — much darker than you instinctively feel comfortable with. It should smell like toffee with just a hint of bitterness. If the caramel is too light, the finished kugel will taste merely sweet and flat; it needs that deep, almost burnt-edged bitterness to achieve its signature flavor. However, if it actually burns (turns black and smells acrid), you must start over.

The moment the caramel reaches the right color, immediately add the well-drained noodles to the pot. Toss them quickly and vigorously with tongs or two forks to coat every strand in the hot caramel. Work fast — the caramel begins to harden as it cools. The noodles will turn a deep golden-brown color.

Let the caramel-coated noodles cool for 5 minutes in the pot. Then add the beaten eggs, salt, and generous amount of black pepper. Stir thoroughly to distribute the eggs and seasoning evenly throughout the noodles.
If you removed the noodles to coat, return the mixture to the greased Dutch oven. Otherwise, make sure the pot is well-greased. Press the noodle mixture firmly into the pot in an even layer.

Bake uncovered at 350°F for 2 hours until the top is very dark brown, almost black, and has formed a thick, crunchy crust. The interior should remain soft and slightly custardy while the exterior becomes deeply caramelized.

Let cool in the pot for 10 minutes, then carefully invert onto a serving platter. The kugel should slide out in one piece, revealing the beautiful dark exterior. Cut into wedges and serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.tip: The caramel must be very dark — darker than you think is right. A too-light caramel produces a kugel that is simply sweet, but missing the complex, bitter-sweet, toffee-like character that makes Yerushalmi kugel unique. Baking in a deep pot rather than a shallow pan creates a taller result with greater contrast between the crusty exterior and soft interior.

recipes.title: Sweet Dairy Noodle Kugel
recipes.description: Wide egg noodles baked in a creamy custard of cottage cheese, sour cream, and milk, studded with orange-soaked raisins. A rich, comforting dish that bridges the gap between side dish and dessert.
ingredients: Juice and zest of 1 large orange
directions: Preheat your oven to 350°F and generously butter a 9x13-inch baking dish. The butter coating is critical — it creates the caramelized, golden crust on the bottom and sides that many consider the best part of the kugel. Some cooks also sprinkle the buttered dish with a thin layer of sugar and cinnamon to amplify this crust.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil and cook the egg noodles until they are just barely al dente — about 1 minute less than the package suggests. The noodles will continue cooking in the oven, so undercooking them now prevents a mushy final texture. Drain the noodles thoroughly and toss them with the melted butter while they are still hot, which coats each strand and prevents clumping.

In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the sour cream, cottage cheese, cream cheese, sugar, eggs, vanilla extract, and cinnamon until the mixture is smooth and uniform. The cream cheese should be at room temperature to avoid lumps — if it is cold, microwave it for 15-20 seconds to soften it first. This custard base is what transforms simple noodles into a rich, creamy dessert.

Fold the buttered noodles into the custard mixture, using a gentle lifting motion to ensure every strand is coated without breaking the noodles. The goal is a uniform distribution — you should not see dry noodles or pools of unmixed custard anywhere in the bowl.

Pour the mixture into the prepared baking dish and spread it evenly with a spatula. Scatter the raisins across the top if using, pressing them gently into the surface so they do not burn during baking. For the topping, combine the cornflake crumbs (or crushed graham crackers), melted butter, sugar, and cinnamon, then sprinkle this mixture evenly over the entire surface.

Bake uncovered for 45 to 55 minutes, until the top is deeply golden and the center is set but still has a gentle jiggle when you shake the pan — similar to a baked custard. The edges should be pulling away slightly from the sides of the dish. Overbaking dries out the kugel, so check at 45 minutes and trust the jiggle test.

Let the kugel rest for at least 15 minutes before cutting. This resting period allows the custard to set fully, making clean slices possible. Serve warm or at room temperature. Kugel is equally delicious cold the next day — many families prefer it chilled, straight from the refrigerator.

For Shabbat, prepare the kugel on Friday and reheat it covered with foil at 300°F for 20 minutes. The flavors meld and deepen overnight, and many experienced cooks insist that day-old kugel is actually superior to freshly baked.
recipes.tip: The secret to an extraordinary kugel is the contrast between the crispy, caramelized crust and the creamy interior — so do not skimp on buttering the pan. This kugel can be made up to 2 days ahead and refrigerated; reheat covered at 300°F for 20-25 minutes. Serve it as a side dish alongside roast chicken or as a dessert with a dollop of sour cream. For an extra indulgent version, fold in 1/2 cup of white chocolate chips before baking — they melt into pockets of sweetness throughout.

recipes.title: Moroccan Moufleta (Mimouna Crepes)
recipes.description: Paper-thin, chewy, stretchy crepes stacked into a tower and doused in melted butter and honey. The signature dish of the Mimouna celebration marking the end of Passover.
ingredients: 1/2 cup neutral oil, plus more for coating the dough balls
Melted butter and honey for serving
directions: In a large bowl, combine the flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast. Add the warm water and the 1/2 cup of oil. Mix with your hands or a wooden spoon until a rough dough forms.

Turn the dough out onto a clean, unfloured surface. Knead vigorously for 12 full minutes. The dough needs to become extremely smooth, elastic, and almost silky to the touch. This extended kneading develops the gluten to the point where the dough can be stretched paper-thin without tearing — which is the entire goal. You will know the dough is ready when you can pull a piece and stretch it translucently thin.
Cover the dough with a damp cloth and let it rise for 40 minutes until it has puffed up noticeably.

Divide the risen dough into 24 equal balls (each about the size of a golf ball). Pour a generous amount of neutral oil into a shallow dish or tray. Roll each ball in the oil to coat it completely, then arrange the oiled balls on the tray, leaving space between them. Let the oiled balls rest for at least 15 minutes — this oil soak is what gives the dough the elasticity to stretch paper-thin without resistance.

When ready to cook, generously oil a clean work surface. Take one dough ball and place it on the oiled surface. Using your fingertips, gently stretch and pull the dough outward from the center, working around the edges, until it is as thin as paper — you should be able to see your hand through it. The dough should not tear if it has been properly kneaded and oiled. If it resists stretching, let it rest for 5 more minutes.
Heat a large, dry skillet or flat griddle over medium heat. Lay the stretched dough onto the hot surface. Cook for about 30 seconds until the bottom sets and shows golden spots.

While the first crepe is cooking, stretch the next dough ball paper-thin. Place this raw crepe directly on top of the cooking one. Flip the entire stack. Continue this process — stretching a new crepe and adding it to the growing stack, flipping the stack each time — until you have built a tower of 8 to 12 crepes.
The finished stack should be golden and spotted on the outside, chewy and layered inside. Transfer to a plate immediately.

To serve, drizzle the stack generously with melted butter and warm honey. Pull individual crepes from the stack, roll them into cigars, and eat with your hands. Some families also serve them with jam, Nutella, or fresh fruit.
recipes.tip: The 15-minute oil soak before stretching is not optional — it is what makes the dough elastic enough to go paper-thin without tearing. If a ball tears when you try to stretch it, it needs more resting time in the oil.

recipes.title: Moroccan Sfenj (Spongy Donuts)
recipes.description: Light, spongy ring donuts made from a very soft, sticky yeast dough and fried to a golden puff. Traditionally dipped in granulated sugar or drizzled with honey while still piping hot.
ingredients: 1 tbsp Arak (anise spirit) or 1 tsp anise extract
Neutral oil for deep frying (at least 3 inches deep)
Granulated sugar or honey for serving
directions: In a very large bowl, combine the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the warm water and Arak. Mix with a wooden spoon or your hands until a very soft, extremely sticky dough forms. Do not be tempted to add more flour — the stickiness is intentional. The high hydration is what creates the spongy, airy interior texture that defines sfenj. The dough should be too wet to knead on a counter.
Cover the bowl with a damp towel or plastic wrap and let the dough rise in a warm place for 30 minutes until it has puffed up and become bubbly.

Punch the dough down firmly in the bowl. Cover again and let it rise for a second 30-minute rise. Do not punch down after this second rise — the air bubbles are what will make the sfenj light and spongy.
While the dough rises for the second time, fill a deep pot or Dutch oven with at least 3 inches of neutral oil. Heat to 350°F, using a deep-fry thermometer to monitor the temperature.

Here is the shaping technique: keep a bowl of water next to your workspace. Dip both hands generously in water — your hands must be very wet at all times when handling this dough. Reach into the bowl and pull off a piece of dough about the size of a plum. Using both hands, gently stretch it into a rough circle and use your thumbs to poke and stretch a hole in the center, forming a ring shape about 3 inches in diameter. The ring does not need to be perfect — rustic is traditional.

Carefully lower the ring into the hot oil. It will sink briefly, then float to the surface and begin puffing up dramatically. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes per side, flipping once with chopsticks or a slotted spoon, until the sfenj is deeply golden brown and puffed on both sides.

Remove with a slotted spoon and let excess oil drip off for just a moment. While the sfenj is still piping hot, either dip it in a plate of granulated sugar, turning to coat all sides, or drizzle it with warm honey. Serve immediately — sfenj are at their absolute best within minutes of frying and do not store well.
recipes.tip: The Arak (anise spirit) in the dough serves a functional purpose beyond flavor — it prevents the dough from absorbing excess oil during frying, resulting in a lighter, crispier donut. If you cannot find Arak, substitute with 1 teaspoon of anise extract or omit it entirely.

recipes.title: Israeli Jelly Sufganiyot
recipes.description: Classic Hanukkah jelly donuts: pillowy fried dough rounds filled with sweet strawberry jam and dusted with a cloud of powdered sugar. The taste of Israeli Hanukkah.
ingredients: 1/2 cup strawberry jam (or flavor of your choice)
directions: In a large bowl or the bowl of a stand mixer, combine the flour, instant yeast, powdered sugar, nutmeg, and salt. Add the egg yolks, oil, and warm water. Mix on low speed with a dough hook (or by hand) until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Increase to medium speed and knead for 8 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls away from the sides of the bowl cleanly.
Shape the dough into a ball, cover the bowl with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place until doubled in size, about 1 to 2 hours depending on the ambient temperature.

Turn the risen dough out onto a lightly floured surface. Use a rolling pin to roll it to an even 1/4-inch thickness. Using a 2-inch round biscuit cutter or glass, stamp out rounds, pressing straight down and twisting slightly to get a clean cut. Re-roll the scraps once to cut additional rounds.

Place the cut rounds on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them 1 inch apart. Cover loosely with a clean kitchen towel and let rise for 15 to 20 more minutes. They should puff up and look slightly puffy.

Heat oil in a deep pot or Dutch oven to exactly 350°F. Use a deep-fry thermometer and monitor the temperature throughout — this is the most critical variable for sufganiyot. Oil that is too hot will burn the outside before the inside cooks; oil that is too cool will result in greasy, heavy donuts that absorb excess oil.

Fry the donuts in batches of 3 to 4, lowering them gently into the oil with a slotted spoon. Fry for approximately 1.5 minutes per side, flipping once, until they are uniformly golden brown and have puffed up into round balls. Remove with a slotted spoon and place on a wire rack to cool slightly.

While the sufganiyot are still warm (but not scorching hot), use a chopstick or the handle of a wooden spoon to poke a small hole into the side of each donut, pushing it about halfway into the center to create a cavity.

Fill a piping bag or squeeze bottle with the strawberry jam. Insert the tip into the hole and squeeze gently, filling each donut with 1 to 2 teaspoons of jam. You should feel the donut become slightly heavier as it fills — do not overfill, or the jam will ooze out.
Dust the filled sufganiyot generously with powdered sugar on all sides. Serve within a few hours of frying for the best texture.
recipes.tip: Oil temperature is everything for sufganiyot. Invest in a deep-fry thermometer and maintain 350°F throughout the frying process. If you do not have a thermometer, drop a small piece of dough into the oil — it should sizzle immediately and float to the surface within 5 seconds.

recipes.title: Classic Jewish Honey Cake (Lekach)
recipes.description: The quintessential Rosh Hashanah dessert: a deeply moist, oil-based cake rich with honey, warm spices, and the subtle complexity of strong coffee. Symbolizes the wish for a sweet New Year.
ingredients: 1 cup warm strong black coffee (or strong tea)
directions: Preheat your oven to 325°F — this lower temperature is essential for honey cake, which burns easily due to its high sugar content. Grease and flour two 9x5-inch loaf pans or one 10-inch tube pan. Line the bottoms with parchment paper for easy release, as honey cake is notoriously sticky.

In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cinnamon, allspice, ginger, and cloves until thoroughly combined. Sifting these dry ingredients together ensures the leavening agents are evenly distributed, which prevents the cake from rising unevenly or developing dense pockets.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the honey, sugar, eggs, vegetable oil, and brewed coffee or orange juice until completely smooth. The coffee is traditional and adds depth without a coffee flavor — it darkens the crumb and balances the sweetness of the honey. Use strong, room-temperature coffee for the best results.

Make a well in the center of the dry ingredients and pour in the wet mixture. Stir from the center outward using a wooden spoon or rubber spatula until just combined — the batter should be smooth and pourable, like thick pancake batter. Do not overmix or use an electric mixer aggressively, as this develops too much gluten and produces a tough, dense cake rather than the tender, moist crumb you want.

If using orange juice, add the orange zest now and fold it in gently. The zest adds fragrant citrus oils that complement the honey beautifully. For a more complex flavor, add 1 tablespoon of brandy or whiskey to the batter.

Pour the batter into the prepared pans, filling them no more than two-thirds full — honey cake rises significantly. Tap the pans firmly on the counter 2-3 times to release any large air bubbles trapped in the batter.

Bake for 50 to 60 minutes for loaf pans, or 60 to 70 minutes for a tube pan, until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with just a few moist crumbs clinging to it. The top should be deeply golden brown and spring back when gently pressed. If the top is browning too quickly, tent it loosely with aluminum foil for the last 15 minutes.

Cool the cake in the pan for 15 minutes, then turn it out onto a wire rack to cool completely. Resist the temptation to cut it while warm — honey cake slices much more cleanly when fully cooled, and the flavor improves dramatically over the next 24 to 48 hours as the honey continues to permeate the crumb.

Wrap the cooled cake tightly in plastic wrap and store at room temperature. Honey cake is one of the rare baked goods that genuinely improves with age — it becomes moister and more flavorful after 2 to 3 days. It keeps beautifully for up to a week and freezes well for up to 3 months.
recipes.tip: The single most important rule with honey cake is patience: do not eat it on the day you bake it. The cake needs at least 24 hours for the honey to fully hydrate the crumb and for the spice flavors to bloom and harmonize. This makes it an ideal make-ahead dessert for Rosh Hashanah — bake it 3-4 days before the holiday. Serve slices with a drizzle of warm honey and a cup of strong tea. For an elevated version, brush the warm cake with a honey-whiskey glaze (2 tablespoons honey heated with 1 tablespoon whiskey) immediately after removing it from the pan.

recipes.title: Ma'amoul (Date-Filled Cookies)
recipes.description: Buttery, melt-in-your-mouth semolina cookies stuffed with a spiced Medjool date paste and dusted with a snowfall of powdered sugar. Shared across Sephardic, Mizrahi, and Arab communities.
ingredients: 2.5 cups all-purpose flour (or 2 cups flour + 1/2 cup fine semolina)
1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, at room temperature
1 cup pitted Medjool dates (about 10 large dates)
directions: Begin with the dough. In a large bowl, rub the softened butter into the flour (or flour-semolina mixture) and sugar using your fingertips. Work the butter in until the mixture resembles coarse, damp sand — every particle of flour should feel greasy to the touch. This rubbing technique creates the tender, shortbread-like crumb that defines ma'amoul.

Sprinkle the rose water and milk over the mixture and stir gently with a fork until the dough just comes together into a cohesive mass. Do not knead or overwork — excessive handling develops gluten, which will make the cookies tough instead of delicate and crumbly. The dough should hold together when squeezed but still feel slightly sandy.

Wrap the dough tightly in plastic wrap and rest it for 30 minutes at room temperature. If using semolina in the dough, refrigerate it overnight — the semolina needs this extended time to absorb the butter and develop the signature melt-in-your-mouth texture.

While the dough rests, prepare the date filling. Place the pitted dates, butter, sesame seeds, cardamom, and cinnamon in a food processor. Process until the dates form a smooth, sticky paste that holds together when squeezed. If the dates are dry, add water 1 teaspoon at a time. Roll the date paste into small balls about 3/4 inch in diameter (you should get about 24 balls).
Preheat the oven to 350°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper.

Take a walnut-sized piece of dough (about 1.5 tablespoons) and roll it into a smooth ball between your palms. Use your thumb to press a deep well into the center of the ball, rotating it as you press to create a cup with thin, even walls. Place a date paste ball into the well.

Close the dough around the date filling, pinching the edges together at the top. Roll the sealed cookie gently between your palms to form a smooth, seamless ball. If you have a traditional wooden ma'amoul mold, press the ball firmly into the mold and tap it out. If not, gently flatten each ball with a fork, pressing a crosshatch pattern into the surface for decoration.

Place the formed cookies on the prepared baking sheets, spacing them 1 inch apart. Bake on the lower rack for 10 minutes, then move the pan to the upper rack and bake for 8 more minutes, until the cookies are set and very lightly golden on the bottom but still pale on top. Ma'amoul should not brown — the pale color is traditional.
Let the cookies cool completely on the baking sheet — they are extremely fragile when warm and will crumble if handled before they set. Once cool, dust them generously with powdered sugar and serve.
recipes.tip: Ma'amoul are extraordinarily fragile when warm — they will break apart in your hands. Let them cool completely on the baking sheet before transferring or dusting with sugar. The overnight refrigeration (if using semolina) is what creates the legendary melt-in-your-mouth texture.

recipes.title: Coconut Cream Malabi
recipes.description: A silky, trembling coconut milk pudding scented with rose water, pooled with ruby pomegranate molasses and scattered with crushed pistachios. Elegant, refreshing, and effortless.
ingredients: 1 can (14 oz) full-fat coconut cream (at least 14% fat content)
1 tsp rose water (start with 1/2 tsp and adjust to taste)
directions: Pour the coconut cream into a medium saucepan. Add the sugar and set over medium heat. Stir gently until the sugar is completely dissolved and the coconut cream is steaming hot, about 2 to 3 minutes. Do not let it boil yet.

While the coconut cream heats, whisk the cornstarch into the 1/3 cup of cold water in a small bowl until completely smooth and lump-free. This is called a slurry — mixing the cornstarch with cold water first prevents lumps from forming when it is added to the hot liquid.

Slowly pour the cornstarch slurry into the hot coconut cream in a thin, steady stream, stirring constantly with a whisk or silicone spatula. This must be done gradually while stirring to prevent any lumps from forming.

Continue cooking over medium heat, stirring without pause, for 3 to 5 minutes. The mixture will thicken noticeably — it should coat the back of a spoon thickly and leave a clean trail when you run your finger through it. It will set up even more firmly as it chills.

Remove the saucepan from the heat. Stir in the rose water. Start with 1/2 teaspoon, taste, and add more if desired — rose water should be subtle and perfumed, not overpowering. A little goes a long way.

Pour the mixture into 4 small bowls, ramekins, or dessert glasses, dividing it evenly. Let cool to room temperature on the counter, then cover each with plastic wrap (pressed directly onto the surface to prevent a skin from forming) and refrigerate for at least 1 hour until completely set and cold.

To serve, drizzle each malabi with a generous spoonful of pomegranate molasses, letting it pool in dramatic ruby streaks on the white surface. Scatter crushed pistachios and pomegranate seeds on top. The visual contrast of white, ruby, and green makes this one of the most beautiful desserts in the Jewish repertoire.
recipes.tip: Use full-fat coconut cream, not light coconut milk — the lower fat content will not set properly. The rose water should be a subtle perfume, not the dominant flavor. Start with 1/2 teaspoon and taste before adding the full amount.

recipes.title: Classic Ashkenazi Chopped Liver
recipes.description: Rich, savory, and deeply traditional, made from broiled chicken livers mixed with deeply caramelized onions, hard-boiled eggs, and schmaltz. A cornerstone of the Ashkenazi appetizer table.
ingredients: 1.5 lbs chicken livers, trimmed of any fat and connective tissue
3 large onions, finely sliced into half-moons
4-6 tbsp schmaltz (rendered chicken fat) or extra virgin olive oil
2 tbsp Kiddush wine, brandy, or cognac
Crackers, challah, or matzo for serving
directions: Begin by caramelizing the onions, which takes the most time and is the foundation of great chopped liver. Heat 3 tablespoons of schmaltz (or olive oil) in a large skillet over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions, spread them out in an even layer, and cook for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring every 3 to 4 minutes. The onions should turn a deep golden brown and become very soft and sweet. Do not rush this step by raising the heat — slow caramelization is what creates the sweet, complex flavor that balances the mineral richness of the liver. Remove half the caramelized onions and set aside for folding in later.

While the onions caramelize, prepare the livers. Line a baking sheet with aluminum foil and set your oven's broiler to high. Arrange the trimmed chicken livers on the foil in a single layer. Broil for 3 to 4 minutes per side until the livers are cooked through but still slightly pink in the very center — they will continue cooking from residual heat. The livers should be firm to the touch but not rubbery. Over-broiling dries them out and makes the final product grainy.

Allow the livers to cool for 5 minutes. In a food processor, combine the broiled livers, half the caramelized onions (the half still in the pan), 3 of the hard-boiled eggs, the wine (or brandy), and the remaining 1 to 3 tablespoons of schmaltz. Pulse 8 to 10 times until the mixture is combined but still retains a coarse, rustic texture. Do not puree it smooth — chopped liver should have character and visible bits of egg and onion, not a paste-like consistency.

Transfer the mixture to a bowl. Chop the remaining 2 hard-boiled eggs into small dice and fold them in along with the reserved caramelized onions. Season generously with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust — chopped liver benefits from a bold hand with the seasoning.
Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate overnight. The flavors need this time to meld and deepen. The chopped liver will also firm up as it chills, making it easier to spread.
To serve, mound the chopped liver on a serving plate, garnish with fresh parsley, and accompany with crackers, sliced challah, or matzo.
recipes.tip: Do not over-process in the food processor — chopped liver should be textured and chunky, not smooth like a pate. The schmaltz is traditional and provides the richest flavor, but good olive oil works well for a lighter version.

recipes.title: Homemade Labneh with Za'atar
recipes.description: Thick, tangy strained yogurt drowned in green olive oil and showered with fragrant za'atar. The simplest and most satisfying appetizer or breakfast spread on the Israeli table.
ingredients: 32 oz (2 lbs) full-fat Greek yogurt or plain whole-milk yogurt
High-quality extra virgin olive oil (generous amount for serving)
Optional toppings: fresh mint, toasted pine nuts, cherry tomatoes, olives
directions: Begin with the highest-quality full-fat yogurt you can find — Greek yogurt works, but regular whole milk yogurt actually produces a smoother, creamier labneh because it has not already been strained. Avoid any yogurt with gelatin, stabilizers, or thickeners added, as these interfere with the straining process and produce an unpleasant texture.

Line a fine-mesh strainer with 3-4 layers of cheesecloth (or a clean, thin cotton kitchen towel) and set it over a deep bowl. The bowl needs to be deep enough that the bottom of the strainer sits well above the base, leaving room for the whey to collect without touching the yogurt.

Stir 1/2 teaspoon of salt into the yogurt and mix well. The salt serves two purposes: it seasons the labneh and it draws moisture out of the yogurt through osmosis, speeding up the straining process. Pour the salted yogurt into the lined strainer, gather the edges of the cheesecloth, and tie them loosely together.

Refrigerate the entire setup for 24 to 48 hours. At 24 hours, you will have a thick, spreadable labneh similar to cream cheese in consistency. At 48 hours, it becomes even firmer and denser — almost like fresh goat cheese. Check it at 24 hours and decide if the consistency is where you want it. You should see a significant amount of yellowish whey collected in the bowl below.

Transfer the strained labneh to a clean bowl. Taste it and adjust the salt if needed. Drizzle with your best extra virgin olive oil — the oil should be fruity and peppery, as it becomes a major flavor component. Sprinkle generously with za'atar, letting the herb mixture fall in an even layer across the surface.

For a beautiful presentation, use the back of a spoon to create a shallow well in the center of the labneh, then pool the olive oil in this depression. Add any additional toppings: sumac, Aleppo pepper, toasted pine nuts, cherry tomatoes, olives, or fresh herbs. The visual contrast of white labneh, green za'atar, and golden oil is stunning.

Serve with warm pita bread, fresh vegetables, or as part of a mezze spread. Labneh is best served at cool room temperature — take it out of the refrigerator 15-20 minutes before serving so the flavors can fully express themselves. Cold labneh tastes muted compared to slightly warmed.
recipes.tip: The quality of your labneh depends entirely on two things: the quality of your yogurt and how long you strain it. Do not rush the straining — 24 hours minimum, 48 for labneh balls. Save the strained whey for baking (use it in place of buttermilk in pancakes, bread, or biscuits). Labneh keeps in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks when stored in an airtight container with a thin layer of olive oil on top. For labneh balls (a traditional preservation method), roll tablespoon-sized portions into balls, place them in a jar, and cover completely with olive oil — these keep for a month and make an impressive gift.

recipes.title: Authentic Israeli Chopped Salad
recipes.description: The freshest, crunchiest salad in the world — finely diced cucumber and tomato dressed with nothing but lemon juice, olive oil, and fresh herbs. The cornerstone of every Israeli meal.
ingredients: 1 lb Persian or seedless cucumbers (about 6 small), finely diced
1 lb firm, ripe tomatoes (about 4 medium), finely diced
1/2 medium red onion, very finely minced
1/2 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
3 tbsp freshly squeezed lemon juice (about 1.5 lemons)
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
directions: The foundation of a perfect Israeli chopped salad is the dice — every piece of vegetable must be cut to roughly the same small size, about 1/4 inch. This uniform cut is not just aesthetic; it ensures that each forkful contains a balanced mix of all the vegetables and that the lemon-olive oil dressing coats everything evenly. Sharpen your knife before you begin — a dull knife crushes tomatoes instead of cutting them cleanly.

Start with the cucumbers. Peel them if the skin is thick or waxy (Persian cucumbers can be left unpeeled). Cut them in half lengthwise, then into long strips, then across into small dice. Transfer to a large mixing bowl. The bowl should be bigger than you think you need — you will be tossing the salad vigorously and need room.

Core the tomatoes by cutting out the stem end with a small paring knife. Cut the tomatoes in half, then into strips, then dice to match the cucumber size. Use the ripest, most flavorful tomatoes you can find — hothouse or Roma tomatoes in winter, heirloom or vine-ripened in summer. The tomatoes are the star of this salad, so their quality matters enormously.

Dice the red onion very finely — smaller than the cucumber and tomato, about 1/8 inch. Red onion provides essential sharpness, but too-large pieces can overwhelm the other flavors. If the raw onion is too pungent for your taste, soak the diced onion in ice water for 5 minutes, then drain thoroughly — this removes the harsh sulfur compounds while preserving the crunch.

Finely chop the fresh parsley and fresh mint. Strip the leaves from the stems and gather them into a tight bundle, then slice across with a sharp knife. Do not use a food processor — it bruises the herbs and turns them into a paste rather than clean, bright flecks of green.

Add all the vegetables and herbs to the bowl. Squeeze the lemon juice directly over the salad, catching any seeds with your other hand. Drizzle with the extra virgin olive oil. Season generously with salt and pepper. Toss everything together with your hands or two large spoons, lifting from the bottom to distribute the dressing evenly.

Taste the salad and adjust: it should be bright and acidic from the lemon, rich from the oil, and well-seasoned with salt. The salt also draws out juice from the tomatoes, creating a natural dressing at the bottom of the bowl. Serve immediately — Israeli salad is best eaten within 30 minutes of preparation, before the salt wilts the vegetables and the tomatoes release too much liquid.
recipes.tip: The secret to an authentic Israeli chopped salad is making it fresh and eating it immediately — this is not a make-ahead dish. In Israel, this salad is prepared minutes before every meal, including breakfast. The lemon-to-oil ratio should be roughly 2:1, leaning acidic and bright rather than rich. For a more substantial version, add diced bell pepper, crumbled feta, or a handful of pitted Kalamata olives. Never refrigerate the finished salad — cold mutes the fresh flavors that make it special.

recipes.title: Zaalouk (Moroccan Eggplant & Tomato Dip)
recipes.description: A smoky, spiced dip of roasted eggplant mashed with tomatoes, cumin, paprika, and fresh cilantro. Served at room temperature with crusty bread, it is an essential part of the Moroccan mezze spread.
ingredients: 2 lbs eggplant (about 2 large), peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
3 large ripe tomatoes, peeled and roughly chopped (or 1 can 14 oz diced tomatoes)
1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil, divided
Crusty bread or pita for serving
directions: Preheat your oven to 450°F. Toss the eggplant cubes with 2 tablespoons of the olive oil, spreading them in a single layer on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Roast for 30 to 35 minutes, tossing once halfway through, until the cubes are deeply browned on the edges and completely soft throughout. The high-heat roasting concentrates the eggplant's flavor and removes excess moisture that would otherwise make the dip watery.

While the eggplant roasts, prepare the tomato base. Heat the remaining olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the chopped tomatoes (or canned diced tomatoes, drained of excess liquid), smoked paprika, cumin, cayenne (if using), and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 15 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick, concentrated sauce.

Add the roasted eggplant to the skillet. Using a fork or potato masher, mash the eggplant into the tomato sauce to your desired consistency — some people prefer it chunky and rustic, while others like it smoother. Either way, it should not be completely smooth like hummus.
Continue cooking the combined mixture over medium-low heat for 10 more minutes, stirring occasionally, to allow the flavors to meld. The dip should be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon.
Remove from the heat and stir in the lemon juice and chopped cilantro. Taste and adjust the salt, lemon, and cayenne to your preference.

Transfer to a shallow serving bowl and let cool to room temperature. Zaalouk is traditionally served at room temperature, not hot, as the flavors become more pronounced as it cools. Serve with crusty bread or warm pita for scooping.
recipes.tip: Roasting the eggplant at high heat rather than sauteing it gives zaalouk a smoky depth that cannot be replicated by stovetop cooking. The dip tastes even better the next day — the spices continue to develop as it sits in the refrigerator.

recipes.title: Keftes de Prasa (Sephardic Leek Patties)
recipes.description: Tender fried patties made from slow-cooked leeks and mashed potatoes, bound with eggs and matzo meal. A Rosh Hashanah tradition symbolizing the desire to cut off enemies.
ingredients: 2 lbs leeks (white and light green parts only), cleaned and roughly chopped
1 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and quartered
1/2 cup matzo meal or fine breadcrumbs
Neutral oil for frying (about 1/2 inch deep)
directions: Trim the leeks by cutting off the dark green tops and the root end. Slice the white and light green parts in half lengthwise and rinse thoroughly under cold running water, separating the layers to flush out any trapped dirt or sand. Leeks are notorious for hiding grit between their layers, so be thorough — nothing ruins these delicate patties faster than a mouthful of sand.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil and blanch the leeks for 5 to 7 minutes until they are completely tender and have lost their raw bite. Drain them in a colander and press firmly with the back of a spoon to squeeze out as much water as possible. This step is critical — excess moisture will make the patties fall apart in the pan. Spread the leeks on a clean kitchen towel and blot them dry.

Finely chop the blanched leeks and transfer them to a large mixing bowl. Add the eggs, breadcrumbs, grated Parmesan or kashkaval cheese, salt, pepper, and a pinch of nutmeg. The cheese adds savory depth and helps bind the mixture. Mix everything together until the ingredients are evenly distributed and the mixture holds together when you squeeze a small handful — if it feels too wet, add another tablespoon or two of breadcrumbs.

With wet hands (to prevent sticking), shape the mixture into oval patties about 2.5 inches long and 1/2 inch thick. Place them on a plate or sheet pan. If you have time, refrigerate the shaped patties for 30 minutes — chilling firms them up and dramatically reduces the chance of them breaking apart during frying.

Heat 1/4 inch of neutral oil (such as vegetable or sunflower) in a large skillet over medium heat. Test the oil temperature by dropping in a small pinch of the mixture — it should sizzle immediately and gently, not violently. If the oil smokes, it is too hot; if the mixture just sits there without bubbling, it is too cool.

Carefully place the patties in the hot oil, leaving at least 1 inch of space between them so they do not steam instead of fry. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side without moving them — resist the urge to flip too early. The patties are ready to flip when the bottom is golden brown and they release easily from the pan. If they stick, they need more time.

Transfer the finished patties to a plate lined with paper towels to absorb excess oil. Squeeze fresh lemon juice over them while they are still hot — the acid brightens the flavor of the leeks and cuts through the richness of the frying oil. Serve warm or at room temperature with additional lemon wedges on the side.
recipes.tip: The make-or-break step is removing enough moisture from the leeks after blanching. Wet leeks mean soggy, crumbly patties — so squeeze, press, and blot them until they feel almost dry. These patties are wonderful as part of a Shabbat lunch spread alongside pickles, hummus, and tahini. They can be made a day ahead and reheated in a 350°F oven for 10 minutes, or served at room temperature. For a gluten-free version, substitute the breadcrumbs with an equal amount of almond flour or matzah meal.

recipes.title: Syrian Lachmagine (Tamarind Meat Pies)
recipes.description: Thin, crispy rounds of dough topped with a tangy, tamarind-laced meat mixture, garnished with pine nuts and pomegranate seeds. A Syrian-Jewish party essential.
ingredients: 24 mini pizza dough rounds (store-bought, or use the challah dough rolled thin)
1 cup tamarind sauce (oot) or 3 tbsp tamarind paste mixed with 3/4 cup water
directions: Begin with the dough. In a large bowl, combine the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the warm water and olive oil, and mix with a wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and springs back when you press it with your finger. The dough should be soft but not sticky — add flour a teaspoon at a time if needed.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap or a damp towel, and let it rise in a warm spot for 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled in size. The ideal rising temperature is around 75-80°F — if your kitchen is cool, place the bowl near a warm oven or in an oven with just the light turned on.

While the dough rises, prepare the meat topping. Combine the ground lamb or beef with the finely diced onion, diced tomatoes, tomato paste, tamarind paste, lemon juice, allspice, cinnamon, salt, pepper, and pine nuts in a bowl. Mix thoroughly with your hands until the mixture is uniform and slightly paste-like. The tamarind is the signature Syrian element — it adds a complex sweet-sour tang that distinguishes lachmagine from other flatbread meats.

Preheat your oven to 475°F (or as high as it will go) with a baking sheet or pizza stone inside. The high heat is essential for creating a crisp bottom and quickly cooking the thin layer of meat. If you have a pizza stone, use it — the direct heat transfer produces superior results.

Divide the risen dough into 12-14 pieces (about the size of golf balls). On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a thin circle, roughly 5-6 inches in diameter. The dough should be thin enough to see your fingers through it when held up to the light — thinner than pizza dough. This thinness ensures the bread bakes crisp while the meat topping stays juicy.

Spread a thin, even layer of the meat mixture over each circle of dough, going almost to the edges. Press the meat down gently so it adheres to the dough — this prevents it from shrinking away during baking. The meat layer should be about 1/8 inch thick — thin enough to cook through quickly.

Transfer the topped rounds to the preheated baking sheet (you may need to work in batches) and bake for 7 to 9 minutes until the edges of the dough are golden and crisp and the meat is cooked through. Watch carefully — the difference between perfectly done and burnt is less than a minute at these high temperatures.

Remove from the oven and immediately squeeze fresh lemon juice over each lachmagine. The acidity brightens every flavor and is absolutely non-negotiable in the Syrian tradition. Serve hot, either flat or folded in half, with a side of yogurt, fresh herbs, and pickled turnips.
recipes.tip: The tamarind paste is what makes this Syrian rather than Turkish or Lebanese — do not substitute with more lemon juice, as it provides a unique fruity sourness that lemon cannot replicate. Lachmagine freeze beautifully: stack cooled flatbreads between sheets of parchment paper, seal in a freezer bag, and reheat directly from frozen in a 400°F oven for 5 minutes. These are traditionally served at Shabbat kiddush, brit milah celebrations, and casual gatherings. For an extra-crisp base, brush the bottom of each dough round with olive oil before adding the meat topping.

recipes.title: Israeli Arayes (Grilled Meat-Stuffed Pita)
recipes.description: Pita pockets stuffed with spiced ground lamb and grilled until the bread is shatteringly crisp and the meat is juicy. The ultimate Israeli street food turned appetizer.
ingredients: 1 lb ground lamb or beef (at least 20% fat content)
4 round pita breads, halved to create 8 pockets
1/2 medium onion, very finely minced and squeezed dry
1/2 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Tahini and Israeli salad for serving
directions: Prepare the meat filling first. In a large bowl, combine the ground lamb or beef with the finely minced onion, chopped parsley, minced garlic, cumin, paprika, cinnamon, allspice, salt, and pepper. Mix thoroughly with your hands for 2-3 minutes until the mixture becomes slightly sticky and cohesive — this indicates the proteins in the meat have begun to bind, which prevents the filling from crumbling out of the pita during grilling.

Cut each pita bread in half to create two pockets. If your pitas are thick, carefully open the pocket by gently separating the two layers with your fingers, starting from the cut edge. Be gentle — if you tear through the outside, the meat juices will leak out during cooking.

Stuff each pita half with a generous amount of the meat mixture, pressing it into an even layer that reaches into the corners of the pocket. The meat should be about 1/2 inch thick throughout — too thick and it will not cook through before the bread burns; too thin and the arayes will be dry. Press the pita closed gently to compact the filling.

Preheat your grill to medium-high heat (around 400°F) or heat a grill pan or heavy skillet over medium-high heat on the stove. If using a grill pan, you want it hot enough that a drop of water sizzles and evaporates on contact. Brush both sides of the stuffed pitas lightly with olive oil — this promotes even browning and prevents sticking.

Grill the stuffed pitas for 3 to 4 minutes per side, pressing down gently with a spatula to ensure full contact with the cooking surface. The bread should develop deep golden grill marks and become crispy, while the meat inside cooks through to a juicy medium. You can check doneness by pressing the center — it should feel firm but not rock-hard.

While the arayes grill, prepare the accompaniments: whisk together tahini with lemon juice and a splash of water to make a pourable sauce, dice fresh tomatoes and cucumbers for a quick salad, and slice pickles. The contrast between the hot, crispy arayes and the cool, creamy tahini is what makes this dish extraordinary.

Remove the arayes from the grill and cut each half into 2-3 triangles for serving. Arrange on a platter and drizzle generously with the tahini sauce. Garnish with chopped parsley, a squeeze of lemon, and a sprinkle of sumac. Serve immediately — arayes are at their absolute best in the first 10 minutes after coming off the grill, when the bread is still crackling-crisp and the meat is steaming and juicy.
recipes.tip: The key to perfect arayes is getting the bread crispy without drying out the meat, which means medium-high heat and patience — do not press too hard or you will squeeze out the juices. These can be assembled up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerated before grilling, making them perfect for entertaining. Serve them as the centerpiece of a mezze spread with hummus, baba ganoush, and Israeli salad. For a smoky upgrade, add 1 tablespoon of harissa paste to the meat mixture and grill over real charcoal rather than gas.

recipes.title: Matbucha (Sephardic Tomato & Pepper Salad)
recipes.description: A thick, jammy, slow-cooked salad of roasted peppers and tomatoes reduced to a concentrated, spicy, sweet spread. A staple of the Israeli mezze table.
ingredients: 1 can (28 oz) diced tomatoes (or 6 large fresh tomatoes, peeled and chopped)
1 serrano or jalapeno pepper, seeded and finely minced
directions: Roast the bell peppers directly over a gas flame, turning with tongs, until the skin is completely blackened and charred on all sides (about 8 to 10 minutes total). Alternatively, broil them on a baking sheet, turning every few minutes. Place the charred peppers in a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let steam for 15 minutes. The steam loosens the skin for easy peeling. Peel off all the charred skin, remove the seeds and stems, and dice the roasted pepper flesh.
Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed saucepan or skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and serrano pepper. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant, stirring constantly.
Add the diced tomatoes (with their juices if using canned), the diced roasted peppers, paprika, sugar, and salt. Stir to combine.

Reduce the heat to the lowest possible setting. Let the mixture simmer uncovered, stirring every 10 to 15 minutes, for 1 to 2 hours. The cooking time is long because the goal is to evaporate nearly all the liquid until the mixture becomes thick, jammy, and concentrated — almost like a thick salsa or chutney. When you draw a spoon across the bottom of the pan, it should leave a clean trail that takes several seconds to fill back in.

Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature. Transfer to a serving dish. Matbucha is always served cold or at room temperature, never hot. It keeps in the refrigerator for up to a week and tastes even better after a day or two.
recipes.tip: The secret to great matbucha is time and patience. It must cook on the lowest possible heat for at least 1 hour — rushing it on high heat will burn the tomatoes before they have a chance to concentrate into that thick, jammy consistency.

recipes.title: Homemade Amba (Iraqi Mango Sauce)
recipes.description: The iconic tangy, mustardy mango condiment that defines Iraqi and Israeli street food. Essential on sabich, falafel, and shawarma.
ingredients: 3 lbs firm, unripe green mangoes, peeled and diced into 1/2-inch cubes
directions: Begin by selecting your mangoes carefully. You need firm, unripe green mangoes with hard, pale flesh and a distinctly sour, astringent taste when raw. Do not use ripe or semi-ripe mangoes, which are sweet and soft and will disintegrate into mush during cooking rather than holding their shape. Peel each mango with a sharp vegetable peeler, working carefully around the large flat pit. Cut the flesh into 1/2-inch cubes, keeping them as uniform as possible so they cure and cook evenly. Discard the pits and any fibrous flesh clinging to them.

Toss the diced mango cubes with the coarse salt in a large glass or ceramic bowl. It is important to avoid metal bowls at this stage, as the acid from the mango can react with reactive metals like aluminum and give the amba an unpleasant metallic taste. Stainless steel is acceptable, but glass or ceramic is ideal. Make sure every cube is coated in salt, then cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate overnight, or for up to 24 hours. During this time, the salt draws out excess moisture from the mango through osmosis, and begins a gentle fermentation process on the surface of the fruit. This curing step is what gives amba its characteristic tangy, complex flavor that cannot be replicated by simply adding vinegar.

The next day, drain the mangoes thoroughly, discarding all the salty, cloudy liquid that has accumulated at the bottom of the bowl. Do not rinse the mangoes, as you want to retain a thin film of salt on the surface. Let the drained cubes sit in the colander for 5 minutes so any remaining liquid drips away. The mangoes should feel noticeably drier and firmer than they did before the overnight cure.

Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and immediately cover the pan loosely with a lid or a splatter screen. The mustard seeds will begin to pop and jump violently within 30 to 60 seconds, and without a cover they will scatter all over your stovetop. Let them pop for 1 to 2 minutes until the popping slows to an occasional crackle. This toasting step is essential because it activates the pungent, sharp compounds inside the seeds that give amba its mustard-like bite. Raw mustard seeds would taste flat and almost flavorless in comparison.

Remove the lid and add the minced garlic, stirring it into the mustard-infused oil. Cook for about 45 seconds, just until the garlic turns fragrant and softens slightly but has not taken on any brown color. Burnt garlic will introduce a harsh bitterness that clashes with the tangy mango. Add the turmeric, fenugreek, and cayenne pepper all at once and stir continuously for 1 minute. The oil should turn a deep, vivid golden-yellow color and the kitchen will fill with a warm, earthy, slightly bitter aroma from the fenugreek. If the spices start to smoke or darken, your heat is too high and you should reduce it immediately.

Add the drained cured mango cubes to the pot and stir them gently into the spiced oil, taking care not to crush them. Pour in the water and vinegar, then stir everything together. Bring the mixture to a steady simmer over medium heat, then reduce to medium-low. Cook uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until the mangoes have softened enough to yield when pressed with the spoon but still hold their shape and have not collapsed into mush. The liquid should have reduced by about one-third and thickened slightly from the natural pectin in the mango.

Remove the pot from the heat. Using an immersion blender inserted directly into the pot (or transferring the mixture in batches to a standard blender), pulse the amba to your desired consistency. Some people prefer a chunky, salsa-like texture with visible mango pieces, while others prefer a smooth, ketchup-like sauce. Either is traditional. If using a standard blender, allow the mixture to cool slightly before blending and leave the lid slightly ajar to allow steam to escape, preventing pressure buildup. After blending, taste the amba and adjust the seasoning: add more salt if it tastes flat, more vinegar if it needs brightness, or more cayenne if you want additional heat.

Let the amba cool completely to room temperature before transferring it to clean, dry glass jars with tight-fitting lids. Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the amba before sealing each jar to prevent oxidation and discoloration. Refrigerate immediately. The amba will keep for up to 3 weeks in the refrigerator and, remarkably, continues to improve in flavor over the first 3 to 5 days as the spices fully permeate the mango and the fermentation flavors deepen. Stir the jar before each use, as the oil may separate to the top during storage.
recipes.tip: The overnight salt cure is the single most important step and cannot be shortened or skipped. It is what creates the fermented tanginess that separates real amba from a simple mango chutney. You can make amba up to 3 weeks ahead and store it in sealed glass jars in the refrigerator, where it actually improves with age. Serve it as the essential condiment on sabich, or drizzle it over falafel, shawarma, grilled chicken, or roasted vegetables for an instant flavor upgrade. For an ambitious variation, add a small handful of dried fenugreek leaves along with the ground fenugreek to create an even more complex, herbaceous version.

recipes.title: Moroccan Chicken Pastilla (B'stilla)
recipes.description: An extraordinary savory pie of shredded chicken, silky egg custard, and sweetened almonds wrapped in crispy phyllo and dusted with powdered sugar and cinnamon. The ultimate Moroccan showpiece.
ingredients: 1 kg (2.2 lbs) bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
1 tsp ground cinnamon, plus more for dusting
Large pinch of saffron threads, bloomed in 2 tbsp warm water
2 tbsp granulated sugar (for the almond mixture)
4 tbsp melted butter (or olive oil for pareve version)
directions: Place the chicken thighs in a large, heavy-bottomed pot with the sliced onions, saffron (along with its soaking water), turmeric, 1/2 teaspoon of cinnamon, a generous pinch of salt, and several grinds of black pepper. Add just enough cold water to barely cover the chicken pieces. Starting with cold water and bringing it up slowly extracts maximum flavor from the chicken and creates a more complex, gelatinous braising liquid. Bring the pot to a boil over medium-high heat, then immediately reduce to a very gentle simmer. Cook for 1 full hour, partially covered, until the chicken is so tender that it is literally falling away from the bone when you lift a piece with tongs. Skim any foam that rises to the surface during the first 15 minutes.

Using tongs or a slotted spoon, carefully remove the chicken pieces from the pot and set them aside on a plate to cool. Leave the onion mixture and all the braising liquid in the pot. Increase the heat to medium and continue cooking this onion sauce, stirring occasionally, for 20 to 30 minutes until nearly all the liquid has evaporated and the onions have broken down into a thick, dark, jammy paste. This concentrated reduction is one of the defining layers of pastilla, transforming a watery onion broth into an intensely savory, almost sweet sauce. Stir more frequently toward the end to prevent scorching as the liquid diminishes.

While the onion sauce reduces, shred the cooled chicken meat with two forks or your fingers, discarding all skin, bones, cartilage, and any fatty pieces. Shred the meat into thin, wispy strands rather than large chunks. Finer shredding allows the chicken to blend seamlessly with the other layers and prevents any single bite from being dominated by a thick piece of meat. Set the shredded chicken aside in a bowl.

This next step is the most technically demanding and also the most important. When the onion sauce is thick and nearly dry, reduce the heat to the lowest possible setting. Whisk the 6 eggs vigorously in a separate bowl until completely smooth. Pour the beaten eggs into the hot onion sauce in a slow, steady stream while stirring constantly and rapidly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula. The key here is that the eggs must cook gently in the residual heat of the thick sauce, forming a soft, creamy, custardy mixture that is uniform and silky. You are not making scrambled eggs. If the heat is too high or you stop stirring, the eggs will curdle into rubbery lumps instead of a smooth custard. This process should take 3 to 4 minutes of constant, patient stirring. When the mixture looks like thick, creamy porridge with no visible liquid remaining, remove it from the heat immediately and set aside.

Toast the blanched almonds in a large, dry skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan every 30 seconds to ensure even browning. Watch them carefully because almonds go from perfectly golden to burnt in a matter of seconds due to their high oil content. They should be uniformly light golden and smell deeply nutty and fragrant. Transfer them immediately to a plate to stop the cooking. Once cooled, place the toasted almonds in a food processor along with the orange blossom water, sugar, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of cinnamon. Pulse 8 to 10 times until you have a coarse, crumbly mixture with visible almond pieces. Do not over-process into a fine powder or paste, as the texture contrast is part of what makes pastilla extraordinary.

Preheat your oven to 375 degrees Fahrenheit and position the rack in the center. Generously brush a 10-inch round baking pan, springform pan, or oven-safe cast-iron skillet with melted butter, making sure to coat the sides as well as the bottom. The butter prevents sticking and also helps the phyllo layers crisp during baking.

Unwrap the phyllo dough and immediately cover the unused sheets with a slightly damp kitchen towel to prevent them from drying out and becoming brittle. Lay the first sheet of phyllo in the prepared pan, pressing it gently into the bottom corners and allowing the excess to drape over the sides. Brush the entire surface generously with melted butter, using a pastry brush and making sure to get into all the creases. Repeat with 3 more sheets, rotating each sheet slightly so the overhanging edges are distributed evenly around the pan. Each sheet should be buttered before the next one is added. The butter between the layers is what creates the shatteringly crisp, flaky crust.

Now build the filling in distinct layers, which is essential to pastilla's architecture. First, spread the egg-onion custard in an even layer over the phyllo base, smoothing it gently with the back of a spoon. Next, distribute the shredded chicken in an even layer over the custard, pressing it down lightly. Finally, spread the almond mixture in an even layer over the chicken. Each layer should be uniform in thickness to ensure every wedge has the same ratio of filling.

Fold the overhanging phyllo edges up and over the filling, one section at a time, brushing each folded section with butter as you go. The phyllo will not cover the center completely, and that is fine. Lay 2 more sheets of phyllo over the top, one at a time, brushing each with butter and tucking the edges down firmly along the inside walls of the pan to create a sealed package. Brush the very top surface with a final coat of butter.

Bake for 20 minutes until the top is golden and the edges are starting to crisp. Remove the pan from the oven. Place a baking sheet or large plate over the pan and, using oven mitts and a confident motion, carefully invert the pastilla onto the baking sheet so the bottom becomes the top. If using a springform pan, you can release the sides first. Return the inverted pastilla to the oven and bake for an additional 15 minutes until both sides are deeply golden brown, crispy, and the phyllo makes a hollow sound when tapped. This double-baking ensures that the bottom, which tends to be soggy from the filling's moisture, gets a chance to crisp up as well.

Remove the pastilla from the oven and immediately dust the top generously with powdered sugar through a fine-mesh sieve, creating a thick, snowy layer. Using the edge of a knife or a stencil if you want to be precise, draw parallel diagonal lines of ground cinnamon across the powdered sugar, creating the traditional diamond or crosshatch pattern. The contrast of white sugar and warm brown cinnamon on a golden, savory pie is the visual hallmark of Moroccan pastilla and should not be skipped. Cut into wedges like a pie and serve immediately, while the phyllo is still crackling and crisp.
recipes.tip: The egg-custard layer is the make-or-break element of pastilla. It must be a creamy, uniform custard, never scrambled eggs. Keep the heat at its absolute lowest, stir without pausing, and pour the eggs in slowly. The pastilla can be assembled up to 6 hours before baking and held in the refrigerator, covered loosely with plastic wrap. Serve it as the dramatic centerpiece of a Rosh Hashanah or special occasion dinner, cutting it at the table for maximum impact. For ambitious cooks, try adding a handful of dried edible rose petals to the almond mixture for an even more authentically Moroccan floral note.

recipes.title: Holishkes (Ashkenazi Stuffed Cabbage)
recipes.description: Tender cabbage leaves wrapped around a savory filling of ground beef and rice, simmered for hours in a sweet-and-sour tomato sauce. A beloved Sukkot tradition.
ingredients: 1 cup grape jelly (or 1/2 cup brown sugar)
directions: Two days before you plan to cook, place the entire head of cabbage, unwrapped, into your freezer. Let it freeze solid for a full 48 hours. This freeze-thaw method is far superior to the traditional boiling approach. When water inside the cabbage cells freezes, it expands and ruptures the cell walls. Upon thawing, the leaves become soft, pliable, and easy to roll without any of the scalding, tearing, and frustration that comes with trying to peel leaves from a boiling head of cabbage. Remove the frozen cabbage from the freezer and let it thaw completely in the refrigerator for 12 to 24 hours. Alternatively, if you did not plan ahead, core the cabbage with a sharp knife and place the whole head in a large pot of boiling water for 8 to 10 minutes, then carefully peel off the softened outer leaves with tongs, returning the head to the water as needed to soften the inner leaves.

Once the cabbage is thawed and pliable, carefully separate 12 to 14 of the largest, most intact leaves. Inspect each leaf for tears or holes, which will cause the filling to leak during cooking. Set aside any damaged leaves to use as a liner for the bottom of your pot later. Using a sharp paring knife held at a shallow angle, shave down the thick, raised central rib of each leaf until it is nearly flush with the rest of the leaf. This step is critical because a thick rib prevents the leaf from rolling evenly and creates a bulge that can cause the roll to unravel. Take your time here, as a well-prepared leaf rolls effortlessly while a poorly prepared one fights you at every turn.

Prepare the filling by combining the ground beef, uncooked rice, eggs, finely minced onion, salt, and pepper in a large mixing bowl. Use your hands to mix and knead the filling for a full 2 minutes until all the ingredients are evenly distributed and the mixture feels cohesive and slightly sticky. The eggs and the starch from the uncooked rice act as binders that hold the filling together during the long cooking process. The rice is added raw intentionally; it will absorb the braising liquid and steam to perfect tenderness inside the cabbage roll, effectively cooking from the inside out.

To assemble each roll, lay a prepared cabbage leaf flat on your work surface with the stem end closest to you. Place about 2 level tablespoons of the meat filling in a compact log shape at the stem end of the leaf, about 1 inch from the bottom edge. Fold the bottom edge of the leaf up and over the filling, then fold both sides inward toward the center like you are wrapping a burrito. Now roll the bundle tightly from the stem end toward the leaf tip, creating a snug, compact, cigar-shaped roll. The tighter you roll, the less likely it is to unravel during the long cooking time. Place each finished roll seam-side down to keep it sealed.

Line the bottom of a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven with any torn or damaged cabbage leaves. This liner serves two purposes: it prevents the bottom rolls from scorching against the hot pot, and it adds extra cabbage flavor to the sauce. Arrange the cabbage rolls seam-side down in the pot, packing them tightly together in a single snug layer. If you have more rolls than fit in one layer, create a second layer on top, placing the rolls perpendicular to the first layer for stability. The tight packing prevents the rolls from unraveling or floating as the sauce cooks.

In a separate bowl, combine the tomato sauce, diced tomatoes with their juices, grape jelly (or brown sugar), lemon juice, golden raisins if using, and a generous pinch of salt. Whisk or stir vigorously until the jelly is mostly dissolved and the sauce is uniform. The combination of grape jelly and lemon juice creates the classic Ashkenazi sweet-and-sour flavor profile that defines holishkes. Pour this sauce evenly over the cabbage rolls, making sure the liquid reaches the bottom of the pot and comes at least three-quarters of the way up the sides of the rolls. Add a splash of water if needed.

Place the pot over medium-high heat and bring the sauce to a gentle boil. You will see bubbles breaking the surface and the sauce will begin to simmer actively. Immediately reduce the heat to the lowest possible setting. Cover the pot tightly with a heavy lid. The goal from this point forward is the gentlest possible simmer, with only the occasional lazy bubble rising to the surface. Simmer for 3 full hours, resisting the urge to stir or disturb the rolls. Check the pot every 45 minutes to ensure there is still sufficient liquid; if the level has dropped significantly, add warm water, pouring it down the side of the pot rather than directly on the rolls.

After 3 hours, the holishkes are done when the cabbage is completely tender and almost translucent, the rice inside the rolls is fully cooked and fluffy when you cut a test roll open, and the sauce has reduced to a thick, glossy, deeply flavored sweet-and-sour glaze that coats the back of a spoon. The long, slow simmer is the entire point of this dish. It transforms a simple tomato sauce into something profoundly complex, as the sugars in the jelly caramelize slowly, the acid from the lemon mellows, and the meat and cabbage release their juices into the surrounding liquid.

Using a large spoon or spatula, carefully transfer 2 to 3 rolls per person to shallow bowls or plates, keeping them seam-side down. Ladle generous spoonfuls of the thick sauce over the top, making sure each roll is well-coated. The sauce is as important as the rolls themselves. Serve hot, with crusty bread to soak up the remaining sauce.
recipes.tip: The freeze-thaw method is the single best technique in this recipe. Plan ahead and put the cabbage in the freezer 2 full days before cooking day. It eliminates the dangerous, frustrating process of peeling leaves from boiling water and produces more uniformly pliable leaves. Holishkes actually taste better the next day after the sauce has had time to concentrate and permeate the rolls, making them an ideal make-ahead dish for Sukkot or Shabbat. Serve them with a side of mashed potatoes to absorb the extraordinary sauce. For an extra depth of flavor, add 2 tablespoons of apple cider vinegar and a bay leaf to the sauce before cooking.

recipes.title: Persian Fesenjan (Pomegranate Walnut Stew)
recipes.description: A deeply complex, velvety stew of chicken thighs braised in a sauce of finely ground toasted walnuts and pomegranate molasses. One of the most sophisticated dishes in the Persian Jewish repertoire.
ingredients: 3.5 cups (400g) walnuts, finely ground in a food processor
1/2 tsp saffron threads, ground and bloomed in 2 tbsp hot water
directions: Begin by toasting the ground walnuts, which is the step that transforms this stew from good to extraordinary. Place the finely ground walnuts in a large, dry skillet over medium heat. Stir them constantly with a wooden spoon, moving them around the pan without pause for 3 to 4 minutes. You will notice the color darkening from pale tan to a warmer, deeper brown, and the kitchen will fill with a rich, nutty aroma. Watch them carefully and do not walk away, because walnuts have a very high oil content and can go from perfectly toasted to acrid and burnt in less than 30 seconds. Toasting accomplishes two things: it drives off the raw, slightly bitter, tannic taste that untreated walnuts carry, and it develops deep, complex nutty flavor compounds through the Maillard reaction. Transfer the toasted walnuts to a bowl immediately to stop the cooking.

Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the finely minced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 to 6 minutes until the onion is soft, translucent, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. The onion provides the savory base upon which the entire stew is built. Add the turmeric and stir it into the onions for 30 seconds, just until the onion turns a vivid yellow and the spice becomes fragrant. Turmeric should be toasted briefly in fat to bloom its flavor but never cooked long enough to turn bitter.

Add the chicken thighs to the pot and sear them lightly on both sides, about 2 minutes per side. The goal here is not to develop a deep, dark brown crust as you would for a braise. Instead, you are simply setting the surface of the meat so it holds together during the long cooking process. The flavor of fesenjan comes from the walnut-pomegranate sauce, not from seared meat fond. Remove the chicken temporarily if it helps you work more easily.

Add the toasted ground walnuts to the pot along with 3 cups of water. Stir well, scraping up any bits from the bottom. Return the chicken if you removed it, nestling the pieces into the walnut mixture. Bring the liquid to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then reduce the heat to low. Cover the pot and cook for 1 full hour, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes. Stirring is critical because the ground walnuts have a tendency to settle to the bottom and scorch if left undisturbed. Each time you stir, use a flat-edged wooden spoon to scrape the bottom of the pot thoroughly. The walnut mixture will thicken gradually during this first hour as it absorbs water and releases its natural oils.

After 1 hour of covered simmering, stir in the pomegranate molasses, sugar, and the bloomed saffron with all of its soaking water. The sauce will transform dramatically, turning from a brownish-tan to a deep, stunning maroon color. This is the moment to begin tasting and adjusting the critical balance that defines fesenjan. The stew should be tangy from the pomegranate, slightly sweet from the sugar, deeply nutty from the walnuts, and subtly floral from the saffron. If the sauce tastes overwhelmingly tart, add sugar a teaspoon at a time. If it tastes too sweet or one-dimensional, add more pomegranate molasses a tablespoon at a time. This balancing act is the soul of the dish and separates a mediocre fesenjan from a transcendent one.

Remove the lid and continue simmering on the lowest possible heat for another 45 to 60 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. During this uncovered phase, the sauce will reduce and thicken considerably. You are looking for several visual and textural cues that tell you the fesenjan is ready: the color should be a deep, rich maroon, almost burgundy; the sauce should be velvety and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon without running off; and a layer of golden-amber walnut oil should glisten on the surface, which is a sign that the nuts have released their fat and the sauce is fully developed. The chicken should be meltingly tender, practically falling off the bone when nudged with a spoon.

Taste the sauce one final time and make any last adjustments to the sweet-sour balance. The flavors will continue to develop as the stew cools slightly, so err on the side of slightly more tart than you think is right. Transfer the chicken and sauce to a large serving platter or serve directly from the pot over a bed of fluffy, steamed basmati rice. Garnish generously with fresh pomegranate seeds, which provide a beautiful jewel-like visual contrast and a burst of fresh, juicy acidity against the rich, velvety sauce.
recipes.tip: Fesenjan is entirely about balance between three elements: the tartness of pomegranate molasses, the richness of toasted walnuts, and the sweetness of sugar. You must taste and adjust multiple times during the second hour of cooking, as the ratios shift as the sauce reduces and concentrates. This stew tastes even better the next day, making it an ideal make-ahead dish for Rosh Hashanah dinner. Pair it with saffron-scented basmati rice and a simple cucumber-yogurt salad to complement the richness. For ambitious cooks, try substituting duck legs for the chicken, as the gaminess of duck creates an even more complex pairing with the pomegranate-walnut sauce.

recipes.title: Ghormeh Sabzi (Persian Herb Stew)
recipes.description: Iran's national dish — a deeply herbaceous stew of slow-braised beef with mountains of fried fresh herbs, kidney beans, and the tangy punch of dried Persian limes.
ingredients: 2 lbs beef chuck, cut into 1.5-inch cubes
4 large bunches fresh flat-leaf parsley (about 4 cups chopped)
2 large bunches fresh cilantro (about 2 cups chopped)
1/4 cup dried fenugreek leaves (or 1 small bunch fresh, chopped)
1 can (15 oz) kidney beans, drained and rinsed
6-8 dried Persian limes (limoo amani), pierced with a knife
directions: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large Dutch oven or heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers. Add the diced onions and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they soften and turn golden. Push the onions to the sides of the pot and add the beef cubes in a single layer. Let the beef sear without moving for 2 to 3 minutes until a brown crust forms on the bottom, then stir and continue searing on all sides for a total of 6 to 8 minutes. Sprinkle the turmeric over the meat and stir to coat evenly. The turmeric provides the warm, golden color that is characteristic of Persian stews. Pour in 6 cups of cold water, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook for 1.5 hours until the beef is becoming tender but not yet falling apart. The beef will finish cooking during the second stage with the herbs.

While the beef simmers, prepare the herb mixture, which is the defining component of this dish and the step that separates an authentic ghormeh sabzi from an imitation. Wash all the herbs thoroughly in several changes of cold water to remove any grit or sand, which can ruin the entire stew. Spin them dry in a salad spinner or spread them on clean kitchen towels and pat them as dry as possible. Moisture is the enemy here because wet herbs will steam instead of fry in the next step. Using a sharp chef's knife, finely chop all the parsley, cilantro, dill, and green onions. You should end up with a massive, impressive mound of chopped green herbs that seems far too large for the pot. This is correct. The herbs will shrink by roughly 75 percent during frying.

This is the most important technique in the entire recipe. Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil in a large, wide skillet over medium heat. Add all of the chopped herbs and the dried fenugreek leaves at once. The pan will be heaping and overflowing, which is expected. Begin stirring and tossing the herbs frequently with a wooden spoon or spatula. Over the next 15 to 20 minutes, the herbs will undergo a dramatic transformation. They will first release a large amount of moisture and steam, then wilt and shrink significantly, and finally turn from bright, vivid green to a deep, dark, almost forest-green color. Keep stirring frequently to prevent burning and to ensure even cooking. This extended frying step is absolutely essential and must not be shortened or skipped. Raw herbs added directly to the stew will taste grassy, vegetal, and unpleasantly bitter. Fried herbs, by contrast, develop a concentrated, complex, almost savory-umami quality that is the heart and soul of ghormeh sabzi. The herbs should smell deeply aromatic and slightly toasty when they are ready.

Add the fried herbs to the pot with the simmering beef, scraping every last bit from the skillet. Take the dried Persian limes and pierce each one in 2 or 3 places with the tip of a sharp knife. This puncturing allows the tart, floral liquid inside the limes to seep into the stew during cooking. Add the pierced limes to the pot, pressing them gently to submerge them in the liquid. The dried limes are a non-negotiable ingredient. They contribute a tangy, slightly bitter, intensely citrusy flavor that is unlike anything else in cooking and cannot be approximated by fresh limes, lemon juice, or any substitute. Continue simmering the stew, partially covered, for another 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the drained and rinsed kidney beans to the pot and stir them in gently. The beans should be added at this later stage rather than at the beginning because they are already cooked and only need to simmer long enough to absorb the herb-infused braising liquid. Continue simmering for 30 more minutes, partially covered, stirring once or twice. During this final phase, the stew should thicken noticeably as the herbs continue to break down and the liquid reduces.

Taste the stew and season generously with salt and freshly ground black pepper.
