The finished ghormeh sabzi should be thick, deeply herbal, and complex, with the dried limes providing a distinctive tangy backbone. If the stew seems too thick, add a splash of water. If it seems too thin, remove the lid and simmer for another 10 to 15 minutes to reduce. Use a spoon to press gently on the dried limes, squeezing out their remaining juice into the stew for maximum flavor impact.

Serve the stew in shallow bowls over a generous mound of perfectly steamed basmati rice. The rice should be fluffy and separate, with each grain distinct, to contrast with the thick, rich stew. Place a dried lime in each bowl as a garnish. Adventurous eaters can bite into the lime for a burst of intense, tangy flavor.
recipes.tip: The fresh herbs must be fried for a full 15 to 20 minutes until they turn dark green. This single technique is what transforms raw, grassy greens into the deep, concentrated, almost meaty flavor base that defines ghormeh sabzi. Dried Persian limes are essential and truly cannot be substituted. They are available at Persian and Middle Eastern grocery stores, and online. This stew improves dramatically overnight, so consider making it a day ahead for Shabbat and reheating gently. Pair it with tahdig (crispy Persian rice) for the ultimate combination. For a more traditional version, use bone-in lamb shoulder instead of beef chuck.

recipes.title: Iraqi Kubbeh Bamia (Okra Soup)
recipes.description: Semolina dumplings stuffed with spiced meat, simmered in a sweet-and-sour okra and tomato broth. A beloved variation in the Iraqi kubbeh soup family.
ingredients: 1 lb ground beef, 1 onion (minced), 1 tsp baharat spice blend, salt and pepper (for filling)
1 lb fresh or frozen okra, trimmed
directions: Begin by preparing the soup base, which needs time to develop before the dumplings are added. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large, heavy-bottomed soup pot over medium heat. Add the diced onions and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they soften and become translucent. Add the minced garlic and stir continuously for 1 minute until it turns fragrant but has not taken on any color. Burnt garlic will introduce a harsh bitterness that will permeate the entire soup. Add the tomato paste and cook for another full minute, stirring to coat the onions and garlic. Cooking the tomato paste briefly in the oil caramelizes its sugars and removes the raw, tinny taste that uncooked paste can have.

Add the okra to the pot, handling it gently. If using fresh okra, leave the pods completely whole and intact. If using frozen okra, add it directly from the freezer without thawing. This is critical: do not trim, slice, or cut the okra in any way. Cutting okra exposes its mucilaginous interior, which will make the soup unpleasantly thick and slimy. Whole okra releases its thickening properties gradually and gently, creating a pleasant, silky body in the broth without any sliminess. Stir the okra gently into the onion mixture, taking care not to break apart any pods, and cook for 5 minutes to lightly coat them in the flavored oil.

Pour in 6 cups of water and add the lemon juice, sugar, and salt. The sweet-and-sour balance is the hallmark of kubbeh bamia and distinguishes it from the other soups in the Iraqi kubbeh family. Taste the broth at this stage and adjust the ratio. It should be noticeably tangy from the lemon with a pleasant undercurrent of sweetness from the sugar. Neither flavor should dominate. If it tastes too sour, add sugar a teaspoon at a time. If it tastes flat and sweet, add lemon juice a tablespoon at a time. Bring the broth to a gentle boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer.

While the soup base comes together, prepare the semolina dough for the dumplings. Place the fine semolina in a large mixing bowl. Add the 1/4 cup of oil and rub it into the semolina with your fingertips until the mixture feels like damp sand. Gradually add the warm water, mixing with your hands, until a smooth, pliable dough forms. It should hold together when squeezed but not feel sticky or wet. If it crumbles, add water a teaspoon at a time. If it sticks to your hands, add semolina a tablespoon at a time. Cover the dough with a damp cloth while you prepare the filling.

For the filling, heat a small skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and minced onion, breaking the meat up with a wooden spoon. Cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the beef is fully browned and no pink remains. Drain off any excess fat through a strainer. Add the baharat spice blend, salt, and pepper, stirring for 1 minute to toast the spices and distribute them evenly through the meat. Transfer the filling to a plate and spread it out to cool. Cold filling is significantly easier to work with when assembling the dumplings, so if you have time, place it in the freezer for 10 to 15 minutes.

Keep a bowl of water beside you and wet your hands thoroughly. This is the golden rule of kubbeh-making: wet hands prevent the semolina dough from cracking, sticking, and falling apart. Take a walnut-sized piece of dough and roll it into a smooth ball between your wet palms. Use your thumb to press a deep well into the center of the ball, rotating it as you press to create a thin-walled cup about 1/4 inch thick. If cracks appear in the walls, smooth them closed with wet fingers. Place 1 tablespoon of the cooled meat filling into the cup. Pinch the opening closed, smoothing the seam with wet fingers, and gently flatten the sealed dumpling into a thick patty about 2 inches in diameter. Repeat with all remaining dough and filling. You should get 15 to 18 dumplings.

Bring the soup broth back to a steady, active simmer. Drop the kubbeh dumplings into the simmering soup one at a time, adding no more than 5 at a time and waiting about 30 seconds between additions. This gradual approach prevents the broth temperature from dropping too quickly, which could cause the dumplings to fall apart before their exteriors set. Once all the dumplings are in the pot, reduce the heat to a gentle simmer. Cover the pot and cook for 30 minutes without stirring, which could break the delicate dumplings.

After 30 minutes, check the soup. The okra should be completely tender when pierced with a fork, the dumplings should be cooked through, slightly swollen, and firm to the touch, and the broth should have developed a thick, slightly viscous, silky texture from the okra's natural thickening properties. Taste the broth one final time and adjust the sweet-sour balance with additional lemon juice or sugar as needed. The flavor should have deepened and mellowed during the cooking process.

Serve the soup in deep bowls, giving each person 2 to 3 dumplings along with several pieces of whole okra and plenty of the fragrant broth. This soup is traditionally served as a first course for Shabbat dinner and is best eaten the day it is made, as the dumplings can become soft if stored in the broth overnight.
recipes.tip: Keeping the okra whole is the single most critical technique. Cut okra releases its mucilaginous interior and turns the soup unpleasantly slimy, while whole pods thicken the broth gently and maintain an elegant, pleasant texture. The soup base can be prepared several hours ahead and kept warm while you shape the dumplings, which is the most time-consuming step. Serve the kubbeh bamia as a dramatic opening course for a Shabbat dinner, followed by a simple grilled meat or rice dish. For ambitious cooks, try making a double batch of dumplings and freezing half of them uncooked on a parchment-lined tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. They can be dropped directly into simmering soup from frozen, adding just 5 extra minutes to the cooking time.

recipes.title: Yemenite Jachnun (Overnight Bread)
recipes.description: A rich, buttery, slow-baked bread that cooks overnight at extremely low heat, emerging deeply caramelized and sweet. Served for Shabbat morning breakfast with grated tomato and fiery zhug.
ingredients: 2 sticks (1 cup) unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
6-8 eggs in their shells (for cooking alongside)
Grated fresh tomato and zhug for serving
directions: In a very large mixing bowl, combine the flour, dark brown sugar, and salt, whisking them together so the sugar is evenly distributed. The brown sugar is important because it contributes to the deep, caramelized sweetness that develops during the overnight bake. Create a well in the center and pour in the lukewarm water. Mix with a wooden spoon until a rough, shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains visible. Turn the dough out onto a clean, unfloured work surface.

Knead the dough vigorously for a full 12 minutes. This is substantially longer than most bread recipes require, and the extended kneading is intentional. You need to develop an exceptionally strong gluten network that will allow the dough to be stretched paper-thin without tearing. Use the heel of your hand to push the dough away from you, fold it back over itself, rotate a quarter turn, and repeat. After 12 minutes, the dough should be very smooth, elastic, slightly shiny on the surface, and spring back immediately when poked with a finger. If the dough tears easily when you try to stretch a small piece, continue kneading for a few more minutes.

Cover the dough with a damp kitchen towel and let it rest on the counter for 30 minutes. This rest allows the gluten strands to relax, which makes the dough easier to handle in the next steps. Without this rest, the dough will fight you when you try to divide and shape it.

Divide the rested dough into 12 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a smooth, tight ball between your palms. Pour a generous amount of neutral oil into a shallow dish or baking pan. Roll each dough ball in the oil until it is completely slick and coated on all surfaces. The oil coating serves a dual purpose: it prevents the balls from drying out during the cold rest, and it lubricates the dough so it can be stretched paper-thin without sticking to itself or to your work surface. Arrange the oiled balls on a tray with space between them, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours and ideally overnight. The cold rest relaxes the gluten completely, firms the dough slightly, and makes the stretching process dramatically easier.

When ready to assemble, remove the dough balls from the refrigerator and let them sit at room temperature for 15 minutes to take the chill off. Generously oil a large, smooth work surface. Working with one ball at a time, place it on the oiled surface. Using your fingertips and the backs of your hands, gently stretch and pull the dough outward from the center, working your way around the edges. The dough should stretch willingly without tearing. Pull it into a paper-thin sheet approximately 17 by 20 inches. You should be able to see the surface beneath the dough, and it should be nearly translucent. Patience and gentleness are essential here. If the dough resists stretching or begins to spring back, walk away and let it rest for 5 minutes, then return to it. Forcing a resistant dough will tear it.

Using your hands or a pastry brush, spread a thin, even layer of the softened butter over the entire surface of the stretched dough, going all the way to the edges. The butter is what creates the flaky, laminated layers inside the finished jachnun and contributes to the rich, caramelized sweetness that develops during the overnight bake.

Fold the buttered dough into a compact package. First, fold the left third of the sheet toward the center. Then fold the right third over the left, creating a long, narrow rectangle. Now fold the top third down toward the center and the bottom third up over it, creating a smaller rectangular packet. Finally, roll this packet into a tight cylinder, tucking the seam underneath. The folding creates multiple alternating layers of dough and butter, similar to the principle behind puff pastry. Repeat the stretching, buttering, folding, and rolling process with each remaining dough ball.

Line a large, deep, heavy pot such as a Dutch oven or a deep stock pot with parchment paper, pressing it into the bottom and up the sides. Place several slices of stale bread in a flat layer on the bottom of the parchment-lined pot. This bread layer is critically important. It acts as an insulating barrier between the bottom jachnun rolls and the direct heat of the pot, preventing them from scorching and burning during the 12-hour bake. Do not skip this step. Arrange the rolled jachnun cylinders in the pot, fitting them snugly together in one or two layers. Nestle the raw eggs, still in their shells, into any gaps between and on top of the jachnun rolls.

Seal the pot tightly with a double layer of protection: first, press a sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil over the top of the pot, crimping it around the edges to create an airtight seal. Then place the heavy lid on top. This double seal traps all the moisture and heat inside, creating a steam environment that prevents the bread from drying out during the extremely long bake. Place the sealed pot in an oven preheated to exactly 200 degrees Fahrenheit. Bake for 12 hours overnight. Do not open the pot during this time.

The next morning, carefully remove the pot from the oven and lift the lid and foil. The transformation will be remarkable. The jachnun rolls will have caramelized to a deep, dark mahogany brown on the outside, while the interior will be soft, flaky, sweet, and almost pastry-like with distinct layers. The eggs will have turned a beautiful amber-golden color throughout, with creamy, custard-like yolks. These are known as huevos haminados, and their flavor is unlike any hard-boiled egg you have ever tasted.

Serve the jachnun immediately by unrolling each cylinder onto a plate, revealing the beautiful spiral layers inside. Accompany with the peeled golden eggs, a bowl of freshly grated tomato made by cutting a ripe tomato in half and grating it on the large holes of a box grater, discarding the skin, and a dish of zhug, the fiery Yemenite cilantro-chili paste. The traditional way to eat jachnun is to tear off pieces, dip them in the grated tomato, and follow with bites of egg.
recipes.tip: The bread slices at the bottom of the pot are the most critical small detail in this recipe. Without them, the bottom layer of jachnun will burn during the 12-hour bake and become inedibly bitter. The 4-hour cold rest on the oiled dough balls is what makes stretching them paper-thin physically possible, as it fully relaxes the gluten. Jachnun can be assembled the evening before and placed directly in the preheated oven before you go to bed, ready to serve for Shabbat morning brunch. For an ambitious twist, add a thin layer of date paste or silan between the butter layers before rolling for an even sweeter, more caramelized result.

recipes.title: Yemenite Kubaneh (Overnight Rolls)
recipes.description: Pull-apart butter rolls baked overnight at the lowest possible oven temperature. They emerge soft, golden, and impossibly tender for Shabbat morning.
directions: In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, sugar, yeast, and salt. Create a well in the center and pour in the warm water. Using a wooden spoon, mix from the center outward until a shaggy dough forms. Turn the dough out onto a clean, lightly floured surface and knead for a full 10 minutes. The dough should transform from rough and sticky to beautifully smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky — when you poke it with your finger, it should spring back slowly. This extended kneading develops the gluten network that gives kubaneh its characteristic pull-apart layers.

Place the kneaded dough in a lightly oiled bowl, turning it once to coat all sides. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and let it rise in a warm, draft-free spot for 1 to 1.5 hours until it has doubled in size. The ideal temperature for rising is around 78°F — if your kitchen is cool, place the bowl inside your oven with just the oven light on, which creates a gentle warmth of about 80°F.

While the dough rises, let the butter soften to room temperature if you have not already. It needs to be spreadable, like thick frosting — not melted and not hard. If your butter is cold, cut it into small pieces and leave it on the counter while the dough rises. You will need it very soft for the stretching step.

Divide the risen dough into 8 equal pieces. Working with one piece at a time (keep the rest covered), use your hands and generous amounts of softened butter to stretch the dough into a thin, nearly transparent rectangle on a buttered work surface. Do not use a rolling pin — the warmth and pressure of your hands, combined with the butter, coax the dough into paper-thin sheets without tearing. You should be able to see the shadow of your hand through the dough. This is the same principle as strudel dough.

Spread an additional thin layer of softened butter across the entire surface of the stretched dough. Fold the dough like a business letter — bottom third up, top third down — creating three layers. Then fold it in half again and roll it into a tight spiral or cylinder. Cut the cylinder in half to create two pieces. This folding and rolling process is what creates the dozens of flaky, buttery layers that define great kubaneh.

Generously butter a round 9-inch baking pan or cast-iron skillet — the butter on the pan creates the golden, caramelized crust that is considered the best part. Arrange all the dough pieces cut-side up in the pan, fitting them snugly together like a puzzle. They should touch each other and the sides of the pan so they will bake into a unified pull-apart bread. Cover with a clean towel and let rise for 45 minutes until the dough pieces are puffy and have expanded to fill any gaps.

Cover the pan very tightly with a double layer of aluminum foil — the seal must be airtight. This traps steam inside, which is what keeps the bread incredibly moist during the long overnight bake. A loose seal will let moisture escape and dry out the bread. Place the sealed pan in an oven set to its absolute lowest temperature — ideally 170°F to 200°F. Most ovens have a 'warm' setting that works perfectly.

Let the kubaneh bake overnight for 8 to 10 hours. The magic of this bread is the long, slow transformation: at low heat, the butter melts between the layers, the sugars in the dough gently caramelize, and the exterior develops a deep golden-brown color while the interior stays cloud-soft. In the morning, your kitchen will smell extraordinary.

Remove the foil and turn the kubaneh out onto a serving board — it should release easily if you buttered the pan well. The bottom (now the top) should be deeply golden and slightly caramelized. Pull the bread apart into individual rolls rather than cutting it. Serve immediately with freshly grated tomato (made by halving ripe tomatoes and grating the cut side on a box grater), zhug (Yemenite hot sauce), and hard-boiled eggs that can be placed in the pan beside the bread to cook overnight.
recipes.tip: The lowest possible oven temperature is everything — on most ovens, the 'warm' setting at 170°F is ideal. Any higher than 225°F and the bread will dry out rather than developing that impossibly tender, buttery texture. Kubaneh is the quintessential Yemenite Shabbat morning bread, traditionally started Friday afternoon before sundown and served Saturday morning. If you do not want to bake overnight, you can bake it at 300°F for 2.5 to 3 hours, though the texture will not be quite as ethereal. The grated tomato accompaniment is non-negotiable — it provides a bright, acidic contrast to the rich, buttery bread.

recipes.title: Yemenite Malawach (Fried Flaky Bread)
recipes.description: A rich, laminated flatbread with dozens of buttery layers that puff and crisp when pan-fried. Like a savory croissant in flatbread form.
directions: In a large bowl, combine the flour and salt. Add the warm water gradually, mixing with your hand until a soft, pliable dough forms. Turn the dough out onto a clean surface and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until it is very smooth, elastic, and does not stick to the surface. The dough should feel alive in your hands — supple and springy. If it tears when you stretch it, knead for another 2-3 minutes.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Oil your hands and the balls generously with vegetable oil, then place them on an oiled plate or tray. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and let them rest for at least 30 minutes, or ideally 1 to 2 hours at room temperature. This rest is essential — it relaxes the gluten, allowing you to stretch the dough paper-thin without it snapping back or tearing. Longer rest equals easier stretching.

Prepare your butter: soften it to a spreadable consistency, or use the traditional method of mixing equal parts softened butter and vegetable oil or margarine. The fat mixture should be very soft, almost the consistency of mayonnaise. You will need generous amounts for each layer.

Working on an oiled surface with oiled hands, take one dough ball and begin pressing and stretching it outward from the center, working in a circular motion. Gradually stretch it into a large, paper-thin rectangle or circle — as thin as you possibly can without tearing. You should be able to read a newspaper through it. If the dough resists, let it rest for 5 more minutes and try again. Spread a thin, even layer of the butter mixture across the entire surface.

Now create the layers: fold the left side of the dough to the center, then the right side over it (like folding a letter). Then fold the bottom third up and the top third down, creating a layered square or rectangle. Alternatively, you can roll it into a tight log and then coil the log into a spiral — both methods create the flaky layers that define malawach. Press the package gently to flatten it slightly.

Repeat with the remaining dough balls. Stack the folded dough pieces between sheets of parchment paper or plastic wrap. At this point, the malawach can be refrigerated overnight or frozen for up to 3 months — in fact, a night in the refrigerator firms the butter layers, which produces even flakier results.

When ready to cook, heat a large, heavy skillet (cast iron is ideal) over medium heat. No additional oil is needed — there is plenty of butter in the dough. Place one malawach in the dry pan and cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side, pressing down gently with a spatula. The bread should develop deep golden-brown spots and feel crispy on the surface while remaining soft and flaky inside. You will hear it sizzle as the butter layers melt and fry the dough from within.

Serve the malawach hot from the pan, accompanied by grated fresh tomato (grate a halved ripe tomato on a box grater, discarding the skin), zhug (Yemenite green chili sauce), and a hard-boiled egg mashed with salt and pepper. The combination of the rich, crispy bread with the cool, acidic tomato and fiery zhug is the classic Yemenite breakfast trifecta.
recipes.tip: The thinness of the stretch determines everything — the thinner you stretch the dough, the more delicate and flaky the layers will be. If you can see your hand through the dough, you have stretched it thin enough. Malawach freezes extraordinarily well: stack the uncooked, folded pieces between parchment paper in a freezer bag and cook directly from frozen, adding 1-2 extra minutes per side. In Israel, frozen malawach is a pantry staple — but homemade is incomparably better. For a savory filling, spread za'atar and cheese between the layers before folding.

recipes.title: Iraqi Ingeryieh (Sweet & Sour Eggplant Stew)
recipes.description: A layered casserole of tender braised meat, fried eggplant slices, caramelized onions, and tomatoes, all bound by a tangy tamarind-sweetened sauce.
ingredients: 2.5 lbs lamb or beef stew meat, cut into 1.5-inch cubes
2 large eggplants, cut into 1/2-inch thick rounds
2 lbs onions (about 4 large), sliced into thin rings
2.5 lbs ripe tomatoes, sliced into thick rounds
6 tbsp tamarind paste mixed with 1/2 cup warm water (or 6 tbsp tamarind liquid)
directions: Begin by preparing the eggplant. Cut it into 1-inch cubes, place them in a colander, and salt them generously. Let them sit for 30 minutes — the salt draws out bitter juices and excess moisture, which prevents the eggplant from absorbing too much oil during cooking and results in a firmer, better texture. After 30 minutes, pat the cubes dry with paper towels, pressing firmly to remove as much moisture as possible.

Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a large, deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches (do not crowd the pan), fry the eggplant cubes until they are golden brown on all sides, about 3-4 minutes per batch. Crowding the pan causes the eggplant to steam rather than fry, resulting in a soggy texture. Transfer the browned eggplant to a plate lined with paper towels.

In the same pan, add another tablespoon of oil and reduce the heat to medium. Sauté the diced onion for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it is deeply golden and sweet-smelling. The caramelized onion provides the sweet base that balances the tangy tamarind in this dish. Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Add the tomato paste to the onion mixture and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens slightly and smells less raw and more complex. This step is called 'blooming' the tomato paste — the heat drives off the tinny, metallic flavor of raw tomato paste and develops deeper, roasted tomato notes.

Stir in the tamarind paste (or pomegranate molasses), sugar, turmeric, salt, and pepper. Add the water or broth and bring the mixture to a simmer. The sauce should taste distinctly sweet-and-sour — adjust the sugar and tamarind until you achieve a balance that is tangy first, sweet second. This flavor profile is the hallmark of Iraqi Jewish cooking.

Return the fried eggplant cubes to the pan, nestling them into the sauce. If using meat, add the browned meat pieces now as well. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover the pot, and cook over low heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the eggplant is meltingly tender and has absorbed the flavors of the sauce. The sauce should reduce and thicken, coating the eggplant in a glossy, caramelized glaze.

Taste the stew and adjust the seasoning — you may need more salt, a squeeze of lemon to sharpen the tang, or a pinch more sugar to round out the sweetness. The final dish should have a complex, layered flavor where the sweetness, sourness, and savory elements are all distinct but harmonious.

Transfer to a serving dish and garnish with fresh chopped parsley or cilantro. Serve over fluffy white rice or alongside warm pita bread. Ingeryieh is even better the next day after the flavors have melded overnight — reheat gently and serve.
recipes.tip: The sweet-and-sour balance is the soul of this dish — taste the sauce before adding the eggplant and adjust until it sings. Tamarind paste is traditional and irreplaceable in flavor, but if you cannot find it, pomegranate molasses is the best substitute. This stew improves dramatically overnight in the refrigerator, making it an ideal Shabbat make-ahead dish. Serve it alongside crispy fried onions on top for textural contrast. For a heartier version, brown lamb shoulder cubes and simmer them in the sauce for an hour before adding the eggplant.

recipes.title: Authentic Ashkenazi Kishke (Stuffed Derma)
recipes.description: A traditional Shabbat side of seasoned flour and schmaltz stuffed into a casing and roasted until crispy on the outside and dense inside. The ultimate comfort food for the cholent pot.
ingredients: 3 feet beef casing (or aluminum foil for a modern version)
1 cup schmaltz (rendered chicken fat) or vegetable shortening
directions: If using traditional beef casing, rinse it very thoroughly under cold running water, flushing water through the inside of the casing several times to remove any salt or brine it was packed in. Then soak the casing in a bowl of warm water for 30 minutes to soften and make it pliable enough to stuff. Inspect the casing for any holes or tears, which would allow the filling to leak during boiling. If using the foil method, which produces results nearly identical to traditional casing and is far more accessible, skip this step entirely.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, matzo meal, finely minced onion, grated carrot, schmaltz (or vegetable shortening), paprika, salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Use your hands to mix and knead the ingredients together for 2 to 3 minutes until you have a thick, cohesive, slightly sticky paste. The schmaltz should be evenly distributed throughout the mixture, coating every particle of flour and matzo meal. Test the consistency by squeezing a handful: it should hold together in a solid clump without crumbling, but it should not be wet or runny. If it crumbles apart, add more schmaltz a tablespoon at a time. If it feels too wet, add flour a tablespoon at a time. The onion and carrot should be minced and grated as finely as possible, as large pieces can create weak spots in the casing.

If using beef casing, stuff the filling loosely into the softened casing using a sausage stuffer, a wide funnel, or your hands. This is the most critical instruction: leave at least 25 percent of the casing volume empty. The filling expands significantly during the boiling and roasting process, and if the casing is packed too tightly, it will burst open in the water, ruining the kishke entirely. Tie or sew both open ends closed securely with kitchen twine. If using the foil method, divide the filling mixture in half. Shape each portion into a compact log approximately 2 inches in diameter and 10 inches long, compressing it firmly with your hands. Place each log on a large sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil and roll it up tightly, twisting both ends like a candy wrapper to create a watertight seal. Double-wrap each log in a second layer of foil for extra protection against water seeping in during boiling.

Bring a very large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Carefully lower the kishke into the boiling water, reducing the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer. Cook for 1 full hour. This initial boil serves a crucial purpose: it sets the filling, partially cooks the flour and matzo meal so they bind together into a dense, cohesive mass, and renders some of the schmaltz, which bastes the interior from within. Do not let the water boil vigorously, as a hard boil can cause the casing or foil to rupture.

After 1 hour, carefully remove the kishke from the water using tongs or a slotted spoon, and let it drain on a cutting board for 5 minutes. If using the foil method, leave the foil on for now. Transfer the kishke to a roasting pan, placing it directly alongside your brisket, roast chicken, or into the cholent pot if you have one going. Roast in a 350 degree Fahrenheit oven for 1.5 hours, basting the kishke every 30 minutes with the pan juices from the surrounding meat. The exterior should become deeply browned, slightly crispy, and almost crackling, while the interior remains dense, savory, and moist. If roasting alongside a brisket, the kishke will absorb the meat's rendered fat and juices, developing an incredible, savory crust that is the most prized part.

Remove the kishke from the oven and let it cool for 5 minutes. If using foil, carefully unwrap it. The foil should peel away cleanly. Using a sharp knife, slice the kishke into rounds about 1 inch thick. The slices should hold their shape firmly, with a crispy, browned exterior ring and a dense, moist, savory interior.

Serve the kishke rounds alongside sliced brisket, or as part of a traditional Shabbat cholent spread. The kishke is the perfect accompaniment to rich, braised meats because its dense, starchy texture absorbs and complements the meat juices beautifully.
recipes.tip: The foil method is the single best tip for home cooks. It produces results virtually identical to traditional beef casing, is far easier to work with, and eliminates the risk of casing bursts. The critical rule is to never pack the filling tightly, whether using casing or foil, as the mixture expands substantially during cooking. Kishke can be boiled up to 2 days ahead and refrigerated, then roasted alongside your brisket or cholent on the day you plan to serve it. For the ultimate experience, nestle the boiled kishke directly into a cholent pot before the long overnight cook, where it will absorb the stew's rich, concentrated flavors for 12 or more hours. For a vegetarian version, substitute the schmaltz with coconut oil and increase the grated vegetables for added moisture.

recipes.title: Potato Knishes from Scratch
recipes.description: Crispy, golden-baked pastries with a thin, flaky dough wrapped around a rich filling of mashed potatoes and caramelized onions. A New York Jewish deli classic made at home.
ingredients: 3 lbs Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and quartered
Salt and white pepper to taste
Egg wash: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water
directions: Start with the dough, as it needs time to rest. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, and salt. In a separate bowl, beat the egg with the schmaltz (or oil), warm water, and vinegar. The vinegar may seem unusual, but it performs a crucial function: it tenderizes the gluten, producing a flaky, pastry-like dough rather than a tough, bready one. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and mix until a soft dough comes together.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 3 to 4 minutes — just long enough for it to become smooth and cohesive, not elastic and springy like bread dough. Over-kneading develops too much gluten and makes the dough tough. Wrap the dough in plastic wrap and let it rest at room temperature for at least 1 hour. This rest is essential — it relaxes the gluten and hydrates the flour, making the dough much easier to roll thin.

While the dough rests, make the filling. Boil the quartered potatoes in generously salted water until completely tender when pierced with a knife, about 18-20 minutes. Drain thoroughly and mash while still hot — a ricer or food mill produces the smoothest texture, but a regular masher works well. Do not use a food processor, which turns potatoes into a gluey paste.

In a skillet, cook the diced onions in schmaltz (or butter) over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes until deeply golden and caramelized. Do not rush this step — properly caramelized onions provide the depth of flavor that elevates knishes from simple potato pastry to something extraordinary. Stir only occasionally to allow browning. Add the caramelized onions and 1 beaten egg to the mashed potatoes. Season generously with salt and white pepper, then taste and adjust.

Preheat the oven to 375°F and line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Roll the rested dough on a floured surface into a very thin rectangle, about 1/8 inch thick. It should be nearly translucent in places — thin dough is key to the proper ratio of filling to crust. Brush the entire surface lightly with melted schmaltz or oil.

Spoon the potato filling in a long log along one long edge of the dough, leaving a 1-inch border. Roll the dough around the filling into a tight log, pinching the seam closed. Using a sharp knife, cut the log into individual knishes, each about 2 inches wide. Pinch the ends of each piece closed and place them cut-side up (filling visible) on the prepared baking sheet.

Brush the tops and sides of each knish with egg wash (1 egg beaten with 1 tablespoon of water). The egg wash is what gives knishes their beautiful, glossy, deep golden finish. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the dough is golden brown and crisp on the edges, and the exposed filling on top has developed a light golden crust.

Let the knishes cool for 5 minutes before serving — they are molten-hot inside straight from the oven. Serve with spicy brown mustard, which is the traditional and irreplaceable accompaniment. Knishes are excellent warm, at room temperature, or even cold the next day.
recipes.tip: The dough must be rolled paper-thin — thick dough produces heavy, bready knishes rather than the delicate, flaky pastry you want. Schmaltz (rendered chicken fat) in both the dough and filling is what makes knishes taste authentic, but butter or oil work well for a dairy or pareve version. These freeze beautifully before baking: freeze them on the sheet pan until solid, then transfer to a freezer bag. Bake directly from frozen, adding 5-7 minutes to the bake time. For a modern twist, add sauteed mushrooms and dill to the potato filling.

recipes.title: Jewish Etrog Jam (Post-Sukkot Tradition)
recipes.description: A precious, fragrant jam made from the etrog (citron) used during Sukkot. The week-long soaking and 7 boiling cycles remove the bitterness, leaving a floral, honey-like preserve.
ingredients: 2 quinces, peeled, cored, and diced (optional — adds body and pectin)
directions: This is a multi-day process that begins immediately after Sukkot ends, when the etrogim used during the holiday are no longer needed for ritual purposes. Rinse each etrog thoroughly under cold running water, gently scrubbing the bumpy surface with a soft brush to remove any wax, dirt, or pesticide residue. Place the whole, uncut etrogim in a large glass or ceramic container. Cover them completely with cold water, making sure every etrog is fully submerged. Place the container in the refrigerator. Every single day for 7 consecutive days, drain the old water completely and refill the container with fresh cold water. This extended soaking period is not optional and cannot be shortened. The etrog's extremely thick pith, which can be an inch or more deep, contains an extraordinary concentration of bitter compounds called limonoids. These must be gradually and patiently leached out through osmosis over the full week. Each daily water change pulls more bitterness out of the pith and replaces it with clean water.

After the full 7 days of soaking, remove the etrogim from the water. They will have softened slightly but will still be firm. Quarter each one lengthwise and carefully remove and discard any seeds. Now slice the peel and fruit together into thin strips about 1/4 inch wide, or dice them into small cubes. Do not separate the peel from the pith. In etrog jam, the entire fruit is used, including the thick white pith, which is the primary ingredient. The pith contributes body, pectin for setting, and, once its bitterness has been removed, a delicate, floral sweetness that is unique to citron.

Place the sliced citron in a large, heavy-bottomed pot and cover with fresh cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat and cook at a steady boil for 20 minutes. Drain the water completely through a colander, discarding it. Return the citron to the pot, cover again with fresh cold water, and repeat the boiling-and-draining process. You must do this a total of 7 times, each time with completely fresh water. Each boiling cycle removes another layer of residual bitterness that the soaking process did not fully eliminate. After each cycle, taste a small piece of the citron. It should become progressively milder. By the 7th boil, the citron should taste only mildly bitter and pleasantly floral, with no harsh, puckering quality.

After the final draining, return the softened citron to the clean pot. Add the fresh lemon juice, the diced quince if using, and all of the sugar. The quince is optional but highly recommended because it is naturally rich in pectin, which helps the jam set firmly, and it adds a subtle, rosy, floral flavor that complements the citron beautifully. Stir the mixture gently to combine, making sure the sugar coats all of the citron pieces. Let the mixture sit for 10 minutes so the sugar begins to dissolve and draw juice from the fruit.

Place the pot over low heat and cook, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon to prevent sticking, for approximately 2 hours. The mixture will go through several stages. First, the sugar will dissolve completely into the fruit juices, creating a thin syrup. Gradually, as the water evaporates, the syrup will thicken and become increasingly viscous. The citron pieces will turn from opaque white to beautifully translucent, almost jewel-like. You will know the jam is approaching readiness when the syrup sheets off the spoon rather than dripping, and when a candy thermometer reads 220 degrees Fahrenheit. If you do not have a thermometer, place a small plate in the freezer for 10 minutes, then drop a spoonful of the hot jam onto the cold plate. If it wrinkles when pushed with your finger after 30 seconds, it is ready. Remember that the jam will thicken considerably as it cools.

Carefully ladle the hot jam into sterilized glass jars, leaving about 1/4 inch of headspace at the top. To sterilize jars, submerge them in boiling water for 10 minutes and let them dry upside down on a clean towel. Wipe the rims of the jars clean with a damp cloth and seal tightly with the lids while the jam is still hot. As the jam cools, it will contract slightly and create a natural vacuum seal.

The finished jam will keep for several months in the refrigerator. It makes a uniquely beautiful and meaningful gift during Tu B'Shvat or at any time during the winter months. The flavor of properly made etrog jam is extraordinary and unlike any other preserve. It tastes of flowers, honey, and citrus, with a subtle, pleasant bitterness that adds complexity and prevents it from being cloyingly sweet.
recipes.tip: The 7-day soak and 7 boiling cycles are the non-negotiable foundation of this recipe. The etrog's thick pith contains bitter compounds so concentrated that no amount of sugar can mask them without this thorough extraction process. Patience over the full week is rewarded with a jam that tastes of flowers and honey rather than bitterness. The jam makes a deeply meaningful gift, especially during Tu B'Shvat, since it transforms the etrog used for the mitzvah during Sukkot into something lasting and delicious. Spread it on toast, dollop it onto yogurt, or serve it on a cheese board alongside aged hard cheeses. For ambitious cooks, try candying thin slices of the etrog peel in the leftover syrup to create an elegant confection coated in granulated sugar.

recipes.title: Persian Faloodeh (Rosewater Noodle Sorbet)
recipes.description: A refreshing frozen dessert of thin rice vermicelli suspended in a rose-scented sugar syrup, frozen to a delicate, icy slush. Topped with sour cherry syrup and lime juice.
ingredients: Sour cherry syrup (or pomegranate syrup) for topping
directions: Begin by making the syrup base, which needs time to cool completely. Combine the sugar and water in a saucepan and bring to a boil over medium-high heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely. Once boiling, reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. The syrup should be clear, slightly thickened, and coat the back of a spoon lightly. Remove from heat and stir in the rosewater and a squeeze of lime juice. Let the syrup cool to room temperature, then refrigerate until completely cold — at least 2 hours or overnight.

While the syrup chills, prepare the noodles. Bring a pot of water to a boil and cook the thin rice vermicelli according to package directions until just tender — usually 2-3 minutes. Be careful not to overcook them; they should be soft but still have some bite, as they will soften further during freezing. Drain immediately and rinse under cold water to stop the cooking and remove excess starch.

Using kitchen scissors or a sharp knife, cut the cooked noodles into short pieces, roughly 1 to 2 inches long. Long, uncut noodles tangle into an unmanageable block during freezing. The short pieces freeze individually and create the characteristic texture of faloodeh — icy strands that shatter and melt on the tongue.

Combine the cold syrup and the cut noodles in a shallow, freezer-safe container (a 9x13 baking dish works perfectly). The noodles should be completely submerged in the syrup. The shallow container is important — a deep container freezes unevenly, with rock-hard edges and a slushy center.

Place the container in the freezer. Every 30 to 45 minutes for the next 3-4 hours, remove the container and scrape the mixture vigorously with a fork, breaking up any large ice crystals and mixing the frozen edges into the still-liquid center. This repeated scraping is what gives faloodeh its distinctive granita-like, crystalline texture rather than becoming a solid ice block. The more diligently you scrape, the finer and more elegant the texture.

After 3-4 rounds of scraping, the faloodeh should be uniformly icy and granular, with the noodle strands frozen into the ice like little worms. It is ready to serve at this point, or you can let it freeze solid and re-scrape with a fork before serving.

To serve, scoop the faloodeh into chilled bowls or glasses. Squeeze fresh lime juice over each portion — the acidity is essential, cutting through the sweetness and making the rosewater sing. Drizzle with a thin stream of sour cherry syrup (the traditional Iranian accompaniment) or pomegranate molasses for a striking ruby-red contrast against the white ice.
recipes.tip: The rosewater quality makes or breaks faloodeh — use a high-quality, food-grade rosewater (the Cortas or Sadaf brands are excellent), and start with less than the recipe calls for, adding more to taste. Too much rosewater tastes soapy; the right amount is subtle, fragrant, and transporting. Faloodeh can be stored in the freezer for up to 2 weeks — re-scrape with a fork before serving to restore the texture. This is the perfect palate cleanser between courses at a Persian Shabbat dinner, or a light, refreshing dessert after a rich meal. For a dramatic presentation, serve it in frozen glasses with a single rose petal floating on top.

recipes.title: Sephardic Bimuelos (Hanukkah Fritters)
recipes.description: Simple, pillowy fried dough puffs soaked in warm honey syrup. The Sephardic answer to sufganiyot, these Ladino-Jewish fritters are faster and easier to make.
ingredients: 1 cup honey mixed with 1/4 cup warm water (for honey syrup)
directions: In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the warm water, yeast, and sugar. Let it sit for 5-10 minutes until the mixture becomes foamy and bubbly on the surface — this confirms your yeast is alive and active. If nothing happens after 10 minutes, your yeast is dead and you need to start over with fresh yeast and slightly cooler water (yeast dies above 110°F).

Add the flour, salt, and eggs to the yeast mixture and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon until a thick, sticky batter forms. This is not a dough you knead — it should be too wet and loose to handle with your hands, more like a thick pancake batter than bread dough. The consistency is key: when you lift a spoonful of batter, it should fall back slowly in thick ribbons, holding its shape for about 2 seconds before sinking back in.

Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and let the batter rise in a warm place for 1 to 1.5 hours until it has at least doubled in volume and the surface is covered in bubbles. The long rise develops both flavor and the airy structure that makes bimuelos light rather than dense. Do not rush this step — underproofed batter produces heavy, doughy fritters.

Fill a deep, heavy pot or Dutch oven with 3 inches of neutral oil (vegetable, canola, or sunflower) and heat it to exactly 350°F. Use a thermometer — guessing the temperature is the number one cause of failed fritters. Too hot and they burn on the outside while staying raw inside; too cool and they absorb oil and become greasy and sodden.

Dip two tablespoons in the hot oil briefly (this prevents sticking), then scoop a generous tablespoon of batter with one spoon and use the other to push it gently into the hot oil. The batter should sizzle immediately and begin puffing up within seconds. Fry 4-5 bimuelos at a time — more than that and the oil temperature drops too much, producing greasy results.

Fry for 2-3 minutes per side, turning them with a slotted spoon, until they are deeply golden brown all over and sound hollow when tapped. They should puff up to nearly double their size and feel very light for their size when lifted from the oil. If they are browning too fast on the outside, reduce the heat slightly.

Transfer the fried bimuelos to a plate lined with paper towels for about 30 seconds to drain excess oil, then immediately drizzle them with warm honey or roll them in cinnamon sugar while still hot. The heat of the fritters helps the honey soak in and the sugar adhere. Serve immediately — bimuelos are at their peak in the first 15 minutes after frying, while the exterior is still shatteringly crisp.

For a Hanukkah variation, dust the bimuelos with powdered sugar instead of honey, or serve them with a small bowl of warm chocolate sauce for dipping. The light, airy texture makes them irresistible no matter the topping.
recipes.tip: Oil temperature is everything with bimuelos — invest in a clip-on thermometer and maintain 350°F throughout frying by adjusting the heat as needed. These must be served immediately; unlike doughnuts, they do not hold well, so plan to fry them right before serving. The batter can be made up to 12 hours ahead and refrigerated — just let it come to room temperature and re-stir before frying. For an aromatic Sephardic twist, add 1/2 teaspoon of orange blossom water to the batter and drizzle the finished bimuelos with orange-blossom honey.

recipes.title: Modern Israeli Tahini Cookies
recipes.description: Crumbly, nutty cookies made with raw tahini and date syrup, coated in sesame seeds. A modern Israeli bakery staple that tastes like halvah in cookie form.
ingredients: 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, melted and slightly cooled
directions: Preheat your oven to 350°F and line two baking sheets with parchment paper. The parchment is important — tahini cookies have a high fat content and will stick aggressively to unlined pans. Position your oven racks in the upper and lower thirds for even baking.

In a large bowl, whisk together the tahini and sugar until smooth and well combined. The tahini should be well-stirred before measuring — tahini separates in the jar, with oil rising to the top and thick paste sinking to the bottom. Pour off the excess oil, stir vigorously until homogeneous, then measure. The consistency should be like thick peanut butter, not runny.

Add the egg, vanilla extract, baking soda, and salt, and mix until the batter is smooth and uniform. It will look slightly oily and feel dense — this is normal. The batter should hold its shape when scooped but still feel soft. If it seems too loose to scoop, refrigerate for 15 minutes to firm up.

Stir in the chocolate chips (or halva chunks, or both) and mix just until distributed. Do not overmix at this stage — overworking the batter after adding the egg activates too much gluten from the residual flour in the tahini and makes the cookies tough rather than tender and crumbly.

Scoop rounded tablespoons of batter onto the prepared baking sheets, spacing them about 2 inches apart. These cookies spread moderately during baking. Sprinkle each cookie with a generous pinch of flaky sea salt (like Maldon) and a few sesame seeds — the salt is not optional, it is what transforms these from merely good to extraordinary by contrasting the sweetness and amplifying the nutty tahini flavor.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are golden and set but the centers still look slightly underdone and soft. This is crucial: tahini cookies firm up significantly as they cool, so pulling them from the oven when they look 'done' means they will be overbaked once cool. The cookies should look almost too soft when you take them out.

Let the cookies cool on the baking sheet for 5 full minutes before transferring them to a wire rack. They will be extremely fragile when hot — the tahini fat needs to solidify to give them structure. After cooling completely, they should be crispy on the edges and chewy in the center with an intense, deeply nutty flavor.
recipes.tip: These are naturally gluten-free and flourless, which makes the quality of your tahini the single most important factor — use a pure, stone-ground tahini with no added oils or stabilizers (Soom and Al Arz are excellent brands). The cookies keep in an airtight container for up to 5 days and actually improve on day two as the flavors meld. Pair them with strong coffee or mint tea for a perfect afternoon treat. For a halvah variation, fold in 1/2 cup of crumbled halvah instead of chocolate chips — it melts into pockets of sweet, sesame-rich flavor.

recipes.title: Traditional Teiglach (Honey Clusters)
recipes.description: Small knots of dough boiled in a sticky honey syrup until golden and caramelized, then tumbled with nuts. An old-world Rosh Hashanah confection that predates honey cake.
ingredients: Shredded coconut or chopped walnuts for coating
directions: Begin by making the dough. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt, and ground ginger. Make a well in the center, add the eggs and vegetable oil, and mix with a fork until a soft dough forms. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead briefly — just 1-2 minutes — until smooth. Do not overwork the dough; you want it pliable, not elastic. If it feels sticky, add flour a teaspoon at a time.

Divide the dough into 4-6 ropes, each about 1/2 inch in diameter. Using a sharp knife, cut each rope into small pieces about the size of hazelnuts — roughly 1/2 inch each. Roll each piece into a ball between your palms. The pieces should be uniform in size so they cook evenly in the honey. Place the balls on a lightly floured surface and cover with a towel while you prepare the honey syrup.

In a large, heavy-bottomed pot (at least 4 quarts — the honey bubbles up dramatically), combine the honey and sugar. Place the pot over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar dissolves and the honey becomes liquid and thin. Bring the mixture to a gentle boil — watch carefully, as honey boils over easily and makes an enormous mess that is almost impossible to clean.

Once the honey is at a steady, gentle simmer, carefully drop the dough balls into the pot in batches, stirring gently with a wooden spoon to prevent them from sticking together. The honey will bubble vigorously when you add the dough — this is normal, which is why you need a large pot. Reduce the heat to maintain a very gentle simmer.

Cook the teiglach in the simmering honey for 25 to 35 minutes, stirring gently every 5 minutes. The dough balls will slowly absorb the honey, swell slightly, and transform from pale and doughy to deep golden amber. The honey itself will darken and caramelize. You will know they are done when the dough pieces are uniformly golden-brown throughout (break one open to check — the center should not be pale or raw) and the honey has thickened to a thick, syrupy consistency.

While the teiglach cook, prepare your finishing station. Line a sheet pan or large plate with parchment paper and have your chopped nuts (walnuts, almonds, or pecans) and ground ginger ready. If using candied cherries, have those prepared as well.

When the teiglach are done, remove the pot from heat. Working quickly (the honey will continue to thicken as it cools), spoon the teiglach and their honey onto the prepared parchment paper in a mound. While still warm and sticky, press the chopped nuts and dried fruit into the surface. Alternatively, you can mix the nuts directly into the pot before pouring. Shape the warm mass into a dome, log, or individual clusters by hand — wet your hands with cold water to prevent the hot honey from sticking to your skin.

Let the teiglach cool completely at room temperature for at least 2 hours. The honey will continue to firm as it cools, becoming chewy and almost toffee-like. Once cool, break or cut into pieces for serving. Store in an airtight container with parchment between layers.
recipes.tip: The temperature of the honey is critical — too high and the outside of the dough balls burn while the inside stays raw; too low and they absorb excess honey and become soggy. Maintain a gentle, steady simmer throughout. Teiglach keeps for weeks in an airtight container at room temperature, making them perfect for Rosh Hashanah preparation. They are traditionally piled into a tall pyramid on the holiday table, symbolizing sweetness and abundance. For an aromatic upgrade, add a cinnamon stick and 3-4 whole cloves to the honey while it simmers — remove them before serving.

recipes.title: Sephardic Date & Nut Charoset
recipes.description: A rich, dark paste of dates, figs, walnuts, and red wine, rolled into balls and coated in chopped nuts. The Sephardic alternative to the Ashkenazi apple-walnut version for the Passover Seder.
directions: Begin by preparing the dates. If using whole dates, pit them by slicing each date lengthwise with a small knife and removing the pit. Medjool dates are the gold standard for charoset — they are naturally soft, sweet, and have a complex caramel-like flavor that dried dates cannot match. If your dates feel firm or dry, soak them in warm water for 15 minutes to soften them, then drain thoroughly.

Place the pitted dates in a food processor along with the walnuts (or almonds, or a combination). Pulse 8-10 times until the mixture is coarsely chopped — you want a chunky, textured paste, not a smooth puree. The texture should resemble the mortar used between bricks, which is the entire symbolic point of charoset. If you do not have a food processor, chop everything finely by hand on a large cutting board.

Transfer the date-nut mixture to a bowl and add the sweet wine (or grape juice), cinnamon, ginger, and a pinch of cloves. Stir everything together with a fork, pressing and mashing gently to blend the flavors while maintaining the chunky texture. The wine serves two purposes: it loosens the mixture to a spreadable consistency and adds an unmistakable depth of flavor that grape juice alone cannot provide.

Taste the charoset and adjust the seasonings. It should be sweet from the dates, warm from the cinnamon, and slightly sharp from the ginger. Add more wine if the mixture is too thick, more cinnamon if it lacks warmth, or a tiny squeeze of lemon juice if it tastes flat and one-dimensional. The balance should lean sweet — this is a celebration food, after all.

Cover the bowl and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or ideally overnight. As the charoset sits, the wine absorbs into the dates and nuts, the spices bloom and harmonize, and the flavors meld into something far greater than the sum of its parts. Cold charoset tastes dramatically better than freshly made charoset.

Before serving, give the charoset a final stir and taste again — you may want to adjust seasoning after chilling. Transfer to a beautiful serving bowl and serve as part of the seder plate, or alongside matzah as a spread. Tradition holds that charoset should be rolled into small balls, but a rustic, scoopable version served in a bowl is equally traditional in many Sephardic communities.
recipes.tip: The quality of the dates determines everything — spring for Medjool dates, which have a natural caramel richness that elevates charoset from a simple condiment to a genuine delicacy. This charoset can be made up to a week before Passover and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator — the flavors only improve with time. Serve any leftovers spread on toast or matzah for breakfast, or swirled into yogurt. For a show-stopping variation, toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 5 minutes until fragrant before adding them — the toasted nuts add a deeper, more complex flavor.

recipes.title: Olive Oil Mandel Bread (Jewish Biscotti)
recipes.description: Twice-baked Jewish cookies studded with chocolate chips and toasted almonds. Similar to Italian biscotti but made with olive oil for a richer, chewier texture. Perfect for dunking.
directions: Preheat your oven to 350°F and line a large baking sheet with parchment paper. Mandel bread (the Jewish biscotti) is baked twice — first as a log, then sliced and toasted — so you will need this sheet pan for both stages.

In a large bowl, whisk together the olive oil, sugar, eggs, vanilla extract, and almond extract until smooth and emulsified. The olive oil is what distinguishes this from Italian biscotti — it produces a more tender, less brittle cookie, and adds a subtle fruity flavor that pairs beautifully with the almonds. Use a mild or medium olive oil, not a strong extra-virgin, which can taste bitter in baked goods.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Add the dry ingredients to the wet mixture in two additions, stirring with a wooden spoon or rubber spatula until just combined. The dough should be soft and slightly sticky but workable — if it is too wet to shape, add 1-2 tablespoons more flour. Fold in the sliced almonds (or chocolate chips, or both) and mix until evenly distributed.

Divide the dough in half. With lightly floured or oiled hands, shape each half into a log roughly 12 inches long, 3 inches wide, and about 3/4 inch thick. Place both logs on the prepared baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart as they will spread during baking. Flatten the tops slightly with your palm — the logs should be more rectangular than round for even slicing later.

Bake the logs for 25 to 30 minutes until they are firm to the touch, lightly golden on top, and just barely cracked on the surface. Remove from the oven and let them cool on the baking sheet for 10 to 15 minutes — this brief rest firms them up enough to slice cleanly. Do not skip this cooling step or the logs will crumble when you cut them.

Using a sharp serrated knife (a bread knife works perfectly), cut the logs on a slight diagonal into slices about 1/2 inch thick. Use a gentle sawing motion rather than pressing down, which crushes the cookies. Lay the slices flat on the baking sheet, cut-side up.

Return the sliced cookies to the oven and bake for an additional 8 to 10 minutes per side, flipping them halfway through, until both cut surfaces are golden and dry to the touch. This second bake is what transforms soft cookie logs into crispy, crunchy mandel bread. The cookies should feel dry and firm when done — they will crisp further as they cool.

Let the mandel bread cool completely on a wire rack. They will become crunchier as they cool. Store in an airtight container at room temperature — mandel bread keeps exceptionally well for 2-3 weeks, and the flavor actually improves after the first day as the olive oil mellows and the almond flavor deepens.
recipes.tip: The second bake is where mandel bread is made or broken — bake until the slices are genuinely dry and golden, not just warm. Underbaked mandel bread will be soft and cakey rather than properly crunchy. These are the ultimate make-ahead cookie: they keep for weeks in an airtight container and are perfect for shipping in care packages. Serve them with coffee, tea, or a glass of sweet wine for dunking. For a chocolate variation, dip one end of each cooled cookie in melted dark chocolate and let it set on parchment paper.

recipes.title: Spinach & Feta Noodle Kugel
recipes.description: A savory twist on the traditional noodle kugel, loaded with crumbled feta, cottage cheese, and fresh spinach, baked until the top is crispy and golden.
ingredients: 1 lb egg noodles (wide or medium width)
1 lb baby spinach, chopped and squeezed dry
1 medium onion, finely minced and sauteed in butter
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
directions: Preheat your oven to 375°F. Generously butter or oil a 9x13-inch baking dish. This kugel benefits from a well-greased pan — the edges become golden and crispy, providing a wonderful textural contrast to the creamy interior.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the egg noodles until just al dente — about 1 minute less than the package recommends. The noodles continue cooking in the oven and will become mushy if fully cooked at this stage. Drain them thoroughly and toss with a tablespoon of olive oil to prevent clumping. Set aside.

While the noodles cook, prepare the spinach filling. If using fresh spinach, wilt it in a hot pan with a splash of water for 2-3 minutes until completely collapsed, then drain in a colander and squeeze out every drop of moisture by pressing it firmly with the back of a spoon. Excess water from spinach is the enemy of kugel — it makes the interior soggy and prevents proper binding. If using frozen spinach, thaw it completely and wring it out in a clean kitchen towel until absolutely dry.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the ricotta cheese, crumbled feta, beaten eggs, sour cream, salt, pepper, and a generous grating of nutmeg. The nutmeg is essential — it has a natural affinity for both spinach and cheese, and transforms the filling from flat to sophisticated. Whisk everything until smooth and uniform.

Add the drained, squeezed spinach and the cooked noodles to the cheese mixture. Fold everything together gently but thoroughly, using a rubber spatula and lifting from the bottom to ensure every noodle is coated and the spinach is evenly distributed throughout. The mixture should look like a creamy, green-flecked mass.

Pour the mixture into the prepared baking dish and spread it evenly with a spatula. Scatter additional crumbled feta over the top — these pieces will bake into golden, salty morsels on the surface. If desired, sprinkle with a light dusting of paprika for color.

Bake uncovered for 35 to 40 minutes until the top is golden brown and the center is set — it should not jiggle when you shake the pan. The edges will be slightly puffed and pulling away from the sides of the dish. If the top is browning too quickly, tent with foil for the last 10 minutes.

Let the kugel rest for 10 to 15 minutes before cutting into squares. This resting time allows the egg custard to set fully, resulting in clean, defined slices rather than a sloppy collapse. Serve warm or at room temperature — this kugel is equally good both ways.
recipes.tip: Squeezing every last drop of moisture from the spinach is the single most important step — wet spinach produces a watery, collapsed kugel that falls apart when sliced. This kugel is a Shavuot staple and makes an excellent brunch dish year-round. It can be assembled up to 24 hours in advance and refrigerated before baking — add 5-10 minutes to the baking time if baking from cold. For a richer version, add 1/2 cup of grated Parmesan to the cheese mixture and sprinkle more on top before baking.

recipes.title: Bukharan Bakhsh (Green Herb Pilaf)
recipes.description: A fragrant Central Asian pilaf where sushi rice is buried under a blizzard of hand-chopped cilantro and dill, then sealed under paper towels and a tight lid to steam into perfectly distinct, herb-scented grains.
ingredients: 2 cups sushi or round-grain rice, rinsed until water runs clear
1 lb beef or lamb, hand-chopped into small pieces
1 large bunch fresh cilantro, finely chopped
1 large bunch fresh dill, finely chopped
directions: Heat the olive oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and sauté for 5 minutes until softened and beginning to turn golden at the edges.
Add the hand-chopped meat and sear, stirring frequently, until the meat is browned on all sides and the onions are deeply caramelized, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the rinsed rice and toss to coat every grain with the oil and meat juices. Toast for 1 minute, stirring constantly.
Pour in the boiling water and add the salt. Bring to a boil uncovered and cook for about 10 minutes until the water level has evaporated down to the level of the rice.
Add all the chopped cilantro and dill and gently fold into the rice. Do not over-stir — the goal is to distribute the herbs while keeping the rice grains intact.
Place a double layer of paper towels directly over the surface of the rice, then press the lid on as tightly as possible. Reduce the heat to the absolute lowest setting and cook for 20 minutes.
Turn off the heat and let the pot stand, still covered, for another 20 minutes. Remove the lid and paper towels, then fluff the rice gently with a fork before serving.
recipes.tip: Placing paper towels under the lid is a Bukharan secret; they absorb condensation that would otherwise drip back onto the rice, ensuring every grain remains distinct and fluffy rather than mushy.

recipes.title: Syrian Bazargan (Bulgur & Tamarind Salad)
recipes.description: A striking Syrian salad of medium bulgur soaked in tamarind paste and lemon juice, tossed with toasted walnuts and roasted red peppers — a dish where tangy, earthy, and sweet flavors are held in perfect tension.
ingredients: 2 cups medium-ground bulgur, rinsed and drained three times
2 roasted red bell peppers, peeled and finely diced
1 cup walnuts, toasted and roughly chopped
1 tsp ground cumin, toasted 30 seconds in a dry pan
directions: Rinse the bulgur three times in cold water, draining thoroughly each time. Place the drained bulgur in a large mixing bowl.
Add the tamarind paste, tomato paste, lemon juice, diced roasted peppers, diced onion, toasted walnuts, toasted cumin, salt, and red pepper flakes to the bulgur. Mix everything together thoroughly.
Cover the bowl and let the mixture rest at room temperature for 1 full hour. During this time the bulgur will absorb the tamarind and lemon juice and hydrate fully.
Stir in the oil and mix to combine. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve cold or at room temperature.
recipes.tip: Tamarind provides a deep 'dark' acidity that vinegar cannot match. Toasting the cumin for 30 seconds before adding it creates a flavor bridge between the earthy walnuts and the tart tamarind.

recipes.title: Ashkenazi Kreplach (Meat Dumplings)
recipes.description: Tender three-cornered pasta dumplings filled with richly seasoned ground brisket and caramelized onions cooked in schmaltz, simmered until plump and silky and served bobbing in golden chicken soup.
ingredients: 1 cup cooked beef brisket or pot roast, ground or very finely chopped
1 large onion, finely diced and caramelized in 2 tbsp schmaltz or oil
directions: Make the dough: combine flour, eggs, oil, salt, and enough cold water to bring the dough together. Knead on a floured surface for 5 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in plastic and rest 30 minutes.
Prepare the filling: grind or very finely chop the cooked meat. Combine with the caramelized onions, egg, salt, pepper, and paprika. Mix until uniform. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Roll the dough very thin on a floured surface — about 1/8 inch thick. Cut into 3-inch squares.
Place 1 teaspoon of filling in the center of each square. Fold one corner diagonally to create a triangle. Press the edges firmly together, dampening with a wet finger if they won't seal.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the kreplach in batches for 12–15 minutes until the dough is tender and cooked through. Remove with a slotted spoon and serve in hot chicken soup.
recipes.tip: If the dough is dry, dampen edges with a finger dipped in water. A perfect kreple should have thin, translucent dough that showcases the rich, dark filling inside.

recipes.title: Yemenite Hilbe (Fenugreek Dip)
recipes.description: A pale, frothy, gelatinous paste made from long-soaked fenugreek seeds whipped with zhug and lemon — a prebiotic powerhouse and the essential condiment of the Yemenite table.
ingredients: 2 tbsp zhug (green or red Yemenite chili paste)
directions: Place the ground fenugreek in a bowl and pour 1/2 cup of cold water over it. Stir briefly, then cover and let soak for at least 3 hours or overnight. Drain off any excess water that has not been absorbed.
Transfer the soaked fenugreek to a blender or use an immersion blender. Add the remaining 1/2 cup cold water, the zhug, lemon juice, and salt.
Blend or whisk vigorously until the mixture becomes thick, pale, frothy, and takes on a gelatinous, mousse-like consistency. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve immediately alongside Yemenite soups, flatbreads, or as a condiment with any Yemenite meal.
recipes.tip: Fenugreek is naturally bitter. The long soak is essential because it draws out the bitter tannins. The resulting froth is a prebiotic powerhouse that perfectly cuts through the fat of Yemenite soups.

recipes.title: Sephardic Aggristada Fish (Lemon-Egg Sauce) — Classic
recipes.description: A detailed classic preparation of pan-fried white fish draped in a luminous, slowly cooked lemon-egg sauce that thickens to the consistency of heavy cream — the signature dish of Syrian and Sephardic Shabbat tables.
ingredients: 2 lbs firm white fish fillets (cod, halibut, or sea bass)
2 eggs, beaten, for coating the fish
directions: Season the fish fillets with salt and pepper. Dredge in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in beaten egg.
Heat a generous layer of neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Pan-fry the fish fillets until deeply golden on both sides, about 3 minutes per side. Remove to a platter and set aside.
For the sauce: whisk the 4 eggs in a bowl until fully blended and slightly frothy.
In a small saucepan, whisk together the warm water and flour until completely smooth with no lumps. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a medium saucepan to catch any remaining lumps.

Add the oil, lemon juice, and salt to the strained mixture. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, for 10–12 minutes until the sauce thickens to the consistency of heavy cream.

Slowly drizzle about 1/4 cup of the hot sauce into the beaten eggs, whisking constantly to temper them. Then pour the tempered egg mixture back into the saucepan while stirring. Cook another 2 minutes until the sauce is glossy and thick. Pour over the fried fish and serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.tip: Never let the sauce boil or the eggs will curdle. If the sauce begins to separate, whisk in a tablespoon of cold water immediately to lower the temperature and re-emulsify.

recipes.title: Syrian Muhammara (Walnut-Pepper Dip)
recipes.description: A bold, textured Syrian dip of roasted red peppers and coarsely ground walnuts bound with pomegranate molasses — smoky, sweet, and faintly spiced, with the perfect contrast between silky and crunchy.
ingredients: 3 large red bell peppers, roasted, peeled, and seeded
3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, plus more for serving
Pinch of cayenne or red pepper flakes
directions: Place the toasted walnuts in a food processor and pulse until they reach the texture of coarse sand. Be careful not to over-process into a paste.
Add the roasted, peeled peppers, pomegranate molasses, lemon juice, garlic, cumin, and cayenne. Pulse several times until the mixture is semi-smooth but still has visible walnut pieces.
Fold in the breadcrumbs with a spatula — these absorb excess moisture and give the dip its characteristic thick, scoopable body.
Drizzle with olive oil, season with salt, and stir to combine. Transfer to a serving bowl, drizzle more olive oil over the top, and serve with pita or flatbread.
recipes.tip: Do not over-process. The beauty of Muhammara is the contrast between the silky roasted peppers and the crunchy, oily walnut pieces. Pulse rather than blend.

recipes.title: Moroccan Fish Patties (Ktzitzot Dagim)
recipes.description: Spiced fish patties simmered directly in a fiery harissa tomato sauce — a Moroccan Shabbat essential where the fish absorbs every drop of the fragrant, garlicky broth as it cooks.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lbs ground white fish (cod, tilapia, or halibut)
1/2 cup breadcrumbs (use matzo meal for Passover)
directions: In a large bowl, combine the ground fish, breadcrumbs, egg, parsley, cumin, paprika, and salt. Mix until uniform. Form into 2-inch balls and set aside on a plate.
Heat the olive oil in a wide, deep skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the harissa paste and cook 30 seconds more.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and water. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook the sauce for 10 minutes until slightly reduced.

Gently lower the fish patties into the simmering sauce one at a time. Cover the pan with a lid and simmer for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. The steam will cook the interior of each patty as the sauce reduces around them.
Serve warm with crusty bread or over rice.
recipes.tip: The key to Moroccan fish patties is letting them cook fully in the sauce without lifting the lid — steam finishes the interior while the sauce reduces around them.

recipes.title: Iraqi Kubbeh Hamusta (Sour Chard Soup)
recipes.description: Semolina dumplings stuffed with spiced ground beef, simmered in a bracingly sour soup of Swiss chard, zucchini, and lemon — a beloved Iraqi variation that balances richness and brightness in every bowl.
ingredients: 1 large bunch Swiss chard, stems and leaves separated
directions: Make the dough: combine semolina, oil, warm water, and salt. Knead for 2–3 minutes until a smooth, pliable dough forms. Cover with a damp towel and rest 10 minutes.
Make the filling: mix ground beef, minced onion, baharat, and salt until sticky and uniform. Refrigerate while you start the soup.

Start the soup: heat olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Sauté the diced onion and sliced chard stems for 5 minutes until softened. Add minced garlic and cook 1 minute more. Add the water and diced zucchini. Bring to a boil.

Shape the kubbeh: with wet hands, flatten a walnut-sized piece of dough into a thin disc. Place 1 teaspoon of meat filling in the center. Bring the edges up and around the filling, sealing completely, then gently flatten into a round disc.

Once the soup is boiling, gently drop the kubbeh discs in one at a time. Add the chard leaves and lemon juice. Reduce heat to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 30 minutes. Season with salt to taste.
recipes.tip: Semolina continues to absorb water as it sits. If your dough cracks while stuffing, add a tablespoon of water; if it's too sticky, keep your hands wet while shaping.

recipes.title: Bukharan Osh Sovo (Overnight Slow-Cooked Rice)
recipes.description: A magnificent Bukharan layered pilaf of seared beef chuck, carrots, prunes, and jasmine rice, baked sealed overnight at the lowest possible temperature until the bottom becomes a golden crust and every layer perfumes the next.
ingredients: 2 lbs beef chuck, cut into large pieces
directions: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over high heat. Sear the beef in batches until dark brown on all sides, creating a rich fond. Remove the meat and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onions and carrots over medium heat until golden, about 10 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 1 minute. Add the prunes.

Return the seared meat to the pot. Level the surface and top with the rinsed rice, spreading it evenly. Carefully pour the water down the side of the pot so as not to disturb the rice layer. Add salt and pepper.
Bring to a boil uncovered, then simmer on low for 20 minutes until the surface water is absorbed.
Cut a piece of parchment paper to fit directly on top of the rice, pressing it down. Seal with a tight-fitting lid. Bake in an oven at 200°F for 10–12 hours.
To serve, run a spatula around the edges, invert onto a large platter so the caramelized bottom crust is on top, and serve family-style.
