recipes.tip: The Maillard reaction is key here. Searing the beef until nearly dark brown creates a 'fond' at the bottom that will infuse the entire rice dish with deep, meaty umami during the long overnight bake.

recipes.title: Syrian Cherry Meatballs (Kibbeh Geraz)
recipes.description: Tiny lamb or beef meatballs simmered in a stunning sweet-and-sour sauce of sour cherries and pomegranate molasses — the ultimate expression of Syrian agrodolce cooking.
ingredients: 1 cup sour cherry jam or pitted sour cherries
directions: Combine the ground meat with allspice and salt. Mix well and form into 1-inch balls. Heat a dry skillet over medium-high heat and pan-fry the meatballs in batches, turning until browned on all sides. Set aside.
Combine the cherry jam, pomegranate molasses, lemon juice, and water in a medium pot. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the sauce is slightly syrupy.
Add the browned meatballs to the sauce. Simmer over medium-low heat, partially covered, for 15 minutes until the meatballs are cooked through and the sauce has thickened to a glossy glaze.
Taste and adjust — add more pomegranate molasses for acidity or a pinch of sugar to balance. Serve over pita or rice.
recipes.tip: Syrian cuisine is defined by agrodolce (sweet and sour). If the sauce is too sweet, add a dash more pomegranate molasses; the acidity provides the 'snap' that prevents the lamb from feeling too heavy.

recipes.title: Moroccan S'china with Wheat Berries
recipes.description: The Moroccan overnight Shabbat hamin built around whole wheat berries sealed in cheesecloth, simmering alongside brisket, chickpeas, and caramel-glazed eggs for over eight hours until everything is impossibly tender.
ingredients: 2 lbs beef chuck, cut into large pieces
6 whole eggs in their shells, scrubbed
1 cup wheat berries, placed in a cheesecloth bag with 3 whole cloves
directions: In a large heavy pot, caramelize 1/4 cup of sugar over medium heat until it turns amber. Add the soaked chickpeas and onions and stir to coat.
Sear the beef chuck separately in oil until well-browned on all sides. Transfer to the pot along with the marrow bones, potatoes, and whole unpeeled eggs.
Tuck the cheesecloth bag of wheat berries and cloves into the pot. Mix the silan, cumin, turmeric, and chili flakes into the 8 cups of water, then pour over everything in the pot.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer. Cover tightly and cook at 230°F in the oven overnight for 8–10 hours.
To serve, remove the cheesecloth bag and peel the eggs — they will have turned into creamy, caramel-colored gems. Serve everything together in deep bowls.
recipes.tip: The whole eggs in their shells cook overnight and transform into creamy, caramel-colored gems — a Moroccan Shabbat delicacy prized alongside the soft, nutty wheat berries.

recipes.title: Iraqi Spayty (Chicken Coconut Curry)
recipes.description: A lesser-known Iraqi-Jewish gem: whole chicken pieces simmered in fragrant coconut cream with bamboo shoots, turmeric, and ginger — a golden, warming curry that reflects the spice trade influences of the Babylonian diaspora.
directions: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Add the diced onions and cook for 5 minutes until soft. Add the turmeric, ginger, and coriander and stir for 1 minute to bloom the spices in the oil.
Add the chicken pieces and sear on all sides until lightly golden, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the coconut cream and add the drained bamboo shoots. Stir to combine, season with salt.
Cover the pot and simmer over medium-low heat for 45–60 minutes until the chicken is completely tender and falling off the bone. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve over white rice.
recipes.tip: Blooming the spices in the oil before adding any liquid is the key to this dish's intense golden color and deep flavor — skip this step and the curry will taste flat.

recipes.title: Syrian Stuffed Zucchini with Dried Fruit
recipes.description: Hollowed zucchini stuffed with spiced beef and rice, simmered in a sweet-tart sauce of tomatoes, apricots, and prunes — a Sukkot and Shabbat classic that celebrates the season's harvest abundance.
directions: Cut the tops off the zucchinis and hollow them out using a long vegetable corer, leaving walls about 1/4-inch thick. Reserve the scooped flesh for another use.
Combine the ground beef, rinsed rice, allspice, and salt. Mix well. Stuff each zucchini 3/4 full — the rice will expand and would cause the zucchini to burst if overfilled.
In a wide pot, stir the tomato paste into the water over medium heat. Add the chopped apricots, prunes, sugar, and lemon juice. Bring to a simmer.

Nestle the stuffed zucchinis into the sauce. Cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 45 minutes, turning the zucchinis once halfway through, until the rice is fully cooked and the sauce has thickened. Season with salt.
recipes.tip: Fill the zucchini only 3/4 full — the rice expands as it cooks and a tightly packed zucchini will burst and fall apart in the pot.

recipes.title: Ashkenazi Sweet and Sour Tongue
recipes.description: Slow-boiled beef tongue, peeled while hot, sliced, and braised in a glossy sweet-and-sour sauce of ketchup, ginger ale, raisins, and brown sugar — a beloved Ashkenazi delicacy that rewards patience.
ingredients: 1 cup ginger ale or dry white wine
directions: Place the tongue in a large pot with the onions, carrots, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Cover with cold water. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 2.5–3 hours until the tongue is fork-tender.
Remove the tongue from the pot while still hot. Immediately peel off the thick outer skin — it will slip off easily while warm but becomes nearly impossible to remove as it cools.
Slice the peeled tongue into 1/2-inch rounds.

Combine all sauce ingredients in a wide pot and bring to a simmer. Add the tongue slices and cook over medium-low heat for 1 hour, turning occasionally, until the tongue is glazed and the sauce is thick. Adjust seasoning.
recipes.tip: The tongue must be peeled while still hot — as it cools, the outer membrane bonds to the meat and becomes nearly impossible to remove cleanly.

recipes.title: Israeli Pletzl (Ashkenazi Onion Flatbread)
recipes.description: A chewy, dense Ashkenazi flatbread blanketed in slow-caramelized onions and poppy seeds — halfway between a bialy and a focaccia, baked at high heat until the edges char and the onions turn jammy and sweet.
directions: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, salt, warm water, and oil. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1.5 hours until doubled.

While the dough rises, cook the diced onions in olive oil over medium heat for 20 minutes, stirring regularly, until deeply golden and soft. Stir in the poppy seeds and kosher salt. Set aside to cool.
Preheat the oven to 450°F. Line a large baking sheet with parchment.
Stretch the dough into a 10x14-inch rectangle directly on the parchment-lined pan. Prick the entire surface all over with a fork — this prevents the dough from rising into a loaf.
Spread the onion and poppy seed mixture evenly over the surface. Bake at 450°F for 15–18 minutes until the edges are dark golden and slightly charred. Cut into squares and serve warm.
recipes.tip: Pricking the dough (docking) prevents it from rising like a loaf, creating the dense, chewy texture typical of traditional bialys. Using unbleached flour will give you a better pull and artisanal crust.

recipes.title: Yemenite Lachuch (Spongy Pancake Bread)
recipes.description: A thick, fermented batter cooked on one side only until the top is riddled with hundreds of tiny holes and completely dry — spongy, slightly tangy, and built to soak up Yemenite soups and honey.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp baking powder (added just before cooking)
directions: Blend the flour, yeast, sugar, salt, and water together until completely smooth, about 2 minutes. Cover and let the batter rest at room temperature for 1 hour until bubbles appear on the surface.
Stir in the baking powder just before cooking.
Heat a non-stick skillet over medium-high heat. Do not add any oil or butter. Pour 1/2 cup of batter into the cold or cool skillet and turn the heat to medium-high.
Cook without flipping for 3–4 minutes until the entire top surface is covered with holes and looks completely dry and set. Do not flip.
Remove the lachuch and immediately run the skillet under cold water to cool it down before making the next one. This thermal shock is essential for the signature bubbly texture.
Serve warm alongside soup or with honey and butter.
recipes.tip: Starting with a cool pan and cooling it between each pancake is mandatory. This thermal shock ensures the batter doesn't set too quickly, allowing the characteristic bubbles to form and reach the surface.

recipes.title: Ethiopian Dabo (Ritual Honey Bread)
recipes.description: A sacred Ethiopian Jewish bread sweetened with honey and baked in a Dutch oven or low oven overnight, emerging with a thick, protective crust and a dense, cake-like, golden interior.
directions: Combine the flour, sugar, salt, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the honey, warm water, and soft butter. Mix until a shaggy dough forms.
Turn out onto a floured surface and knead for 10 minutes until smooth and supple. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rest for 1 hour.
Shape the dough into a single large round loaf. Wrap in parchment paper.

Bake in a preheated Dutch oven at 350°F for 1 hour until the crust is deep golden brown and a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Alternatively, bake at 200°F overnight for the traditional method.
Cool on a wire rack before slicing.
recipes.tip: Traditionally, Dabo was baked in the ground under hot coals. Using a preheated Dutch oven mimics this radiating heat, creating a thick, protective crust and a dense, cake-like interior.

recipes.title: Ashkenazi Arbes (Ritual Peppery Chickpeas)
recipes.description: Cooked-until-creamy chickpeas showered with coarse black pepper and kosher salt while still steaming hot — a deceptively simple Ashkenazi tradition served in paper cones at Purim and on Shabbat.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in cold water
2 tsp coarse black pepper (or more to taste)
directions: Drain the soaked chickpeas and place in a large pot. Cover with fresh cold water by at least 3 inches. Add the baking soda.
Bring to a boil, skimming any foam that rises. Reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 45–60 minutes until the chickpeas are very soft — they should mash easily between two fingers.
Drain the chickpeas thoroughly. While still steaming hot, immediately toss with the coarse black pepper and kosher salt.
Serve at once in small bowls or paper cones. The pepper should be assertive and abundant.
recipes.tip: The pepper should be coarse and aggressive. Adding the seasoning while the chickpeas are hot allows the spices to penetrate the skin and stick to the creamy interior.

recipes.title: Moroccan T'faya (Caramelized Onion Topping)
recipes.description: Slow-cooked onions rendered into a mahogany jam with honey-soaked raisins, cinnamon, and ginger — a Moroccan sweet topping poured over couscous, briouats, or used as a spectacular bread spread.
ingredients: 4 large onions, peeled and thinly sliced
1/2 cup raisins, soaked in warm water 15 min and drained
directions: Melt the butter in a wide, heavy pan over the lowest possible heat. Add the sliced onions and stir to coat. Cook over very low heat for 40 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the onions have completely collapsed into a dark, jammy mass.

Add the drained raisins, honey, cinnamon, and ginger. Stir to combine and continue cooking over low heat for another 15 minutes until the mixture turns a deep mahogany color and is very thick and sticky.
Serve warm poured over couscous, grilled meats, or as a topping for challah and flatbreads.
recipes.tip: Do not rush the onions. High heat creates bitterness; low heat releases the natural fructose sugars which then caramelize to create the deep mahogany color.

recipes.title: Ashkenazi Mushroom Barley Soup
recipes.description: A thick, deeply savory soup of sautéed cremini and shiitake mushrooms, pearled barley, and root vegetables in a rich broth — old-world Ashkenazi comfort that improves enormously the next day.
ingredients: 4 oz shiitake mushrooms, stems removed, sliced
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
directions: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer — do not stir for the first 5 minutes. Let them sit undisturbed until a golden-brown crust forms on the bottom. Then stir and continue cooking until all liquid has evaporated, about 10 minutes total.
Push the mushrooms to one side. Add the diced onions, carrots, and celery to the same pot. Sauté for 5 minutes until softened.
Add the barley and pour in the stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 1 hour until the barley is tender and the soup has thickened naturally.
Stir in the fresh dill, season generously with salt and pepper, and serve.
recipes.tip: Never stir the mushrooms for the first 5 minutes. Letting them sit undisturbed on high heat creates a golden-brown crust that adds a deep, meaty umami to the soup.

recipes.title: Sephardic Pan de España (Spanish Sponge Cake)
recipes.description: A magnificent oil-free sponge cake leavened entirely by whipped eggs, scented with lemon zest, and baked in an ungreased tube pan — the jewel of the Sephardic Passover dessert table and a year-round celebration cake.
ingredients: 1 cup all-purpose flour (or potato starch for Passover)
directions: Preheat the oven to 325°F. Do not grease the tube pan — the batter needs to cling to the sides to rise properly.
In a completely clean, grease-free bowl, beat the egg whites with a pinch of salt until frothy. Gradually add half the sugar and beat until stiff, glossy peaks form.
In a separate bowl, beat the egg yolks with the remaining sugar, lemon zest, and vanilla until the mixture is pale yellow, thick, and falls in ribbons from the beater, about 3–4 minutes.
Gently fold the yolk mixture into the beaten whites using a rubber spatula, making slow, sweeping figure-eight motions to avoid deflating the foam.
Sift the flour or potato starch over the batter in three additions, folding gently after each addition until just incorporated.
Pour the batter into the ungreased tube pan. Bake at 325°F for 50 minutes until the top is golden and springs back when lightly pressed.
Immediately invert the pan over its feet (or over a bottle neck) and leave to cool completely upside down before unmolding.
recipes.tip: Ensure your mixing bowl is 100% grease-free. Even a drop of yolk or oil will prevent the whites from reaching full volume, which is the only leavening agent in this cake.

recipes.title: Sephardic Orange Chiffon Cake
recipes.description: A towering, cloud-light chiffon cake with an intense fresh orange flavor, made pareve with oil instead of butter — the iconic Israeli celebration cake that graces every holiday table from Rosh Hashanah to Shavuot.
directions: Preheat the oven to 325°F. Do not grease the tube pan.
Whisk together the flour and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the egg yolks, 1 cup of the sugar, oil, orange juice, and orange zest. Beat until smooth and well combined.
In a separate clean bowl, beat the egg whites with a pinch of salt until frothy. Gradually add the remaining 1/2 cup sugar and beat until stiff, glossy peaks form.
Fold the whites into the batter in three additions, using gentle sweeping motions to preserve the volume.
Pour into the ungreased tube pan. Bake at 325°F for 60 minutes until the top is golden and a skewer comes out clean.
Invert immediately and cool completely upside down before unmolding.
recipes.tip: The orange juice is not just for flavor; the acidity helps stabilize the egg white foam, resulting in a cake that is exceptionally tall and airy.

recipes.title: Moroccan Spiced Kumquat Jam
recipes.description: Whole kumquat halves cooked into a luminous, amber-colored jam spiced with cardamom and cinnamon — a jewel-like Moroccan preserve that belongs on every Mimouna table and Shabbat morning spread.
directions: Soak the halved kumquats in a large bowl of water with the baking soda for 10 minutes. Rinse thoroughly under cold water.
Combine the sugar, water, cinnamon stick, cardamom pods, and cloves in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Add the rinsed kumquats. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer for 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the peel is soft and the syrup has thickened.
To test the set, place a teaspoon of jam on a cold plate; push with your finger — if it wrinkles, it's done.
Pour into sterilized jars and seal. Store refrigerated for up to 3 weeks.
recipes.tip: Kumquats are high in natural pectin. To check if the jam is done, place a spoonful on a cold plate; if it wrinkles when pushed with a finger, it has reached the set point.

recipes.title: Israeli Sabich Salad (Deconstructed)
recipes.description: Everything beloved about the iconic Iraqi-Israeli sabich sandwich — golden fried eggplant, hard-boiled eggs, chickpeas, and Israeli salad — deconstructed into a dramatic layered bowl and showered with tahini and amba.
ingredients: 2 cups Israeli salad (diced tomato, cucumber, parsley)
1/2 cup tahini, loosened with water and lemon juice
directions: Salt the eggplant cubes generously and let them sit 20 minutes. Pat dry with paper towels.

Heat 1/2 inch of neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Fry the eggplant cubes in batches without crowding the pan, turning until deeply golden on all sides, about 4 minutes per batch. Drain on a wire rack and season with salt.
Layer the fried eggplant and chickpeas in the bottom of a wide serving bowl. Add the Israeli salad on top. Arrange the quartered hard-boiled eggs over the salad.
Drizzle generously with loosened tahini and amba just before serving. Serve immediately.
recipes.tip: The secret to this salad is frying the eggplant cubes until they are deeply golden on all sides — undercooked eggplant is bitter and spongy, while properly fried eggplant is creamy and rich.

recipes.title: Sephardic Pastelicos (Meat and Rice Pies)
recipes.description: Three-cornered meat and rice-filled pastries that echo Haman's hat, made from a tender oil dough brushed with egg wash and scattered with sesame seeds — a beloved Purim and Shabbat tradition across the Sephardic world.
directions: Make the dough: mix flour, oil, water, and salt together until a soft dough forms. Knead briefly until smooth. Cover and rest 20 minutes.
Make the filling: brown the ground beef in a skillet with the allspice and salt. Drain any excess fat. Mix in the cooked rice and pine nuts. Cool completely.
Roll the dough thin on a lightly floured surface. Cut into 3-inch circles using a cookie cutter or glass.
Place 1 teaspoon of filling in the center of each circle. Fold up three sides to create a triangular hat shape, pinching the corners firmly to seal.
Brush each pastelico generously with beaten egg and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake at 350°F for 25 minutes until golden.
recipes.tip: The three-cornered shape is a nod to Haman's hat — making pastelicos a popular Purim tradition. Pinch the corners firmly and brush generously with egg wash for a glossy, bakery-quality finish.

recipes.title: Yemenite Zhug (Cilantro Chili Paste)
recipes.description: The fiery, herbaceous green chili paste that defines the Yemenite table — a vibrant blend of cilantro, serrano peppers, and garlic that elevates every soup, flatbread, and roasted meat it touches.
ingredients: 1 large bunch fresh cilantro (leaves and stems)
3–4 serrano peppers, stemmed (seeds removed for milder version)
directions: Place the garlic cloves and serrano peppers in a food processor. Pulse until finely minced.
Add the cilantro leaves and stems, cumin, and salt. Pulse until a coarse, vibrant green paste forms.
With the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil until the paste comes together and looks glossy.
Taste and adjust salt. Transfer to a glass jar and store in the refrigerator, covered with a thin layer of olive oil, for up to 2 weeks.
recipes.tip: The heat lives in the seeds and ribs of the peppers. For a milder zhug, remove the white pith before processing.

recipes.title: Israeli Malawach Pizza (Modern Fusion)
recipes.description: A genius Israeli kitchen hack: frozen malawach rounds pan-fried crispy, then flipped and topped with tomato sauce and melted mozzarella — a laminated flatbread pizza that requires no oven and no dough-making.
directions: Heat a large non-stick skillet or cast-iron pan over medium heat with a drizzle of olive oil.
Place the frozen malawach round directly in the pan. Cook for 3–4 minutes until the bottom is golden and crispy.
Flip the malawach. Working quickly on the cooked side, spread tomato sauce, then scatter mozzarella and olives over the top. Sprinkle with oregano.
Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid. Cook for 3 more minutes until the cheese is fully melted and bubbling and the bottom is deep golden and crispy.
Slide onto a cutting board and cut into wedges. Serve immediately.
recipes.tip: Using frozen malawach straight from the freezer (without thawing) gives you an even crispier result — the moisture from the dough steams the cheese as it cooks.

recipes.title: Ashkenazi Apple Noodle Kugel
recipes.description: Wide egg noodles baked with freshly grated Granny Smith apples, raisins, cinnamon, and a shattering cinnamon-sugar crust — a sweet, autumnal Ashkenazi kugel that bridges side dish and dessert.
ingredients: 1 lb wide egg noodles, cooked and drained
3 Granny Smith apples, peeled and grated at the last moment
6 tbsp melted butter or neutral oil
2 tbsp sugar mixed with 1/2 tsp cinnamon
directions: Preheat the oven to 350°F. Grease a 9x13-inch baking pan.
Cook and drain the egg noodles. While still warm, toss with the melted butter.
Grate the apples directly into the bowl of noodles — do this at the very last moment to prevent browning. Add the beaten eggs, sugar, cinnamon, raisins, and salt. Fold everything together thoroughly.
Pour into the prepared pan and spread evenly. Sprinkle the cinnamon-sugar mixture over the top.
Bake uncovered for 1 hour until the top is crunchy and caramelized and the center is set. Let rest 10 minutes before cutting into squares.
recipes.tip: Grate the apples at the last moment and immediately fold them into the noodles — exposed apple flesh oxidizes quickly and will turn brown and bitter if left to sit.

recipes.title: Syrian Tamarind Meatballs
recipes.description: Feather-light ground beef meatballs made tender by grated onion, simmered in a glossy tamarind and tomato sauce that sings with acidity and warmth — a Syrian family staple that disappears within minutes.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated on the large holes of a box grater
directions: Combine the ground beef with the grated onion, allspice, and salt. Mix well — the onion juice will be absorbed into the meat. Form into small 1-inch balls.
Heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add the meatballs in batches and brown on all sides, about 3 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same skillet, whisk together the tamarind paste, tomato paste, lemon juice, and water over medium heat until smooth. Bring to a simmer.
Return the meatballs to the sauce. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes until the meatballs are cooked through and the sauce has thickened. Season with salt.
recipes.tip: The grated onion in the meat mixture is the secret to a light, almost cloud-like meatball — the onion juice tenderizes the protein fibers during cooking.

recipes.title: Yemenite Hawaij Coffee (Ritual Spice Blend)
recipes.description: The Yemenite spice blend for coffee — cardamom-forward, warming, and faintly sweet — stirred into ground coffee before brewing and served with dates for a ritual morning cup that is unlike anything else.
directions: Combine all the ground spices with the ground coffee in a small bowl. Mix thoroughly.
Brew the spiced coffee as you normally would — in a drip machine, French press, or stovetop moka pot.
Serve in small cups alongside fresh or dried dates. The dates are an integral part of the experience — they provide natural sweetness that complements the spiced coffee.
recipes.tip: Hawaij for coffee (as opposed to hawaij for soup) contains warming, sweet spices. Cardamom is the dominant note — adjust the ratio to your preference, but never omit it.

recipes.title: Kubbeh Selek (Iraqi Beet Dumpling Soup)
recipes.description: Semolina dumplings filled with spiced beef, bobbing in a stunning ruby-red beet soup brightened with lemon and sweetened with a whisper of sugar — one of the most visually dramatic dishes in Iraqi Jewish cooking.
ingredients: 4 large beets, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch cubes
directions: Make the filling: combine ground beef, minced onion, baharat, and salt; mix until sticky. Refrigerate 30 minutes.
Make the dough: mix semolina, water, oil, and salt. Knead 2–3 minutes until a soft, pliable dough forms. Cover with a damp towel and rest 20 minutes.

Make the soup: in a large pot, sauté the diced onion in oil until translucent. Add the beets and tomato paste, stir 2 minutes. Add the broth, sugar, lemon juice, and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce and simmer 15 minutes.
Shape the kubbeh: with wet hands, flatten a walnut-sized piece of dough into a thin disc. Place a teaspoon of filling in the center. Bring edges up to seal completely and roll into a smooth ball.

Bring the beet soup to a full boil. Gently drop the kubbeh in one at a time. Once they float (about 5 minutes), reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 45–50 minutes until the beets are completely tender and the soup is a deep ruby color.
recipes.tip: If you find shaping difficult, roll the meat filling into tiny balls and freeze them for 1 hour. This hard center makes it significantly easier to wrap the soft semolina dough around the meat without tearing.

recipes.title: Msabaha (Warm Chunky Hummus)
recipes.description: The hummusiya's insider secret — warm whole chickpeas folded into a punchy, lemony tahini sauce, served immediately in wide bowls with olive oil, pine nuts, and parsley while still steaming from the pot.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas, soaked 12 hours with 1/2 tsp baking soda
Generous drizzle of extra virgin olive oil
directions: Drain the soaked chickpeas. Place in a large pot and cover with fresh cold water by 4 inches. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then simmer 1–2 hours until the chickpeas are very soft and crushable between two fingers. Do not drain.
Whisk together the tahini, lemon juice, crushed garlic, cumin, and salt in a large bowl.
Slowly ladle in 1/2 cup of the hot chickpea cooking liquid, whisking constantly. The tahini will first seize up then loosen into a white, creamy sauce.
Use a slotted spoon to transfer 2/3 of the hot chickpeas into the tahini bowl. Roughly mash about half of them with a fork, leaving the rest whole for texture. Stir gently to combine.
Serve immediately in wide, shallow bowls. Pool olive oil in the center, scatter pine nuts and parsley, and dust with paprika.
recipes.tip: Traditional Msabaha is defined by its punchy, bright acidity. If the dish feels heavy, add a teaspoon of lemon juice just before serving. The acid cuts through the fat of the tahini, waking up the earthy chickpea flavor.

recipes.title: Kubbeh Patata (Iraqi Potato-Meat Dumplings)
recipes.description: Crispy fried patties with a mashed Yukon Gold potato shell encasing fragrant ground beef spiced with cinnamon and allspice — the Iraqi Passover and Hanukkah essential made from the most humble ingredients.
ingredients: Neutral oil for frying (about 1/2 inch deep)
directions: Boil the whole, unpeeled potatoes for 25 minutes until completely tender. Peel while warm and mash completely smooth — do not add any liquid. Stir in the egg yolks, matzo meal, salt, and pepper. Refrigerate the potato mixture for 1 hour.

While the potatoes cool, sauté the minced onion in a splash of oil until golden. Add the ground beef and cook until browned, breaking up lumps. Season with cinnamon, allspice, and salt. Drain excess fat. Cool completely.

Take a golf-ball-sized portion of cold potato dough. Flatten it into a thick disc. Place a tablespoon of meat filling in the center. Fold the dough over and around the filling, sealing completely. Flatten gently into a thick patty.
Heat 1/2 inch of neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Fry the kubbeh patata for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden brown. Drain on a wire rack and serve hot.
recipes.tip: Do not add any liquid to the potatoes while mashing. Any added milk or water will make the dough too soft to hold the meat. The egg yolks and matzo meal act as the structural glue that allows the potato to withstand the heat of the frying pan.

recipes.title: Mina de Carne (Sephardic Meat & Matzo Pie)
recipes.description: Layers of broth-soaked matzo encasing a savory filling of allspice-scented ground beef and parsley, sealed with egg wash and baked golden — the Sephardic Passover centerpiece that is both rustic and deeply satisfying.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (1 for the filling, 2 for the egg wash)
1 1/2 cups beef broth (for soaking the matzo)
directions: Preheat the oven to 350°F. Grease a 9x13-inch baking dish with olive oil.
Sauté the onion in olive oil until golden. Add the ground meat and cook until browned with the allspice and salt. Stir in the parsley and one beaten egg to bind. Set aside.
Pour the beef broth into a shallow tray. Dip each matzo sheet into the broth for 30–60 seconds until pliable but not falling apart. Remove and lay on a clean towel.
Lay three softened matzo sheets in the bottom of the baking dish, overlapping to cover the entire surface. Spread the meat mixture evenly over them.
Cover with the remaining three softened matzo sheets. Beat the remaining two eggs and pour over the top of the pie, tilting the dish so the egg seeps into the edges.
Sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake at 350°F for 35–40 minutes until golden-brown. Let rest 10 minutes before cutting into squares.
recipes.tip: If a matzo sheet breaks while dipping, don't worry. Use the broken pieces to patch the layers like a puzzle. Once the egg wash bakes, it will fuse the pieces into a single, cohesive crust that slices like a traditional pie.

recipes.title: Maakouda (Moroccan Potato Fritters)
recipes.description: Golden, puffed Moroccan potato cakes dipped in a baking powder batter before frying — crispy, airy shells giving way to a cumin and turmeric-spiced mashed potato interior that is impossibly creamy.
ingredients: 2 lbs large potatoes, peeled and boiled
1/2 cup all-purpose flour (or matzo meal for Passover)
Neutral oil for frying (1 inch deep)
directions: Mash the hot boiled potatoes until completely smooth. Add the garlic, parsley, cumin, turmeric, 1 egg, and generous seasoning. Mix thoroughly. Cool for 30 minutes.
Make the batter: whisk 2 eggs with flour, baking powder, and water until a thick, smooth batter forms.
Shape the potato mixture into 2-inch round cakes, about 1/2 inch thick.
Heat 1 inch of neutral oil in a large skillet to 350°F. Dip each potato cake into the batter, coating all sides.
Fry the fritters for 2–3 minutes per side until puffed, golden-yellow, and crispy. Drain on a wire rack. Serve immediately.
recipes.tip: The baking powder in the batter is the key to the Maakouda's airy texture. It reacts with the heat of the oil to create tiny bubbles, resulting in a shell that is crisp and light rather than heavy and doughy.

recipes.title: Sefa (Moroccan Sweet Ceremonial Couscous)
recipes.description: A tower of buttered, cinnamon-dusted couscous studded with honey-soaked raisins and toasted almonds, crowned with pomegranate arils — the Moroccan sweet couscous served at celebrations and royal feasts.
ingredients: 4 tbsp butter or pareve margarine, melted
1/2 cup raisins, soaked in warm water and drained
directions: Cook the couscous in boiling salted water according to package directions. Once all the water is absorbed, fluff aggressively with a fork for several minutes to separate every grain.
While still hot, pour the melted butter over the couscous. Add the sugar and 1 teaspoon of the cinnamon. Toss until every grain looks glossy and is coated.
Fold in the soaked raisins and half the toasted almonds.

Pile the couscous onto a large round serving platter, shaping it into a cone or pyramid. Use the remaining cinnamon to draw decorative lines down the sides. Top with the remaining almonds and scatter the pomegranate arils over everything.
Serve at room temperature as a dessert or a sweet side.
recipes.tip: Coating the couscous in butter while it is hot is essential. The fat prevents the starch from bonding, which is what keeps the grains from clumping together and ensures a velvety, fluffy mouthfeel.

recipes.title: Huevos Haminados (Sephardic Slow-Cooked Eggs)
recipes.description: Eggs simmered overnight in onion skins and coffee grounds until the whites turn caramel-beige and the yolks become velvety and creamy — a Sephardic Shabbat and Passover tradition going back centuries.
ingredients: 2 tbsp ground coffee or used coffee grounds
directions: Spread the onion skins across the bottom of a heavy pot. Scatter the coffee grounds over the skins.
Nestle the raw eggs, still in their shells, on top of the skins in a single layer.
Add the oil and salt. Pour in room-temperature water until the eggs are completely submerged by at least 2 inches.
Bring to a very gentle simmer over medium-low heat. Once simmering, cover the pot tightly and reduce the heat to the absolute lowest setting.
Cook for at least 8 hours, ideally 12–15 hours overnight. Check periodically to ensure the eggs remain submerged, adding hot water if needed.
Serve the eggs at room temperature, peeled, alongside Shabbat salads or as part of a Passover Seder spread.
recipes.tip: The addition of oil to the water creates a thin film on the surface that prevents the water from evaporating too quickly. This ensures the eggs remain submerged and cook evenly without constant monitoring.

recipes.title: Abgoosht with Gondi (Persian Lamb & Chickpea Stew)
recipes.description: The Persian Jewish equivalent of cholent — braised lamb and chickpeas with dried limes in a golden turmeric broth, enriched with cardamom-scented gondi dumplings that expand as they absorb the savory liquid.
ingredients: 2 lbs lamb leg or shoulder, cut into 2-inch cubes
3 dried Persian limes (limu omani), pierced with a fork
directions: Sear the lamb cubes in oil in a large pot over high heat until a dark brown crust forms on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Add the whole onion and turmeric to the pot. Sauté 2 minutes until fragrant. Return the lamb. Add the chickpeas, potatoes, dried limes, and 6 cups of water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer covered for 2 hours until the lamb is fork-tender.
Meanwhile, make the gondi: combine ground chicken, chickpea flour, grated onion, cardamom, salt, and oil. Mix thoroughly. Refrigerate 30 minutes. Wet hands and roll into golf ball-sized dumplings.
Gently drop the gondi into the simmering stew. Do not stir. Cover and cook another 45 minutes — the dumplings will expand as they absorb the lamb broth.
Serve the broth in soup bowls and the meat, potatoes, and gondi on a separate platter.
recipes.tip: Traditionally, the stew solids are removed from the broth, mashed into a paste called 'Gousht-e Koobideh,' and served separately from the clear broth — providing two distinct experiences from a single pot.

recipes.title: Hamod (Lebanese Lemon and Potato Soup)
recipes.description: A bright, lemony Lebanese soup of whole braised garlic cloves, diced potatoes, and celery in chicken stock — warming, restorative, and wonderfully aromatic, with the garlic turning sweet and mellow after its long simmer.
ingredients: 3 large potatoes, peeled and diced into 1-inch cubes
1 whole head of garlic, cloves separated and peeled
directions: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the whole peeled garlic cloves and the chopped celery. Sauté for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened but not browned.
Add the diced potatoes and turmeric. Stir to coat. Pour in the stock and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer for 20 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender.
Stir in the lemon juice and fresh mint. Simmer another 5 minutes. Taste and adjust salt and pepper.
Serve in wide bowls, making sure each serving has several whole garlic cloves — by now they are as soft as butter and entirely sweet.
recipes.tip: Leaving the garlic cloves whole allows them to confit in the soup. By the time the soup is finished, the garlic will be as soft as the potatoes, providing a sweet, mellow garlic flavor in every bite.

recipes.title: Biscochos de Huevo (Sephardic Bracelet Cookies)
recipes.description: Light, sesame-encrusted ring cookies with a pale golden exterior and a firm, dry bite — the Sephardic biscotti, made for dunking in coffee or tea, served at every holiday from Purim to Rosh Hashanah.
directions: Beat the 3 eggs with the sugar for 3 minutes until very light and foamy. Whisk in the oil and vanilla.
Sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Gradually stir the dry ingredients into the wet, mixing until a smooth dough forms. Knead briefly until uniform.
Cover the dough with a bowl and rest for 15 minutes — this allows the gluten to relax so the dough doesn't spring back during shaping.
Divide into walnut-sized balls. Roll each into a 6-inch rope. Join the ends to form a ring, or fold in half and twist before joining to form a braid.
Brush each ring with the beaten egg and dip into sesame seeds to coat generously.
Bake at 325°F for 20–25 minutes until pale golden and firm. For extra crunch, turn the oven to 160°F and leave the cookies inside for another hour to dry out completely.
recipes.tip: Let the dough rest under a bowl for 15 minutes before shaping. This allows the gluten to relax, which prevents the dough from springing back when you try to roll it into long, thin ropes.

recipes.title: Saluf (Yemenite Soft Pita)
recipes.description: A soft, pillowy Yemenite flatbread cooked directly in a cast-iron skillet — with a high-hydration dough stretched by hand in the pan until it blisters and chars, perfumed with a hint of fenugreek.
directions: Combine all ingredients. The dough will be wetter and stickier than standard pita dough — this is correct. Knead for 5 minutes until elastic. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled.
Punch the dough down. Divide into 8 equal balls. Place on a floured surface, cover, and rest 20 more minutes.
Heat a large cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat and brush with a little olive oil.

Wet your hands thoroughly. Take one dough ball and use your fingers to stretch it directly in the hot pan until it forms a round, roughly 1/4-inch thick. Work quickly as the dough will begin cooking immediately.
Cover the pan with a tight lid. Cook 2–3 minutes until the top is set and covered in bubbles and the bottom is golden-brown. Remove and keep wrapped in a clean towel. Repeat for remaining pitas.
recipes.tip: Adding a small amount of ground fenugreek to the dough is what distinguishes Yemenite Saluf from Arab pita. It creates a maple-like aroma that pairs perfectly with Yemenite soups.

recipes.title: Tunisian Fricassee (Fried Sandwich Buns)
recipes.description: Pillowy fried buns stuffed with tuna, harissa, boiled potato, hard-boiled egg, and preserved lemon — Tunisia's iconic street food sandwich, best made fresh and eaten while the bun is still warm and crispy.
ingredients: Neutral oil for frying (2 inches deep)
1/4 preserved lemon, rinsed and thinly sliced
directions: Make the dough: knead all bun ingredients for 10 minutes until very smooth and shiny. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled.
Divide dough into 12 balls. Roll each into a slightly elongated oval. Place each on its own small square of parchment paper. Cover and rise another 20 minutes.
Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a wide, deep pot to 350°F. Use a thermometer — temperature precision is critical here.
Pick up each bun by its parchment square and lower into the oil. The parchment will release on its own. Fry 2 minutes per side until puffed and golden-brown. Drain on a wire rack.
Spread harissa on both cut sides of each warm bun. Stuff with potato slices, tuna, quartered egg, olives, and preserved lemon.
recipes.tip: If the oil is too cold, the buns will soak up fat and become greasy; if too hot, the outside will burn before the inside cooks. Use a thermometer to maintain exactly 350°F.

recipes.title: Israeli Baked Cheesecake (Shavuot Style)
recipes.description: Israel's beloved light, cloud-like cheesecake made with white soft cheese and carefully folded egg whites — baked at low temperature and left to cool in the oven to emerge crack-free and impossibly tender.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups Petit Beurre or graham cracker crumbs
2 lbs Gvina Levana, Quark, or Farmer's cheese
directions: Mix the biscuit crumbs with melted butter. Press firmly into the bottom of a 9-inch springform pan. Freeze 15 minutes to set.
Preheat the oven to 325°F.
Beat the cheese, 3/4 cup of the sugar, egg yolks, cornstarch, and vanilla until completely smooth.
Beat the egg whites with the remaining 1/4 cup sugar until stiff, glossy peaks form. Gently fold the whites into the cheese mixture in three additions.
Pour the filling over the crust. Bake at 325°F for 45–50 minutes until the edges are set but the center still has a slight jiggle.
Turn off the oven. Leave the cheesecake inside with the oven door slightly ajar for 1 hour. Then remove and cool completely at room temperature before refrigerating for at least 4 hours.
recipes.tip: The key to a crack-free Israeli cheesecake is the cool-down method — leaving the cake in the turned-off oven allows it to contract slowly and evenly, preventing the dramatic temperature change that causes the top to split.

recipes.title: Moroccan Cumin Beet Salad (Barba)
recipes.description: Whole boiled beets, slipped from their skins and dressed while warm in a lemony, toasted-cumin vinaigrette — a vibrant Moroccan salad that only improves after hours of marinating in the refrigerator.
ingredients: 1 1/2 tsp whole cumin seeds, toasted in a dry pan until fragrant
directions: Place the whole, unpeeled beets in a pot and cover with cold water. Bring to a boil and simmer for 45 minutes until a fork slides easily into the center. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes.
Rub off the skins under cold water — they will slide off easily. Cut the peeled beets into 1/2-inch cubes.
Shake together the olive oil, lemon juice, minced garlic, toasted cumin seeds, salt, and pepper in a jar until emulsified.
Toss the warm beets with the dressing and half the parsley. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
Serve cold or at room temperature, garnished with the remaining parsley and a pinch of extra cumin.
recipes.tip: Always toast whole cumin seeds in a dry pan for 60 seconds until they release a nutty aroma before adding them to the salad. This unlocks the essential oils and provides a much deeper flavor than pre-ground cumin powder.

recipes.title: Meorav Yerushalmi (Jerusalem Mixed Grill)
recipes.description: Jerusalem's famous market mixed grill — chicken breast, thighs, hearts, and livers tossed with onions and an aromatic spice blend of turmeric, cumin, cardamom, and paprika in a smoking hot pan, served stuffed into pita.
ingredients: 1/2 lb chicken hearts, trimmed of connective tissue
directions: Parboil the chicken hearts in boiling water for 3 minutes. Drain and pat dry.
Pat all the chicken pieces and livers completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear.
Heat oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the onions and cook until soft and beginning to brown at the edges, about 5 minutes. Remove the onions and set aside.
In the same pan, add more oil. When smoking hot, add the chicken breast and thigh pieces. Fry on high heat 3 minutes without stirring, then add the hearts and livers.
Stir constantly for 2 minutes. Add all the spices, return the onions to the pan, and toss everything together for 2 more minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Serve immediately stuffed into pita with hummus, Israeli salad, and hot sauce.
recipes.tip: Do not crowd the pan. Too much meat will release juices and boil instead of sear, resulting in grey, tough meat instead of the crispy, flavorful bits found at a Jerusalem market. Cook in batches if needed.

recipes.title: Red Schug (Fiery Yemenite Chili Paste)
recipes.description: A deep-crimson, smoky chili paste made from dried red chilies, garlic, and cumin — the Yemenite condiment that turns any soup, bread, or egg dish into something electric.
directions: Soak the dried chilies in warm water for 30 minutes until soft. Drain and squeeze out excess liquid. Remove the stems; remove seeds for a milder paste or leave them for maximum heat.
Place the soaked chilies, garlic cloves, salt, cumin, and black pepper in a food processor. Pulse several times until the mixture is finely chopped but still has a slightly rustic texture.
With the motor running, slowly drizzle in the olive oil until the paste comes together and looks glossy.
Transfer to a glass jar. To store, top with a 1/4-inch layer of olive oil to create an airtight seal. Refrigerate for up to 3 weeks.
recipes.tip: When storing the schug in a jar, always top it with a 1/4-inch layer of olive oil. This creates an airtight seal that prevents the vibrant red color from darkening and keeps the garlic from fermenting too quickly.

recipes.title: Green Schug (Yemenite Herbal Chili Paste)
recipes.description: A verdant, aromatic paste of fresh jalapeños, cilantro, parsley, and cardamom — the cooling yet fiery Yemenite condiment that is the essential counterpart to hilbe on any Yemenite Shabbat table.
ingredients: 4–5 fresh jalapeños, stemmed (seeds removed for milder version)
1 large bunch fresh cilantro (leaves and tender stems)
directions: Roughly chop the jalapeños into large chunks.
Place the cilantro, parsley, and garlic in a food processor. Pulse a few times to break down the leaves.
Add the jalapeño chunks, salt, cardamom, and olive oil. Process until the mixture resembles a coarse pesto — not a smooth purée.
Taste and adjust salt and heat. Transfer to a jar and cover with a thin layer of olive oil. Refrigerate for up to 10 days.
recipes.tip: Cardamom is the secret ingredient in Yemenite green schug. It provides a floral, cooling top-note that balances the intense capsaicin heat of the jalapeños and the pungency of the garlic.

recipes.title: Lisan el Qathi (Iraqi Stuffed Eggplant Rolls)
recipes.description: Long eggplant strips broiled until pliable, then rolled around finger-shaped beef sausages and baked in a sweet-and-sour pomegranate molasses glaze — an Iraqi Shabbat main of quiet, elegant complexity.
ingredients: 3 long eggplants, sliced lengthwise into 1/2-inch strips
directions: Brush the eggplant strips with olive oil and season with salt. Broil in the oven for 5 minutes per side until soft, pliable, and golden.
Mix the ground beef with minced onion, baharat, and salt. Roll the meat mixture into small finger-sized sausages, one for each eggplant strip.
Place one meat sausage at the end of each eggplant strip and roll up tightly. Arrange seam-side down in a baking dish.
Whisk together the tomato paste, beef stock, and pomegranate molasses. Pour over the rolls until half-submerged. Cover with foil.
Bake at 350°F for 40 minutes. Remove foil and bake another 10 minutes until the sauce has reduced into a thick, sweet-and-sour glaze.
recipes.tip: Always place the eggplant rolls with the seam facing the bottom of the dish. The weight of the roll and the heat of the oven will seal the seam, ensuring the meat stays tucked inside without the need for toothpicks.

recipes.title: Classic Potato Kugel (The Fluffy Method)
recipes.description: A golden, deeply crispy potato kugel with a fluffy, custardy interior — made with the critical step of preheating the oiled pan so the batter sizzles the moment it lands, creating the legendary crust.
directions: Preheat the oven to 450°F. Pour 2 tablespoons of the oil into a 9x13-inch baking pan and place the empty pan in the oven to heat for 15 minutes.
Grate the onion first using the coarse side of a box grater. Coarsely grate the potatoes. Place the grated potatoes in a colander and press out as much liquid as possible with your hands.
Whisk the eggs, remaining oil, salt, and pepper until combined. Fold in the drained potatoes and grated onion quickly.
Remove the blazing hot pan from the oven. Pour the batter in — it should sizzle dramatically immediately. Spread evenly and sprinkle with paprika.
Bake at 450°F for 30 minutes, then lower to 350°F and bake another 60 minutes until deep golden-brown on top and the center is set. Let rest 10 minutes before cutting.
recipes.tip: If the kugel is browning too quickly, cover loosely with foil for the last 20 minutes. The high initial temperature is required to set the starch, but the lower temperature ensures the interior cooks through without burning.

recipes.title: Shirin Polo (Persian Wedding Rice)
recipes.description: Iran's most celebratory rice — basmati layered with candied orange peel, carrots, jewel-like barberries, and saffron water, forming a golden tahdig crust at the bottom that is the most prized bite at the table.
ingredients: Peel of 2 oranges, julienned (white pith removed)
1/2 cup dried barberries (zereshk), soaked in warm water 10 min
1/4 tsp saffron threads dissolved in 3 tbsp hot water
directions: Blanch the julienned orange peel in boiling water for 1 minute, drain, and repeat 3 times to remove bitterness. Sauté the drained orange peel and julienned carrots with the sugar and a splash of water until glazed and translucent. Set aside.
Drain the barberries. Sauté in a teaspoon of oil with a pinch of sugar for 60 seconds only. Set aside.
Boil the rice in heavily salted water for 7 minutes — it should be lengthened but still firm in the center. Drain and rinse with cool water.

Pour the oil into the bottom of a large non-stick pot. Layer half the rice. Scatter the candied carrot-orange mixture and the barberries evenly. Top with the remaining rice. Pour the saffron water over the top.
Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel. Cook over medium-low heat for 45 minutes until a golden tahdig crust has formed at the bottom.
Serve by scooping the fluffy top rice onto a platter. Then invert the pot to reveal the golden tahdig crust on top.
recipes.tip: Barberries are extremely delicate. Only sauté them for 60 seconds with a teaspoon of sugar just before adding them to the rice. If they cook too long, they will lose their vibrant red color and turn brown.

recipes.title: Iraqi Chicken Shorba (Hearty Rice Soup)
recipes.description: A thick, golden Iraqi chicken soup where short-grain rice cooks so long it breaks down into the broth, creating a naturally creamy, porridge-like consistency — rich, restorative, and deeply comforting.
ingredients: 3/4 cup short-grain (Arborio or sushi) rice, washed
directions: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onions and cook until translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the chicken pieces and cook on all sides until they release their fat and turn golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric and salt — the turmeric should coat the chicken and onions, turning everything a deep golden color.
Add the washed rice and pour in the 8 cups of water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very gentle simmer.

Simmer uncovered for 1.5–2 hours. As the rice cooks for this long, it will begin to break down, naturally thickening the broth into a creamy, porridge-like consistency. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
Adjust salt and serve in wide bowls.
recipes.tip: Use a starchy short-grain rice like Arborio or sushi rice for Shorba. Long-grain basmati won't release enough starch, resulting in a thin, watery broth rather than the comforting thick soup traditional in Iraqi homes.

recipes.title: Couscous-au-Lait (Moroccan Mimouna Special)
recipes.description: Israeli pearl couscous simmered slowly in whole milk with butter, sugar, and cinnamon until it turns thick and creamy like rice pudding — the beloved Moroccan Mimouna sweet that celebrates the return of chametz.
ingredients: 1 tsp ground cinnamon, plus more for dusting
directions: Cook the pearl couscous in a pot of boiling salted water for 8 minutes until tender but with a slight bite. Drain thoroughly.
Return the couscous to the pot over medium-low heat. Add the butter, sugar, and milk. Stir to combine.
Simmer, stirring constantly, for 10–12 minutes until the couscous has absorbed most of the milk and the mixture is thick and creamy — like a loose rice pudding.
Serve warm in bowls, dusted generously with ground cinnamon.
recipes.tip: Pearl couscous (Israeli couscous) is the correct variety here — it holds its shape and provides a satisfying chew that regular fine couscous cannot. The slow simmer in milk transforms it into something close to a classic rice pudding.

recipes.title: Libyan Asida (Semolina Pudding)
recipes.description: A thick, silky Libyan semolina pudding, stirred until smooth and poured into a bowl where a well is made in the center and filled with melted butter and golden honey — simple, nurturing, and ancient.
directions: Bring the liquid to a boil in a medium, heavy-bottomed saucepan with the sugar and salt.
Reduce heat to medium. Gradually pour in the semolina in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly to prevent any lumps from forming.
Switch to a wooden spoon. Cook over medium heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring continuously, until the pudding thickens significantly and pulls away from the sides of the pot.
Pour into a wide, deep serving bowl. Use the back of a spoon to create a well in the center. Pour the melted butter and honey into the well.
Serve immediately while still warm and steaming.
recipes.tip: Pour the semolina in a slow, steady stream while whisking constantly — if you pour it all at once, it will clump immediately and create an unworkable, lumpy paste rather than a smooth, silky pudding.

recipes.title: Sephardic Travados (Walnut-Filled Pastries)
recipes.description: Crisp, delicate half-moon pastries made from an orange-juice dough encasing a fragrant walnut and cinnamon filling, rolled in powdered sugar while still warm — a treasured Sephardic cookie served at every major holiday.
directions: Make the dough: mix flour, oil, orange juice, sugar, and baking powder together to form a soft dough. Rest under a bowl for 20 minutes.
Make the filling: combine chopped walnuts, sugar, cinnamon, and orange blossom water. Mix well.
Roll the dough very thin on a lightly floured surface. Cut into 3-inch circles.
Place a teaspoon of walnut filling in the center of each circle. Fold over into a half-moon shape and press the edges firmly with the tines of a fork to create a decorative seal.
Bake at 350°F for 20–25 minutes until pale golden. While still warm, toss generously in powdered sugar.
recipes.tip: The orange juice in the dough is both a leavening agent and a tenderizer. The resulting pastry should be crisp but not hard — it should shatter gently when bitten, not crack.

recipes.title: Iraqi Amba Fish (Mango Braised Fish)
recipes.description: Firm white fish fillets braised over sautéed onions and garlic in a tangy, mustardy amba mango sauce — one of the most distinctive flavor profiles in Iraqi Jewish cooking, equally wonderful at room temperature.
ingredients: 4 firm white fish fillets (cod, sea bass, or grouper), about 6 oz each
directions: Heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add the onions and cook for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more.
Stir in the cumin and turmeric and bloom for 30 seconds.
Nestle the fish fillets into the pan. Spoon the amba sauce over each fillet and pour the water around the sides.
Cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, basting the fish once with the sauce, until the fish is just cooked through and flakes easily.
Serve warm or at room temperature over rice.
recipes.tip: Amba's fermented, tangy quality is the entire flavor base of this dish. Use good-quality jarred amba or make your own — there is no substitute for the distinctive mustardy-mango flavor it provides.

recipes.title: Yemenite Saltah (Fenugreek Stew)
recipes.description: Yemen's national dish — a bubbling stew of slow-braised lamb or beef with potatoes and tomatoes, crowned table-side with a dramatic spoonful of hilbe fenugreek froth and served with fiery zhug and fresh flatbread.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lbs lamb shoulder or beef chuck, cut into small pieces
directions: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add the onions and garlic and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the meat and brown on all sides. Add the diced tomatoes and cook until they break down into a thick sauce, about 5 minutes.
Add the cubed potatoes and enough water to cover everything by 1 inch. Season generously with hawaij and salt.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer covered for 1–1.5 hours until the meat is completely tender and the broth is rich.
Ladle into heavy bowls. Place a large spoonful of hilbe directly in the center of each bowl — it will float on the surface. Serve immediately with zhug on the side and fresh flatbread.
recipes.tip: Saltah is traditionally served in a pre-heated heavy stone bowl. The goal is to bring the stew to the table still simmering and bubbling — this is considered a mark of quality in Yemenite restaurants.

recipes.title: Libyan Couscous with Seven Vegetables
recipes.description: The Libyan Jewish Shabbat centerpiece — braised lamb shoulder surrounded by seven symbolic harvest vegetables, served over couscous steamed above the stew so every grain is infused with the aroma of the lamb and spices below.
ingredients: 2 lbs lamb shoulder, cut into 2-inch cubes
directions: Sear the lamb cubes in batches in hot oil until browned on all sides. Place in a large pot.
Add the tomato paste, harissa, turmeric, cumin, cinnamon, and saffron. Add enough water to cover the lamb by 2 inches. Bring to a boil, then simmer covered for 45 minutes.
Add the vegetables in order of cooking time: turnips first, then potatoes, carrots, and squash. After 10 more minutes, add chickpeas, zucchini, and cabbage last.

Meanwhile, place the dry couscous in a couscoussière top tray or a fine-mesh colander that fits snugly over the pot. Steam the couscous over the simmering stew for 20 minutes. Remove, fluff with a fork, toss with butter, and return to steam another 10 minutes.
Serve the couscous on a large platter. Ladle the stew and vegetables over the top.
recipes.tip: Steaming the couscous over the simmering stew infuses every grain with the aromatic steam from the lamb and spices below — this is what gives Libyan couscous its characteristic depth that boiled couscous can never replicate.

recipes.title: Honey-Ginger Teiglach with Nuts
recipes.description: A ginger-spiked variation on the traditional Ashkenazi honey clusters — baked dough pieces and mixed nuts tumbled in a boiling honey-ginger syrup until they turn a deep, brittle amber.
directions: Mix the dough ingredients together to form a soft, pliable dough. On a floured surface, roll into thin ropes and cut into 1/2-inch pieces.
Spread the pieces on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Bake at 375°F for 10 minutes until very lightly golden.

In a large pot, combine honey, sugar, and ground ginger. Bring to a boil over medium heat. Add the baked pieces and mixed nuts. Cook, stirring constantly, for 20–25 minutes until everything is a deep amber color.
Wet your hands with cold water. Working quickly, form the mixture into balls or shape into a mound on a parchment-lined surface. Let cool completely until hardened.
recipes.tip: The teiglach are done when they turn a deep amber — not golden. The darker color means the honey has properly caramelized and the pieces will have a satisfying, brittle crunch rather than a soft, sticky chew.

recipes.title: Sephardic Borekas de Spinaka (Spinach Cheese Triangles)
recipes.description: Individual flaky triangles of phyllo or puff pastry filled with a creamy blend of feta, ricotta, and wilted spinach — the quintessential Sephardic dairy appetizer for Shavuot and Shabbat.
ingredients: 1 package (1 lb) phyllo dough or puff pastry sheets
1 lb fresh spinach, wilted and squeezed absolutely dry
4 tbsp melted butter (for phyllo) or 1 egg wash (for puff pastry)
directions: Wilt the spinach in a hot pan with a splash of water. Drain in a colander and squeeze in a clean kitchen towel until every drop of moisture is gone.
Combine the drained spinach, feta, ricotta, egg, nutmeg, and pepper. Mix well.

For phyllo: cut sheets into 3-inch-wide strips. Brush each strip with melted butter. Place 1 teaspoon of filling at the bottom of the strip. Fold flag-style into triangles, brushing each fold with butter.
For puff pastry: cut into 3-inch squares. Place filling in center. Fold into a triangle and crimp the edges with a fork.
Brush all triangles with egg wash (for puff pastry) or additional butter (for phyllo). Sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Bake at 375°F for 20–25 minutes until golden and puffed.
recipes.tip: The single most important step when using spinach in baked pastries is to remove ALL the water. After wilting, squeeze the spinach in a clean kitchen towel as firmly as possible — any residual moisture will create steam that makes the pastry soggy.

recipes.title: Israeli Krembo (Chocolate Marshmallow Cookies)
recipes.description: The iconic Israeli childhood treat — a round tea biscuit crowned with a dome of homemade Swiss meringue marshmallow and enrobed in a crisp, dark chocolate shell — made from scratch at home for the first time.
ingredients: 20 round tea biscuits (Petit Beurre or similar)
directions: Make the marshmallow: combine egg whites and sugar in a heatproof bowl set over a pot of simmering water (double boiler). Whisk constantly for 10 minutes until the mixture reaches 160°F and the sugar is fully dissolved.
Remove from the heat. Beat with an electric mixer on high speed for 10 minutes until stiff, glossy peaks form and the bowl feels cool to the touch. Add vanilla.
Transfer the marshmallow to a piping bag fitted with a large round tip. Pipe a generous dome onto each biscuit. Refrigerate for 1 hour until completely set and firm.
Melt the chocolate with the coconut oil in a double boiler until smooth. Let it cool to approximately 90°F.
Working quickly, dip each krembo base-first into the chocolate, tilting and rotating to coat the entire marshmallow dome. Let excess drip off. Place on a parchment-lined tray.
Refrigerate for 30 minutes to set the chocolate completely before serving.
recipes.tip: The chocolate must be at around 90°F for dipping. Too hot and it will melt the marshmallow; too cold and it will set unevenly. Work quickly once the chocolate is ready and always dip from the base of the biscuit upward.
